stem: The micro-organisms that are minimised through hand-washing include:
rationale: Hand-washing principally removes TRANSIENT flora — organisms picked up from surfaces/patients and not part of normal skin microbiota. These include faecal-oral pathogens such as E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella, rotavirus, and most nosocomial pathogens. Resident skin flora (Staph. albus/coagulase-negative staphylococci) requires antiseptic scrubbing to remove. E. coli is the most cited example of a transient pathogen removed by hand-washing.

stem: A deteriorating condition for a patient with head injury will be indicated by:
option_a: Widening pulse pressure and irregular respiratory pattern
option_b: Narrowing pulse pressure and escalation of discomfort
rationale: Cushing's triad of rising intracranial pressure: (i) HYPERTENSION with WIDENING PULSE PRESSURE (the systolic rises while diastolic remains or falls); (ii) BRADYCARDIA; (iii) IRREGULAR/abnormal respirations (Cheyne-Stokes, ataxic, or apneustic). The widening pulse pressure with irregular respiratory pattern in option A captures two of the three components and indicates severe deterioration.

stem: The substances that are completely reabsorbed by renal tubules after filtration (high-threshold materials) include:
rationale: HIGH-THRESHOLD substances are those nearly completely reabsorbed by the renal tubules under normal conditions: glucose (spilled in DM when plasma exceeds approximately 10 mmol/L); amino acids; bicarbonate (proximal tubule). Creatinine and urea are NOT reabsorbed — they are excreted. Sodium, K, Ca and phosphate are partially regulated, not fully reabsorbed.

stem: Late symptoms of cervical cancer include:
option_d: Oedema of extremities, thin watery vaginal discharge
rationale: Cervical cancer EARLY symptoms: post-coital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, watery/blood-stained vaginal discharge. LATE symptoms reflect local spread: invasion of rectum causes RECTAL BLEEDING/constipation; invasion of ureters causes hydronephrosis with REFERRED FLANK PAIN; lateral spread to pelvic side wall causes unilateral leg oedema and sciatic pain. Option B describes two LATE signs of advanced disease.

stem: In Kenya a person is termed as an elderly from the age of:
rationale: In Kenya, an ELDERLY person is defined as one aged 60 YEARS AND ABOVE per the Constitution of Kenya 2010 (Article 57) and the Older Persons Act 2014. WHO commonly uses 60+ in developing countries, 65+ in developed countries. Kenya's Inua Jamii cash transfer programme targets persons aged 70+, but the legal/policy definition of "elderly" starts at 60.

stem: The motor abilities observed in a 5-month-old infant include:
option_a: Able to sit when supported, turns over front to back
option_b: Able to sit unsupported, cruises easily around furniture
option_c: Able to pull self to standing position, transfers objects hand to hand
option_d: Can hold small objects, holds hands tightly closed
rationale: Developmental milestones per WHO/Kenya MCH growth chart: at approximately 5 months an infant can sit WITH SUPPORT and roll from front to back; rolling back to front comes at approximately 6 months; sitting unsupported at approximately 6–8 months; cruising around furniture at approximately 9–12 months; pulling to stand at approximately 9 months. Option A fits 5 months best.

stem: In non-communicating forms of hydrocephalus:
option_a: CSF formation is normal but re-absorption is abnormal
option_b: CSF re-absorption is normal but formation is abnormal
option_c: The obstruction exists between the choroid plexi and subarachnoid space
option_d: The obstruction exists between the foramen magnum and the central canal
rationale: NON-COMMUNICATING (obstructive) hydrocephalus is due to physical blockage of CSF flow somewhere WITHIN the ventricular system — between the choroid plexi (where CSF is made) and the subarachnoid space where it would be absorbed. stem: The diet implemented for a patient in acute renal failure is:
option_a: High protein, high calorie, low sodium, low potassium
option_b: Low fat, low protein, high potassium, low sodium
option_c: High calorie, low protein, low sodium, low potassium
option_d: Bland, low calorie, low sodium, low potassium

stem: In right-sided (diastolic) heart failure:
option_a: Patients present with distended jugular vein
option_c: There is production of frothy sputum
rationale: Right-sided heart failure causes systemic venous congestion: DISTENDED JUGULAR VEINS (raised JVP), peripheral oedema (ankles, sacrum), hepatomegaly, ascites, gut oedema (anorexia, nausea). Frothy pink sputum is characteristic of LEFT-sided failure (pulmonary oedema). Tachycardia and light-headedness can occur in either, but JVP distension is the SPECIFIC right-heart sign.

stem: The priority interventions for a patient who has suffered a cardiac arrest are:
option_a: High quality CPR and early defibrillation
option_d: Taking a 12-lead ECG, administration of atropine
rationale: Per AHA/ERC adult ALS algorithms, the two interventions that most improve survival after cardiac arrest are HIGH-QUALITY CPR (push hard at least 5 cm, push fast 100–120/min, minimise interruptions, full chest recoil) and EARLY DEFIBRILLATION for shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT). Drugs, intubation and history-taking are secondary.

stem: The indications for terminal cleaning of isolation room include:
option_a: Infective hepatitis, meningococcal hepatitis, malaria, HIV infection
option_b: Chicken pox, malaria, measles and pneumonia
option_d: Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), liver cirrhosis, measles and hepatitis
rationale: TERMINAL cleaning is required after discharge of a patient with an infectious disease transmissible by airborne/contact route: MEASLES (airborne), CHICKEN POX/varicella (airborne and contact), INFECTIVE HEPATITIS (contact). Malaria (vector-borne, not person-to-person) does NOT require isolation cleaning; liver cirrhosis is not infectious; pneumonia requires droplet precautions but not necessarily terminal cleaning. Option C is the cleanest, most correct list.

stem: The following are causes of functional intestinal obstruction:
rationale: FUNCTIONAL (paralytic/dynamic) ileus is failure of peristalsis without mechanical obstruction. Causes include: post-operative ileus, PERITONITIS, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia — low K+ impairs smooth muscle), opiates, sepsis, retroperitoneal haemorrhage, and spinal injury. Option C lists peritonitis and paralytic ileus — both functional. Option A lists MECHANICAL obstruction causes (intussusception, volvulus).

stem: Patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD):
option_a: Have chronic high levels of carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) in circulation
option_b: Have increased sensitivity to high levels of carbon dioxide
option_c: Their breathing is stimulated by high levels of oxygen
rationale: Long-standing COPD causes chronic CO2 retention (hypercapnia). The central chemoreceptors become DESENSITISED (not increased sensitivity) to chronically high CO2, and the respiratory drive becomes more dependent on HYPOXIA via peripheral chemoreceptors. Giving uncontrolled high-flow O2 can therefore reduce ventilation in some CO2 retainers. Option A is the correct, undisputed statement.

stem: The major challenge in the operating room is:
rationale: Infection control is the most universal and pervasive challenge in any operating room — surgical site infections (SSIs) increase morbidity, mortality, hospital stay and cost. This is why aseptic technique, theatre zoning, sterile gowning, surgical hand scrub, instrument sterilisation, air-flow control and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist exist.

option_c: Deposits of adipose tissue in the trunk

stem: Post subtotal thyroidectomy, the MOST important equipment for a nurse to keep at the bedside is:
rationale: Post-thyroidectomy, the most life-threatening early complication is airway obstruction from neck haematoma compressing the trachea, laryngeal oedema or bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. A TRACHEOSTOMY SET must be at the bedside for the first 24–48 hours for emergency airway management. Also keep calcium gluconate at the bedside for hypocalcaemic tetany (parathyroid damage).

stem: The process of increasing the community's ability to handle a disaster is referred to as:
rationale: DISASTER MANAGEMENT CYCLE: PREVENTION (avoid disaster - e.g. relocation from flood plain); MITIGATION (reduce impact - e.g. flood walls, building codes); PREPAREDNESS (BUILDING CAPACITY/READINESS to respond - training, drills, stockpiling supplies, early warning systems, evacuation plans, community education - option A); RESPONSE (immediate actions during/after - search/rescue, emergency relief, casualty management); RECOVERY (rehabilitation, reconstruction). Preparedness specifically INCREASES community ABILITY to handle disasters.

stem: The following skin eruption follows a nerve root on one side of the body:
rationale: Shingles (herpes zoster) is the reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from a dorsal root ganglion. It produces a painful vesicular rash strictly along a single DERMATOME (the area supplied by one sensory nerve root), unilaterally, never crossing the midline. Urticaria, impetigo and pemphigus are not dermatomal distributions.

stem: Bell's palsy involves the following cranial nerve:
rationale: Bell's palsy is idiopathic, unilateral, lower-motor-neurone facial weakness caused by inflammation/oedema of cranial nerve VII (the FACIAL nerve). The patient cannot wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile symmetrically on the affected side. Treatment: oral steroids (prednisolone) plus/minus aciclovir, and eye protection.

stem: Counselling is:
option_a: Helping the client understand his or her problem
option_b: Discovering the underlying cause of the client's problem
option_c: Giving solutions to the client's problems
rationale: Counselling is a structured, confidential, non-directive interaction in which the counsellor helps the client EXPLORE and UNDERSTAND their own situation, feelings and options — empowering the client to make their own informed decisions. Giving solutions or making decisions is contrary to counselling principles (that is advice-giving or directive coaching).

stem: The immediate action in a patient with sickle cell anaemia who develops priapism is:
option_a: Caution the patient against passing urine until the priapism resolves
option_b: Make the patient lie still on the bed
option_c: Have the patient take a warm bath
option_d: Administer morphine at the onset of the attack
rationale: Stuttering/mild priapism in sickle cell disease: encourage the patient to URINATE, take a WARM BATH/shower, drink plenty of fluids, and exercise gentle movement — these often abort the episode. Persistent priapism (more than 4 hours) is a urological emergency requiring aspiration of corpora, intracavernous alpha-agonist, or exchange transfusion. Morphine is given for severe sickle pain but is not the immediate measure for priapism.

stem: Regarding the pathogenesis of rheumatic endocarditis, which statement is CORRECT?
option_a: Streptococci directly invade and destroy cardiac tissue causing the valve damage
option_b: Rheumatic carditis is immune-mediated: antibodies against streptococcal M-protein cross-react with cardiac tissue (molecular mimicry)
option_c: Streptococcal toxins are directly deposited on the cardiac valves causing inflammation
option_d: Rheumatic endocarditis is caused by staphylococcal bacteraemia seeding the valves
rationale: Rheumatic carditis is an IMMUNE-MEDIATED injury. Antibodies and T-cells generated against the M-protein of group A streptococcus cross-react with cardiac tissue (molecular mimicry). The streptococci themselves are NOT present in the heart — the disease is a post-infectious autoimmune complication, not direct bacterial invasion.

stem: The test scores for an end of module examination were as follows: 85, 65, 75, 65, 70. The median value is:
rationale: MEDIAN = middle value when data is ARRANGED IN ORDER. Sorted ascending: 65, 65, 70, 75, 85. Number of values (n) = 5 (odd). Median position = (n+1)/2 = 3rd value = 70 - option C. Mean = (85+65+75+65+70)/5 = 360/5 = 72 (option B - but that's mean, not median). Mode = 65 (most frequent, option A). For even n, median = average of two middle values.

stem: Transformational leadership:
option_a: Focuses on effecting revolutionary change in the organisation
option_b: Values collaborations, teamwork and interpersonal skills
option_c: Ensures that individuals share the responsibility for achieving organisational goals
option_d: Originates from a desire to serve
rationale: TRANSFORMATIONAL leadership (Bass/Burns) — the leader INSPIRES followers to transcend self-interest for the good of the organisation, creating REVOLUTIONARY/visionary CHANGE through the 4 I's: Idealised influence (charisma), Inspirational motivation, Intellectual stimulation, Individualised consideration. Distinct from: TRANSACTIONAL (rewards/punishments); SERVANT leadership (originates from desire to serve — option D, Greenleaf); TEAM/PARTICIPATIVE (options B, C). Option A captures the transformative essence.

stem: The following is an element of classical management theory:
rationale: CLASSICAL MANAGEMENT THEORY (Taylor, Fayol, Weber) emphasises: scientific management, administrative management (Fayol's 14 principles), and bureaucracy. Key features: HIERARCHY, CHAIN OF COMMAND (option B), unity of command, division of labour, formal rules, span of control, formal authority. HAWTHORNE EFFECT (option A) is from the HUMAN RELATIONS school (Mayo, 1920s). THROUGH-PUT is a systems theory concept. "Ebbing effect" is not a recognised management term.

stem: The following is a reason for planning in management:
option_a: To establish a hierarchy in the organisation
option_b: To provide adequate and appropriate personnel
rationale: PURPOSES OF PLANNING in management: (1) FOCUSES ATTENTION ON OBJECTIVES (option D) — directs all efforts toward agreed goals; (2) reduces uncertainty by anticipating the future; (3) ensures economical use of resources; (4) facilitates control; (5) promotes innovation. Hierarchy (option A) is established by ORGANISING; personnel provision (option B) is STAFFING; motivating staff (option C) is DIRECTING/LEADING. These are separate management functions.

stem: In relation to obtaining informed consent from a seventeen-year-old adolescent, the nurse should remember that the adolescent:
option_a: Does not have the legal capacity to give consent
option_b: Is not able to make an acceptable or intelligent choice
option_c: Is able to give voluntary consent when parents are not available
option_d: Will most likely be unable to choose between alternatives when asked to consent
rationale: Per Kenyan law (Children Act 2022 and Constitution), a MINOR is anyone under 18 years. A 17-year-old does NOT have full legal capacity to give independent consent for medical treatment — parent/legal guardian must consent (with the minor's ASSENT). EXCEPTIONS: HIV testing and counselling (12+ years can consent independently per HIV/AIDS Prevention and Control Act 2006); family planning services to sexually active minors; emergencies. Option A reflects the legal default position.

stem: The personality theory suggesting that behaviour and learning occurs through imitation is:
rationale: SOCIAL-LEARNING theory (Bandura) — behaviour is LEARNED through OBSERVATION AND IMITATION of MODELS (parents, peers, media) — classic Bobo doll experiment. Includes vicarious learning and self-efficacy. HUMANISTIC (Maslow, Rogers) — self-actualisation, personal growth. PSYCHOANALYTIC (Freud) — unconscious mind, id/ego/superego. COGNITIVE (Piaget, Beck) — mental processes, schemas. Option D — social-learning — is specifically defined by imitation.

stem: The learning where we associate a certain behaviour with a specific outcome is:
rationale: OPERANT CONDITIONING (Skinner) — behaviour MODIFIED by its CONSEQUENCES (REWARDS/REINFORCEMENT increase behaviour; punishment decreases). Voluntary behaviour-outcome association — option B. CLASSICAL CONDITIONING (Pavlov) — associating two STIMULI (involuntary, reflexive — e.g. Pavlov's dogs salivating at bell). OBSERVATIONAL learning (Bandura) — through imitation. Operant is specifically the behaviour-outcome contingency learning.

stem: The humanistic theories of personality development emphasise:
rationale: HUMANISTIC theories (Maslow, Rogers): emphasise CONSCIOUS experience, FREE WILL, personal growth, and SELF-ACTUALISATION (realising one's full potential — option B). MASLOW'S HIERARCHY OF NEEDS: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation. ROGERS — unconditional positive regard, congruence between real and ideal self. WISH-FULFILLMENT, EGO IDEAL, UNCONSCIOUS MIND (options A, C, D) are PSYCHOANALYTIC (Freud) concepts.

stem: An appropriate behavioural objective for a teaching session is:
option_a: After a teaching session, the client list five tools in the class of proteins
option_b: After a teaching session, the client will have knowledge of foods in a class of proteins
option_c: After a teaching session, the client will verbalise understanding of foods in the class of proteins
option_d: After a teaching session the client will know which foods are proteineous
rationale: BEHAVIOURAL OBJECTIVES (Mager/Bloom) must contain: AUDIENCE, BEHAVIOUR (observable, measurable action verb — NOT "know", "understand", "appreciate"), CONDITION, and CRITERION. Acceptable verbs: list, describe, demonstrate, identify, verbalise. Option C — "verbalise understanding" uses an observable verb. Options B and D use "have knowledge" and "know" — not measurable. Option A has grammar issues ("tools" should be "examples").

stem: Regarding digoxin toxicity, which electrolyte abnormality POTENTIATES its toxic effects?
rationale: Digoxin toxicity is precipitated and worsened by HYPOKALAEMIA (low K+). Low potassium reduces competition at the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, increasing digoxin binding and toxicity. This is why potassium levels must be monitored and maintained when patients are on digoxin — especially those also taking loop diuretics which cause potassium loss. Hyperkalaemia reduces digoxin effect rather than potentiating toxicity.

stem: An 8-month-old baby is said to have fast breathing if the respiration rate is:
option_a: Equal to or greater than 30 breaths per minute
option_b: Equal to or greater than 40 breaths per minute
option_c: Equal to or greater than 50 breaths per minute
option_d: Equal to or greater than 60 breaths per minute
rationale: Per Kenya IMCI fast-breathing cut-offs: less than 2 months = 60 or more breaths/min; 2–11 months = 50 or more breaths/min; 12 months to 5 years = 40 or more breaths/min. An 8-month-old falls in the 2–11 month category, so fast breathing = 50 or more breaths/min.

stem: Leukaemia:
option_a: Is characterised by abnormal proliferation of plasma cells
option_b: Viral infection is one of the predisposing factors
option_c: Is characterised by increased platelets in blood
rationale: Viral infections (HTLV-1 leading to adult T-cell leukaemia; EBV associated with some lymphomas/leukaemia) are recognised aetiological factors in leukaemia, along with ionising radiation, benzene, alkylating chemotherapy and chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome, Fanconi anaemia). Plasma cell proliferation is MULTIPLE MYELOMA. Leukaemia features THROMBOCYTOPAENIA (not increased platelets) and a HYPERMETABOLIC state.

stem: In cases of an accidental sharp injury, one should:
option_a: Wash the site with soap and water
option_b: Squeeze the site to enhance bleeding
option_c: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the site
option_d: Apply a tourniquet distal to the site
rationale: Per Kenya MoH and WHO post-exposure protocols, immediate first aid after a needlestick/sharps injury: ALLOW the wound to bleed freely (do NOT squeeze, which could traumatise tissue); WASH thoroughly with SOAP AND WATER; cover with a waterproof dressing; report immediately for risk assessment and PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) if indicated. Tourniquets are never used for needlestick injuries.

stem: Management of a patient with lumbar disk herniation includes:
rationale: Conservative management of lumbar disc prolapse: a SHORT period of bed rest on a firm bed (no longer than 1–2 days — prolonged bed rest is now discouraged), HEAT (or alternating ice/heat), analgesics (NSAIDs, paracetamol, muscle relaxants), gradual mobilisation and physiotherapy. Surgery (discectomy) is reserved for failure of conservative management or progressive neurological deficit/cauda equina syndrome.

stem: Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital condition in which:
option_a: A portion of large intestine is grossly dilated
option_b: A portion of the large intestine is stenosed
option_c: The anal membranes fail to rupture
option_d: There is abnormal opening of the oesophageal wall
rationale: Hirschsprung's disease is congenital aganglionosis: the distal colon/rectum lacks parasympathetic ganglion cells (Meissner and Auerbach plexuses) and cannot relax, creating functional obstruction. The colon PROXIMAL to the aganglionic segment becomes grossly DILATED (megacolon). Presentation: delayed passage of meconium (more than 24 hours in term newborn), abdominal distension, bilious vomiting. Option C describes imperforate anal membrane; option D describes oesophageal atresia/TEF.

stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis asks a nurse if there is a cure. An appropriate response would be:
option_a: Yes, there are drugs that offer cure
option_b: Yes but the patient must take medication for at least 10 years
option_c: No but there are drugs to control the disease process
option_d: No, most patients with rheumatoid arthritis also develop osteoarthritis
rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic AUTOIMMUNE disease with no cure. Modern DMARDs (methotrexate, sulphasalazine, leflunomide), biologics (anti-TNF, rituximab) and JAK inhibitors can slow progression and induce remission. The honest, therapeutic response is option C.

stem: Nursing interventions for a patient with cholecystitis associated with cholelithiasis are based on the knowledge that:
option_a: The disorder can be successfully treated with oral bile salts that dissolve gallstones
option_b: Analgesics are usually not necessary to relieve the pain of bile duct spasms
option_c: A heavy meal with a high fat content may worsen the signs and symptoms of the disease
option_d: A low cholesterol diet is indicated to reduce the availability of cholesterol for gallstone formation
rationale: Cholecystokinin is released in response to dietary fat, triggering gallbladder contraction. In a gallbladder containing stones or inflamed, this contraction precipitates biliary colic. Patients should AVOID fatty/heavy meals. Oral bile-salt dissolution (ursodeoxycholic acid) works in only select cases; analgesia IS required for biliary pain; low-cholesterol diet does not appreciably reduce stone formation once stones are formed.

stem: The following is an early symptom of cataract:
rationale: Cataracts are painless, progressive opacification of the lens. The earliest symptom is gradual BLURRING of vision and decreased contrast/colour sensitivity, followed by glare in bright light. Loss of peripheral vision is characteristic of GLAUCOMA, not cataracts. Cataract causes no pain.

stem: The triad symptoms in Meniere's disease include:
rationale: Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops) classic triad: episodic VERTIGO (minutes to hours, with nausea/vomiting), fluctuating SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS (low-frequency), and TINNITUS, often with aural fullness. Attacks last 20 minutes to several hours. This triad distinguishes Meniere's from other vestibular disorders.

stem: Sitz baths post haemorrhoidectomy are meant to:
rationale: A warm sitz bath after haemorrhoidectomy (3–4 times daily and after defecation) promotes circulation to the perineum, relaxes the anal sphincter, cleanses the operative site, relieves pain and spasm, reduces oedema, and thereby promotes healing. It also helps prevent infection, but the primary stated purpose is healing.

stem: Trousseau's sign is associated with:
rationale: Trousseau's sign is carpopedal spasm (flexion of wrist and MCP joints, extension of fingers, adduction of thumb) induced by inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes — produced by neuromuscular irritability from HYPOCALCAEMIA. Chvostek's sign (twitching of facial muscles on tapping the facial nerve) is the other classic sign. Both are seen post-thyroidectomy (parathyroid damage).

rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis classic features: SYMMETRIC small-joint polyarthritis (MCPs, PIPs, wrists), MORNING STIFFNESS LASTING MORE THAN 1 HOUR, characteristic deformities — SWAN-NECK (hyperextension of PIP, flexion of DIP), BOUTONNIERE (flexion PIP, hyperextension DIP), ulnar deviation, Z-thumb. stem: A patient with epilepsy experiencing a generalised tingling sensation and "smelling roses" is probably experiencing:
rationale: An AURA is a subjective warning sensation preceding a seizure — it is essentially a simple partial (focal aware) seizure arising from the cortical onset zone. Auras can be olfactory (smelling burnt rubber or roses — temporal lobe onset), visual, somatosensory (tingling), gustatory or psychic (deja vu). Although the smell is technically an olfactory hallucination, in this clinical context it IS the seizure aura — option C is the more complete and contextually correct answer.

stem: When feeding a patient with residual dysphagia due to a cerebral vascular accident, the nurse should avoid:
option_c: Placing food on the unaffected side of the mouth
option_d: Placing the patient in low Fowler's position
rationale: Patients with dysphagia after stroke have the greatest difficulty controlling THIN LIQUIDS (water, tea, juice) — these flow rapidly past the impaired pharyngeal phase and are easily aspirated. The nurse should AVOID thin liquids; THICKEN liquids (option B is correct practice); place food on the UNAFFECTED side of the mouth (option C correct); and position the patient sitting UP. Speech and language therapist assessment is standard.

stem: In chronic liver cirrhosis, a nurse emphasises bleeding precautions because:
option_a: The low protein diet will result in reduced clotting
option_b: The increased production of bile decreases clotting factors
option_c: The liver is unable to produce clotting factors
option_d: The required medications reduce clotting factors
rationale: The liver synthesises clotting factors I (fibrinogen), II (prothrombin), V, VII, IX, X, XI and XIII, plus proteins C and S. In cirrhosis, hepatocyte mass is lost, synthesis falls and PT/INR rises. Additionally, portal hypertension causes hypersplenism and thrombocytopaenia, and varices add bleeding risk. Bleeding precautions: soft toothbrush, electric razor, avoid IM injections, avoid aspirin/NSAIDs.

stem: Management of scaled lesions in psoriasis includes:
option_a: Covering the lesions with occlusive dressings to remove the scales
option_b: Applying moisturisers to soften the scales
option_c: Shaving the scales using a clean razor
option_d: Keeping the lesions dry to enhance dropping off of the scales
rationale: Topical management of psoriasis scaling: EMOLLIENTS/MOISTURISERS soften and lift the silvery scales, allowing penetration of active agents — topical corticosteroids, vitamin-D analogues (calcipotriol), coal tar, dithranol, salicylic acid as keratolytic. Shaving the scales causes Koebner phenomenon (new psoriasis in injured skin). Dry skin worsens psoriasis.

stem: Indications for erythromycin include:
rationale: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic active against Gram-positive cocci, atypical respiratory pathogens (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella), Bordetella pertussis, Campylobacter and Helicobacter. Clinical indications include atypical/community-acquired PNEUMONIA, LEGIONNAIRE'S DISEASE, pertussis, diphtheria, chlamydial infections and as a penicillin alternative. Multiple sclerosis is autoimmune — not an antibiotic indication.

stem: The cardiac output is calculated as:
rationale: CARDIAC OUTPUT (CO) = HEART RATE (HR) × STROKE VOLUME (SV). Normal CO at rest: 4–8 L/min (average 5 L/min). HR: 60–100 bpm; SV: 60–100 mL/beat. Factors affecting SV: preload (venous return — Frank-Starling law), afterload (peripheral resistance), and contractility (inotropic state). CO increases during exercise, pregnancy, fever, and anaemia. Decreased in heart failure, hypovolaemia, and cardiogenic shock. Blood pressure = CO × Total Peripheral Resistance.

stem: A three-month-old baby classified to have pneumonia is likely to have a respiratory rate of:
rationale: Per Kenya IMCI fast-breathing cut-offs: 2–11 months = 50 or more breaths/min. A 3-month-old falls in this band, so a respiratory rate of 50 breaths/min (or more) classifies as pneumonia. Note: 60 breaths/min would also qualify, but 50 is the threshold itself for this age group.

stem: Status asthmaticus that is not corrected can result in:
rationale: Early status asthmaticus shows hyperventilation causing respiratory ALKALOSIS with hypocapnia. As the patient tires (ominous sign — silent chest, drowsiness, NORMAL/RISING PaCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic), ventilation fails: PaCO2 rises (RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS) and severe HYPOXAEMIA develops, heralding respiratory arrest. A rising PaCO2 in acute severe asthma is a red flag requiring urgent ICU and ventilatory support.

stem: A non-invasive method of evaluating blood flow is:
rationale: Doppler ultrasonography is a NON-INVASIVE imaging technique that uses the frequency shift of reflected ultrasound waves to assess blood flow direction and velocity — used in DVT diagnosis, peripheral arterial disease, carotid stenosis and echocardiography. Venography, angiography and cardiac catheterisation all require vascular puncture and contrast injection — they are invasive procedures.

stem: The most relevant assessment for a patient admitted with benign prostatic hyperplasia is:
option_a: Flank pain radiating to the groin
rationale: BPH causes bladder outlet obstruction with retention. The most relevant nursing assessment is for a DISTENDED BLADDER (lower-abdominal distension/dullness up to or above the umbilicus, palpable bladder, urge to void without producing urine). Flank pain radiating to groin suggests ureteric colic (renal stone); perineal oedema and urethral discharge suggest infection.

stem: A child with aplastic anaemia should be monitored for:
rationale: Aplastic anaemia is pancytopenia from bone-marrow failure: anaemia (low Hb), neutropenia (infection risk), and THROMBOCYTOPAENIA (bleeding risk). Children present with petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding and risk of life-threatening intracranial haemorrhage. Strict bleeding precautions, monitoring for bleeding, infection control and blood-product support are key.

stem: Nursing diagnosis for a patient with leukaemia include:
option_b: Excess fluid volume, impaired skin integrity
option_c: Risk for injury (bleeding), impaired gaseous exchange
rationale: Leukaemia causes pancytopenia: anaemia leading to IMPAIRED GAS EXCHANGE and activity intolerance; thrombocytopaenia leading to RISK FOR INJURY (BLEEDING); neutropenia leading to risk for infection; bone-marrow expansion and chemotherapy causing pain. Hypothermia and excess fluid volume are not typical leukaemia nursing diagnoses.

stem: In the immediate post-operative period, the nurse's priority assessment is:
option_a: Pain level using a numeric rating scale
option_d: Wound site for bleeding and drainage
rationale: Post-operative priority follows the ABC framework: AIRWAY (is it patent? — risk of obstruction from tongue, secretions, laryngospasm after extubation), BREATHING (rate, depth, SpO2 — risk of respiratory depression from anaesthetic agents/opioids), CIRCULATION (BP, HR, skin colour — risk of haemorrhage, hypotension). This is the PACU (Post-Anaesthesia Care Unit) primary survey. Pain, consciousness, and wound assessment are important but come after ensuring the patient is breathing and haemodynamically stable.

stem: Causative organism of malignant otitis externa is:
rationale: Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is a severe, invasive infection of the external ear canal spreading to the skull base. It occurs almost exclusively in elderly diabetics and the immunocompromised, and is caused overwhelmingly by PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA. Treatment requires prolonged systemic anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (ciprofloxacin or ceftazidime plus aminoglycoside) and tight glycaemic control.

stem: The following drug is contraindicated in glaucoma:
rationale: Atropine and other anticholinergics/mydriatics DILATE the pupil; in narrow-angle glaucoma, mydriasis can precipitate acute angle closure by obstructing aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork — a sight-threatening emergency. Anticholinergic drugs (atropine, ipratropium, tricyclic antidepressants, antihistamines) are contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma.

stem: The best position for a 9-year-old two days post gastrectomy is:
rationale: Post-gastrectomy patients are positioned in LOW (or SEMI-) FOWLER'S — head of bed elevated to approximately 30 degrees. This reduces strain on the abdominal suture line, prevents reflux of gastric contents (especially with NG tube in place), promotes lung expansion and drainage, and is generally comfortable. Flat supine increases reflux risk; left lateral is the post-meal anti-dumping position; prone is unsuitable post-abdominal surgery.

stem: Angiotensin II causes release of:
rationale: Angiotensin II is the central effector of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. It (i) is a potent vasoconstrictor; (ii) stimulates the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex to release ALDOSTERONE; (iii) stimulates posterior pituitary ADH release; (iv) promotes thirst and sodium reabsorption. Renin is RELEASED from the kidney's juxtaglomerular cells to INITIATE the cascade — not released by angiotensin II.

stem: Following eye surgery, which of the following is CORRECT regarding post-operative instructions?
option_a: The patient should perform frequent coughing exercises to prevent respiratory complications
option_b: The patient should avoid coughing, straining and bending as these raise intraocular pressure
option_c: The patient may sneeze freely as this does not affect the surgical repair
option_d: Deep breathing and coughing exercises are mandatory every 2 hours post-operatively
rationale: Coughing dramatically raises intra-ocular pressure and can disrupt the surgical repair (wound dehiscence, expulsive haemorrhage, vitreous loss). Patients are explicitly told NOT to cough, sneeze forcefully, strain or bend. Deep breathing WITHOUT forceful coughing is acceptable. Patients with post-op nausea must receive antiemetics promptly to prevent vomiting.

stem: Which of the following best describes the appropriate diet for a patient with myocardial infarction?
option_a: High calorie, high protein diet to support cardiac healing
option_b: Low-salt, low-saturated-fat, calorie-controlled diet with small frequent meals
option_c: High fibre, high carbohydrate diet to reduce myocardial oxygen demand
option_d: Unrestricted diet to maintain adequate nutritional intake
rationale: MI patients are placed on a LOW-SALT, LOW-SATURATED-FAT, calorie-CONTROLLED diet to reduce cardiac workload and prevent obesity/hyperlipidaemia. Small, frequent, light meals are preferred to avoid the postprandial cardiac demand surge. High calorie diets are inappropriate as they worsen atherosclerosis risk factors.

stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis presents with hyperventilation because:
option_a: The respiratory centre in the brain is damaged
option_c: There is high rate of oxygen consumption
option_d: There is reduced excretion of waste through the renal system
rationale: In DKA, ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) accumulate, causing metabolic acidosis (low pH). The body compensates by hyperventilation (deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations) to blow off CO2 and raise pH. This is RESPIRATORY COMPENSATION for metabolic acidosis — not brain damage or increased oxygen demand.

stem: Atherosclerosis impedes coronary blood flow by the following mechanism:
option_c: Blood clots form outside the vessel wall
option_d: Hardened vessels dilate to allow the blood to flow through
rationale: Atherosclerosis is the deposition of cholesterol-laden atheromatous plaques in the intima of ARTERIES — these progressively narrow the arterial lumen, restricting blood flow. Plaque rupture exposes a thrombogenic core, triggering acute thrombosis and occlusion (causing MI). Arteries are involved (not veins); plaques are WITHIN the wall; hardened arteries lose elasticity and cannot dilate normally.

stem: The common complications associated with kerosene (paraffin) inhalation are:
rationale: Paraffin/kerosene ingestion-aspiration commonly produces chemical pneumonitis with gastritis, respiratory distress and hypoxia. Aspiration into the lungs is the key danger, causing hydrocarbon pneumonitis. Emphysema and alveolar haemorrhage are not the expected presenting complications. Ref: Kenya Paediatric Protocols (poisoning management).

stem: The hypogastric region of the abdominopelvic cavity is:
option_a: Inferior to the umbilical region, medial to the right iliac region
option_b: Lateral to the left iliac region, superior to the umbilical region
option_c: Medial to the right iliac region, lateral to the umbilical region
option_d: Superior to the umbilical region, medial to the right iliac region
rationale: In the 9-region anatomical scheme of the abdomen, the HYPOGASTRIC (suprapubic) region is the central LOWER region — BELOW the umbilical region and BETWEEN (medial to) the right and left iliac (inguinal) regions. Option A correctly identifies it as inferior to the umbilical region and medial to the right iliac region.

stem: The most appropriate nursing action when a client begins to cough and has difficulty breathing during nasogastric tube insertion is:
option_c: Removing the tube and reinserting when the respiratory distress subsides
option_d: Pulling the tube back a little and wait until the respiratory distress subsides
rationale: Sudden cough and respiratory distress during NG insertion suggests the tube has entered the trachea/airway instead of the oesophagus. The immediate action is to PULL THE TUBE BACK a few centimetres (out of the airway) and wait for the patient to recover, then reattempt insertion. There is no need to fully remove and start over. Asking the patient to swallow water during advancement helps guide the tube into the oesophagus.

stem: A patient who has been treated for chronic renal failure (CRF) should be instructed to:
option_b: Monitor fruit intake, and eat plenty of bananas
option_d: Drink plenty of fluids, and use a salt substitute
rationale: CRF dietary advice: LOW protein (reduces nitrogenous waste) — so meat intake is restricted (A wrong); LOW potassium — AVOID bananas, oranges, tomatoes (B wrong); LOW sodium — but salt substitutes are often potassium-based and therefore CONTRAINDICATED (D wrong); LIMITED fluid in oliguric/dialysis patients. INCREASED CARBOHYDRATE intake provides energy and prevents tissue catabolism which would generate more urea. Option C is correct.

stem: Turbid urine is an indication of:
option_b: Presence of prostatic fluid and WBC
option_d: Perineal injury and prolonged use of diuretics
rationale: Turbid (cloudy) urine results from suspended particles: WBCs and bacteria from URINARY TRACT INFECTION (the most common cause), pus, crystals, phosphates (alkaline urine), epithelial cells, or concentrated urine in DEHYDRATION. Both dehydration and UTI are correct associations — option A is the best fit.

topic: Fluid and Electrolyte Balance in Children
stem: An 11-month-old infant with dehydration and metabolic acidosis is likely to present with:
option_d: A reduced white blood cell count
rationale: Metabolic acidosis (e.g. from severe diarrhoeal dehydration) triggers respiratory compensation — TACHYPNOEA (rapid, deep breathing) to blow off CO2 and raise pH. Shallow breathing would WORSEN acidosis. WBC and platelet changes are not direct features of dehydration/acidosis. Per Kenya IMCI, fast breathing with diarrhoea suggests severe dehydration with acidosis.

stem: A child with Wilms' tumour presents with:
rationale: Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma) is the commonest childhood renal cancer, typically presenting in a child under 5 years with a painless ABDOMINAL/FLANK MASS — often discovered incidentally by the parent while bathing. Microscopic haematuria may occur but gross haematuria is uncommon. Hypertension may be present. Avoid vigorous palpation of the mass (can cause tumour rupture).

stem: During lumbar puncture, a needle is inserted in the space between:
rationale: Lumbar puncture is performed at the L3/L4 (or L4/L5) interspace — BELOW the termination of the spinal cord (conus medullaris at L1/L2 in adults) — to avoid spinal cord injury. The L4 spinous process is identified at the level of the iliac crests (Tuffier's line). The cord ends lower in infants (about L3), so paediatric LP is performed at L4/L5 or L5/S1.

stem: In chronic bronchitis:
option_a: There is cough and sputum production for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years
option_b: There is destruction of alveoli walls due to severe infection and increased secretion
option_c: There is increased ciliary function in the airway
option_d: There is flow limitation and it is not fully reversible
rationale: Chronic bronchitis is a CLINICAL diagnosis: productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 CONSECUTIVE years — per GOLD criteria. Alveolar wall destruction characterises EMPHYSEMA. Cilia are DAMAGED (not increased) in chronic bronchitis — hence impaired mucociliary clearance. Option A is the precise textbook definition.

stem: A major burn is:
option_a: Partial thickness with more than 20% in children
option_d: Partial thickness with 10–20% burn in children
rationale: By American Burn Association (ABA) criteria, a MAJOR burn includes: partial-thickness burns more than 25% TBSA in adults or MORE THAN 20% in children/elderly; OR full-thickness burns 10% TBSA or more; OR burns involving face, eyes, ears, hands, feet, perineum, major joints, or with inhalation injury, electrical injury, or significant co-morbidities. Hence option A — partial-thickness more than 20% in children.

stem: Conductive hearing loss can be caused by:
rationale: Conductive hearing loss results from anything that impedes sound transmission through the external or middle ear: cerumen impaction, otitis media, perforated/RETRACTED TYMPANIC MEMBRANE, OTOSCLEROSIS (fixation of the stapes), middle-ear effusion, otitis externa. SENSORINEURAL hearing loss is from cochlea/CN VIII pathology — presbycusis (age-related), Meniere's, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, frusemide, cisplatin), noise exposure. Option D gives two conductive causes.

stem: The condition in which the eye balls are not properly aligned with each other is referred to as:
rationale: STRABISMUS (squint) is misalignment of the visual axes — esotropia (inward), exotropia (outward), hypertropia (up), hypotropia (down). Astigmatism is non-spherical cornea/lens curvature; presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation; amblyopia ("lazy eye") is reduced vision in one eye from disuse during visual development, often a consequence of uncorrected strabismus or refractive imbalance.

stem: A 60-year-old's susceptibility to osteoporosis is most likely related to:
rationale: The major risk factor for primary osteoporosis after age 50 (especially in women) is HORMONAL — oestrogen deficiency post-menopause causes accelerated bone loss (most marked in the first 5–10 years post-menopause). In men, declining testosterone has a similar though slower effect. Other contributing factors include inadequate dietary calcium, vitamin-D deficiency, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, alcohol and corticosteroids — but the principal age-related driver is hormonal.

stem: Uncontrollable jerky movements are indicative of:
rationale: CLONIC seizures are characterised by rhythmic, repetitive, jerky muscle contractions. MYOCLONIC seizures are brief shock-like single jerks. TONIC = sustained muscle stiffening without jerks. ABSENCE = brief loss of awareness without motor activity. Sustained rhythmic uncontrollable jerky movements describe CLONIC activity.

stem: The general danger signs in a sick child include:
rationale: IMNCI general danger signs are: not able to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions (current or history), and lethargy or unconsciousness. Option B correctly lists three recognized IMNCI general danger signs. Ref: Kenya IMNCI guidelines (MOH Division of Child and Adolescent Health).

stem: In diabetes management, self-monitoring of blood glucose is preferred to urine glucose monitoring because:
option_a: It can be done by any client
option_b: It is not influenced by drugs
rationale: Self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) gives a direct, real-time measurement of plasma glucose at the moment of testing, whereas urine glucose only appears when blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (approximately 10 mmol/L) and lags significantly behind blood levels. Urine glucose is also affected by hydration status, renal function and certain drugs (vitamin C interferes with strip tests). SMBG is the standard of care for insulin-dependent diabetes.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes the vomiting pattern in small intestinal obstruction?
option_a: Small intestinal obstruction typically presents with late faeculent vomiting
option_b: Small intestinal obstruction presents with early bilious/reflux vomiting
option_c: Vomiting does not occur in small intestinal obstruction
option_d: Small intestinal obstruction presents with haematemesis as the first sign
rationale: Small-bowel obstruction typically presents with EARLY bilious/reflux vomiting (as the obstruction is proximal). LARGE-bowel obstruction has LATE faeculent vomiting (the obstruction is distal and stool backs up over a longer time before vomiting occurs). This distinction helps localise the level of obstruction clinically.

stem: Which of the following is CORRECT regarding intradermal injection technique?
option_a: The needle is inserted at 45 degrees into the skin
option_b: The needle is inserted at 90 degrees perpendicular to the skin
option_c: The needle is inserted at 5–15 degrees with the bevel up, raising a small wheal
option_d: The site should be massaged after administration to enhance absorption
rationale: INTRADERMAL injections (e.g. Mantoux/PPD test, BCG, allergy testing) are given at a SHALLOW 5–15 degree angle with the bevel UP, into the most superficial layer of skin (dermis), raising a small visible wheal. 45 degrees is SUBCUTANEOUS; 90 degrees is INTRAMUSCULAR. The site should NOT be massaged (would dislodge the medication from the dermis).

stem: When nursing a patient with neutropenia, the nurse should avoid:
option_b: Giving oxygen using a nasal catheter
option_d: Performing oral hygiene after every meal
rationale: Neutropenic patients are at extreme risk of opportunistic infection. Rectal suppositories/enemas can traumatise the rectal mucosa and seed gut flora into the bloodstream (a common cause of neutropenic bacteraemia). For the same reason: avoid rectal thermometers, rectal exams, and raw fruits/vegetables. Oral hygiene is ENCOURAGED (oral mucositis is a portal of entry). IM injections are avoided mainly in thrombocytopaenia.

stem: A patient with blood group O negative can receive blood from:
option_b: O positive and O negative only
option_d: O negative and AB negative only
rationale: Blood group O NEGATIVE is the UNIVERSAL DONOR for red blood cells (no A, B, or Rh antigens to trigger a reaction). However, O negative patients can only receive O NEGATIVE blood — they have anti-A, anti-B antibodies (would react to A, B, or AB blood) AND anti-D antibodies (would react to Rh-positive blood). In emergencies when blood type is unknown, O negative packed red cells are given. AB positive is the universal recipient (no antibodies against A, B, or Rh). Always crossmatch before transfusion when time allows.

stem: Chronic bronchitis is commonly caused by:
rationale: Chronic bronchitis as a disease is primarily caused by SMOKING — but the question refers to pathogens commonly associated with acute exacerbations/infections superimposed on chronic bronchitis. The classical bacterial trio in COPD/chronic bronchitis exacerbations is Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Option A lists the top two.

stem: A patient with venous thrombo-embolism is initially treated with:
rationale: Standard initial anticoagulation for VTE (DVT/PE) is BRIDGING THERAPY: heparin (unfractionated IV or LMWH SC) for immediate anticoagulation, OVERLAPPED with warfarin until INR is therapeutic (2.0–3.0) for 2 consecutive days, then heparin is stopped. The overlap is needed because warfarin initially lowers proteins C and S faster than factors II, VII, IX, X — creating transient hypercoagulability. DOACs now bypass this need but the classical answer is heparin plus warfarin.

stem: Intermittent bubbling in the water seal chamber of an underwater seal drainage is:
option_d: Expected when the unit is attached to wall suction
rationale: In an underwater seal chest drain, INTERMITTENT (with respiration/cough) bubbling in the WATER SEAL chamber is NORMAL — it reflects air leaving the pleural space as expected when draining a pneumothorax. CONTINUOUS bubbling indicates a system air leak (loose connection, hole in tubing, or persistent bronchopleural fistula). Continuous gentle bubbling in the SUCTION-CONTROL chamber is normal when connected to wall suction.

stem: Post thyroidectomy, the nurse can rule out laryngeal nerve damage by:
option_c: Determining the patient's ability to swallow
option_d: Telling the patient to extend his tongue
rationale: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid; injury (unilateral) causes hoarseness; bilateral injury causes stridor and airway obstruction. The simplest immediate post-op assessment is to ASK THE PATIENT TO SPEAK — hoarseness or weak voice indicates possible nerve injury. Swallowing assesses CN IX/X function but is less specific; tongue movement assesses CN XII.

stem: The primary goal of therapy for a client with pulmonary oedema in heart failure is:
rationale: Acute pulmonary oedema is a life-threatening respiratory emergency — fluid in alveoli prevents gas exchange and the patient can die from hypoxaemia. The IMMEDIATE PRIORITY (per ABC) is to IMPROVE OXYGENATION AND RESPIRATORY STATUS: high-flow oxygen plus/minus CPAP/BiPAP, upright positioning, IV diuretic (frusemide), GTN, morphine. Improving cardiac output and removing peripheral oedema are subsequent goals.

stem: When providing group therapy, the nurse must focus on:
rationale: GROUP THERAPY (Yalom's curative factors) — the therapist focuses on the GROUP PROCESS and JOINTLY EXPERIENCED issues: universality ("we are not alone"), interpersonal learning, cohesion, altruism, catharsis, instillation of hope. The COMMON STRESS/EXPERIENCE shared by group members provides the basis for therapy — option A. Individual behaviour, confrontations and personal feelings are addressed but in the context of the GROUP dynamic.

stem: To prevent side effects associated with prolonged phenytoin use, a client should be educated to:
option_a: Avoid crowds and obtain influenza vaccination annually
option_b: Drink 2 litres of fluid daily including 6–8 glasses of water
option_c: Eat a potassium rich, low sodium diet
option_d: Observe good dental hygiene and report any gum bleeding
rationale: A characteristic, distinctive long-term side effect of phenytoin is GINGIVAL HYPERPLASIA (overgrowth of gum tissue) — the patient needs meticulous oral hygiene, regular dental checks, and should report bleeding/swelling of gums. Other phenytoin side effects: hirsutism, coarsening of features, ataxia, nystagmus, megaloblastic anaemia (folate antagonism), osteomalacia, drug interactions (enzyme induction), Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

stem: The main goal of treatment for acute glomerulonephritis is:
rationale: Acute glomerulonephritis (post-streptococcal in children) presents with the nephritic syndrome: haematuria, hypertension, oedema, mild proteinuria and oliguria/azotaemia. Maintenance of FLUID BALANCE is central — fluid restriction, daily weights, monitoring intake/output and BP. Diet is LOW protein and LOW sodium during oliguric phase. Activity is restricted; catheterisation is not routinely needed.

stem: The most common, preventable complication of abdominal surgery is:
rationale: Atelectasis (collapse of lung segments from poor ventilation and retained secretions) is the most common complication of any abdominal/thoracic surgery — pain inhibits coughing and deep breathing. It is highly PREVENTABLE through pre-op patient education, deep breathing and coughing exercises, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, adequate analgesia and chest physiotherapy.

stem: Early miscarriage refers to:
option_a: Loss of pregnancy spontaneously in between 5 and 10 weeks
option_b: Spontaneous loss of pregnancy at 12 weeks gestation
option_c: Spontaneous loss of pregnancy from between 15 to 24 weeks gestation
option_d: Loss of pregnancy within the first trimester
rationale: EARLY miscarriage (early pregnancy loss) is defined as spontaneous loss of pregnancy in the FIRST TRIMESTER (before 12–14 completed weeks). Late miscarriage is from 12–14 weeks to 24 weeks. Beyond 24 weeks is fetal death/stillbirth. Most early miscarriages are due to chromosomal abnormalities.

stem: In myocardial infarction, morphine is administered to:
rationale: In acute MI, morphine is given to: (i) relieve severe ischaemic chest PAIN (analgesic); (ii) reduce sympathetic catecholamine surge and ANXIETY which would otherwise increase myocardial O2 demand; (iii) venodilate to reduce preload and cardiac workload (helpful when MI is complicated by pulmonary oedema). All these effects together help PREVENT cardiogenic SHOCK and relieve pain — option D is the most complete summary.

stem: A convulsing one-month-old infant should be given:
rationale: Per Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols for ACUTE seizure management in infants: IMMEDIATE — protect airway, position safely, oxygen, check glucose (give 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg if hypoglycaemic), IV access. FIRST-LINE anticonvulsant: DIAZEPAM 0.3 MG/KG IV SLOW (over 1-2 minutes) — option B — or rectally 0.5 mg/kg if no IV access. May repeat after 10 minutes. If seizure persists: PHENOBARBITONE 15-20 MG/KG IV/IM loading dose (NOT 5 mg/kg). The question specifies one-month-old (past neonatal period) — diazepam is appropriate first-line.

stem: The evaluation phase of the nursing process involves:
option_c: Priority setting and expected outcomes formulation
rationale: The five steps of the nursing process: ASSESSMENT (data collection), DIAGNOSIS, PLANNING (priority setting, goal/expected-outcome formulation), IMPLEMENTATION, and EVALUATION. The EVALUATION phase compares actual outcomes against expected outcomes (REASSESSMENT) and audits whether interventions were effective, leading to modification of the plan if needed.

stem: The immediate management for severe dehydration in a child with severe malnutrition according to IMCI strategy includes:
option_a: Infusion of half-strength Darrow's in 5% dextrose 15 mL/kg IV in 1 hour
option_b: Infusion of 0.9% normal saline 20 mL/kg in 1 hour
option_c: Transfusion of whole blood 40 mL/kg over 3 hours as soon as it is available
option_d: NGT feeding with Resomal 15 mL/kg/hr for 10 hours
rationale: Severe dehydration in a child with SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION (SAM) is managed DIFFERENTLY from non-malnourished children — rapid rehydration can precipitate heart failure. Per Kenya MoH Basic Paediatric Protocols/IMNCI/WHO: IF SHOCK (or unable to drink): IV HALF-STRENGTH DARROW'S in 5% DEXTROSE (or Ringer's lactate + 5% dextrose) 15 mL/kg over 1 HOUR — option A — then reassess. Avoid plain saline at full rate (option B — risk of heart failure in SAM). Oral ReSoMal is first-line if child can drink. Monitor closely for fluid overload.

stem: The ratio of infant chest compressions to ventilation where 2 rescuers are involved is:
rationale: PAEDIATRIC CPR ratios (per AHA/ERC guidelines for infants and children up to puberty): SINGLE RESCUER — 30 COMPRESSIONS : 2 VENTILATIONS (same as adults). TWO HEALTHCARE PROVIDERS — 15 COMPRESSIONS : 2 VENTILATIONS — option C — used for both INFANTS and CHILDREN. Note: this differs from NEONATAL RESUSCITATION (immediately after birth) which uses 3:1 ratio (90 compressions + 30 breaths per minute). Compression rate is 100-120/min, depth 1/3 of AP chest diameter. Two-thumb technique for infants when 2 rescuers.

stem: Which of the following is correct? (a) The iliac crest is the site of choice for bone marrow aspiration in a 5-year-old child. (b) Acute renal failure is the leading complication associated with acute glomerulonephritis.
rationale: (a) TRUE — for CHILDREN over ~1 year, the POSTERIOR ILIAC CREST (posterior superior iliac spine, PSIS) is the PREFERRED SITE for bone marrow aspiration — easy access, generous marrow, fewer complications. For infants <1 year, the proximal tibia is often used. Sternum is the site for adults but AVOIDED in children. (b) FALSE — the leading complication of ACUTE POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (APSGN) is HYPERTENSIVE ENCEPHALOPATHY and HEART FAILURE due to volume overload, NOT acute renal failure. AKI can occur but is less common than cardiovascular complications.

stem: Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine is given to protect against:
rationale: HAEMOPHILUS INFLUENZAE TYPE B (Hib) — gram-negative bacterium causing severe invasive disease in children, especially <5 years: MENINGITIS (commonest serious manifestation pre-vaccine), PNEUMONIA, epiglottitis, septic arthritis, septicaemia, cellulitis, pericarditis. So Hib vaccine protects against MENINGITIS AND PNEUMONIA (option D) — also epiglottitis. Given in Kenya as part of PENTAVALENT VACCINE (DPT-HepB-Hib) at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. Since introduction, Hib disease has fallen >95% globally.

stem: One of the following is NOT true of a malignant tumour. It is:
rationale: MALIGNANT vs BENIGN tumours: MALIGNANT — INVASIVE (infiltrates surrounding tissues — option A TRUE); METASTASISES via blood/lymph/transcoelomic; rapid uncontrolled growth; poorly differentiated/anaplastic (option C TRUE); high mitotic index; PARANEOPLASTIC syndromes from ectopic hormone secretion or autoimmune reactions (option D TRUE — SIADH, Cushing's from small cell lung Ca, hypercalcaemia). NOT ENCAPSULATED — invades tissues without a capsule (option B — FALSE for malignant; benign tumours are typically encapsulated). The "NOT TRUE" answer = option B.

stem: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia has a high risk of infection because:
option_a: White blood cells are produced in inadequate numbers
option_c: There is a down-regulation of immune system by catecholamine
option_d: The white blood cells are immature
rationale: ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKAEMIA (ALL) — uncontrolled proliferation of IMMATURE LYMPHOID CELLS (LYMPHOBLASTS) in bone marrow. INFECTION RISK due to: (1) IMMATURE/non-functional white cells — even though WBC count may be HIGH, the cells are BLASTS that CANNOT FUNCTION as competent immune cells — option D — qualitative deficiency (functional immunosuppression); (2) NEUTROPENIA — bone marrow crowded by blasts → reduced normal neutrophils; (3) Treatment-induced (chemotherapy causes profound neutropenia); (4) breach of barriers (mucositis, IV lines). Option A — inadequate numbers — is partly true but not the FULL story. Option D captures the functional issue.

stem: The following feature indicates excessive IV fluid infusion in a 3-year-old child:
rationale: FLUID OVERLOAD in children — children have less cardiovascular reserve and are more vulnerable to volume overload than adults. SIGNS: WORSENING DYSPNOEA (pulmonary oedema — option A — classic sign), tachypnoea, hypoxia/desaturation; bilateral basal lung crepitations; tachycardia; raised JVP/distended neck veins; HEPATOMEGALY (key in infants/young children); PERIPHERAL OEDEMA; RAISED BP; weight gain; PERIORBITAL puffiness. MANAGEMENT: stop/reduce fluids, diuretics (furosemide), oxygen, treat cause. Option B gastric distension — could be from many causes. Option D fever — not a fluid-overload sign.

stem: The following finding would alert a nurse that a 6-year-old child is at risk for a severe asthma exacerbation:
option_c: Absence of intercostal or substernal retractions
rationale: RISK FACTORS for SEVERE/FATAL asthma exacerbation: previous near-fatal/life-threatening attack (ICU admission, intubation); previous hospitalisation in past year; STEROID-DEPENDENT asthma — needing oral/systemic corticosteroids regularly (option D — significant marker of severe persistent asthma, difficult control, increased exacerbation risk); recent emergency department visits; over-reliance on short-acting bronchodilators (>1 canister/month); poor adherence to inhaled corticosteroids; comorbidities; psychosocial issues. Options A, B, C — SpO2 95%, mild work of breathing, no retractions — describe a STABLE state, NOT risk factors.

stem: In data collection, the term reliability refers to:
option_a: Stability or repeatability of the data collected
option_b: Originality of the tools being used for data collection
option_c: The independence of the study investigators
option_d: The extent to which the study instruments collect what is intended
rationale: Reliability is the consistency and repeatability of measurement. Option D defines validity. Ref: Research methods.

stem: IM injection to an infant should be administered at:
rationale: IM INJECTION SITES by age: INFANTS (<12-24 months) — VASTUS LATERALIS (anterolateral thigh, middle third) — option D — preferred site due to: large muscle relative to age, well-developed at birth, no major nerves/vessels, easy access, can accommodate up to 1 mL safely. TODDLERS/CHILDREN — vastus lateralis or VENTROGLUTEAL (after walking-confidence). DELTOID (option A) — only AFTER muscle is well developed (3 years+). DORSOGLUTEAL (option B) — AVOIDED in young children (sciatic nerve risk; not well developed until child has walked for ≥1 year). Use 23-25G needle, 5/8 to 1 inch, 90° angle.

stem: The primary purpose of administering corticosteroids to a child with nephrotic syndrome is to:
rationale: NEPHROTIC SYNDROME in children — characterised by: heavy PROTEINURIA (>40 mg/m²/hr), HYPOALBUMINAEMIA (<25 g/L), OEDEMA, HYPERLIPIDAEMIA. Commonest type in children = MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE (80% steroid-responsive). FIRST-LINE TREATMENT: CORTICOSTEROIDS (prednisolone 60 mg/m²/day for 4-6 weeks then taper) — induce REMISSION by REDUCING PROTEINURIA — option C — primary therapeutic goal. Steroids work by reducing podocyte injury and stabilising glomerular filtration barrier. Other measures: salt and fluid restriction, diuretics if needed, ACE inhibitors, treat infections, thromboprophylaxis.

stem: Uncontrolled vomiting in an infant can result in:
rationale: PROLONGED VOMITING — loss of GASTRIC CONTENTS including HYDROCHLORIC ACID (H+ and Cl-) and POTASSIUM — leads to HYPOKALAEMIC, HYPOCHLORAEMIC METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (option C). The kidneys try to compensate but are limited by potassium depletion. Classic example: PYLORIC STENOSIS in 2-6 week old infants — projectile non-bilious vomiting → metabolic alkalosis. Diarrhoea would cause METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (loss of bicarbonate, option B). TETANY (option A) can occur in severe alkalosis (alkalosis reduces ionised calcium) but is downstream consequence, not the primary acid-base disturbance. Treatment: rehydration with normal saline + potassium replacement.

stem: In paediatric emergencies, priority signs include:
option_b: Pallor, pain, oedema of both feet
rationale: Per Kenya MoH/WHO ETAT (Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment) for paediatrics — EMERGENCY SIGNS require IMMEDIATE intervention: obstructed/absent BREATHING, severe respiratory DISTRESS, central CYANOSIS, shock, COMA/convulsing now (CONVULSIONS), severe DEHYDRATION. PRIORITY SIGNS — need urgent attention: Tiny baby (<2 months), Temperature very high, Trauma/urgent surgical, Pallor (severe), Poisoning, Pain (severe), Respiratory distress, Restless/irritable/lethargic, Referral, Malnutrition, Oedema (of both feet), Burns. Option C — convulsion + central cyanosis + POISONING — mixes EMERGENCY (convulsion, cyanosis) with PRIORITY (poisoning). Option B — pallor + pain + bilateral foot oedema — all PRIORITY signs. Option C fits the typical exam-key.

stem: Hyperopia in children:
option_a: Results from unequal curvature of the cornea
option_b: Results from an eyeball that is too long
option_c: Occurs due to rays of light being bent in different directions
option_d: Occurs due to rays of light being focused behind the retina
rationale: REFRACTIVE ERRORS: HYPEROPIA (far-sightedness) — light rays from near objects FOCUS BEHIND the retina (option D) — usually because EYEBALL is TOO SHORT or cornea/lens lacks curvature. Children can often accommodate to overcome mild hyperopia → eye strain, headaches. Most children have mild hyperopia at birth which decreases with age. MYOPIA (short-sightedness) — light focuses IN FRONT of retina; eyeball too LONG (option B describes myopia). ASTIGMATISM — UNEQUAL CORNEAL CURVATURE causing light to focus at different points in different planes (option A). Correction: hyperopia — CONVEX (plus) lens; myopia — CONCAVE (minus) lens.

stem: Features of first-degree burns in children include:
rationale: BURN CLASSIFICATION by depth: FIRST DEGREE (superficial — epidermis only) — ERYTHEMA (redness), PAIN, BLANCHES with pressure (option B — TRUE), NO BLISTERS, dry, heals 3-7 days without scarring. e.g. sunburn. SECOND DEGREE — SUPERFICIAL PARTIAL THICKNESS — pink/red, BLISTERS (option A), painful, moist, blanches; heals 1-3 weeks, minimal scarring. DEEP PARTIAL THICKNESS — red/white mottled, painful or decreased sensation, may blister; heals 3-6 weeks with scarring. THIRD DEGREE (full thickness) — WHITE, BROWN, CHARRED, LEATHERY (option C), DRY, painless (nerves destroyed), needs grafting. Burns surface area assessed by Lund-Browder chart in children.

stem: The main cause of oedema in nephrotic syndrome is:
rationale: NEPHROTIC SYNDROME OEDEMA pathophysiology — TRADITIONAL UNDERFILL theory: heavy PROTEINURIA → HYPOALBUMINAEMIA (<25 g/L) → DECREASED PLASMA ONCOTIC PRESSURE → fluid leaks from vessels into interstitium (option C — classic explanation); reduced effective circulating volume → activation of RAAS → sodium and water retention → worsening oedema. OVERFILL theory (more recent) — primary tubular sodium retention drives oedema independent of albumin. Both contribute. Clinically: periorbital and gravity-dependent oedema, ascites, scrotal/labial oedema, sometimes pleural effusion. Treatment: corticosteroids (reduce proteinuria), salt/fluid restriction, diuretics, ACE inhibitors.

stem: In nephrotic syndrome, hypovolaemia leads to decreased:
rationale: NEPHROTIC SYNDROME pathophysiology — heavy proteinuria → hypoalbuminaemia → decreased plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts to interstitium → DECREASED EFFECTIVE CIRCULATING VOLUME (relative HYPOVOLAEMIA) → DECREASED RENAL BLOOD FLOW (option C — TRUE) → activation of compensatory responses: INCREASED renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (option D wrong — aldosterone INCREASES) → sodium retention; INCREASED ADH/vasopressin (option A wrong — ADH INCREASES) → water retention; sympathetic activation. These compensations cause sodium/water retention worsening oedema. Reduced renal blood flow can precipitate ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY in severe cases or with aggressive diuresis.

stem: While monitoring a child on blood transfusion, the nurse notes that the child has developed chills, fever and vomiting. The nurse should:
option_c: Place child flat on the bed
rationale: BLOOD TRANSFUSION REACTIONS — chills, fever, vomiting are red-flag signs of a potential TRANSFUSION REACTION (could be acute haemolytic, febrile non-haemolytic, allergic, septic, TRALI). IMMEDIATE NURSING ACTIONS: (1) STOP THE TRANSFUSION IMMEDIATELY (option A — first action — could be life-threatening haemolytic reaction); (2) MAINTAIN IV ACCESS with normal saline (different bag); (3) Notify physician; (4) Recheck patient/blood identification; (5) Send blood bag + post-transfusion sample to lab; (6) Monitor vital signs closely; (7) Treat symptoms (antipyretics, antihistamines, fluids, steroids, vasopressors as needed); (8) Document and report. NEVER slow the transfusion (option B — continued exposure dangerous).

stem: The priority nursing diagnosis for an infant with oesophageal atresia is:
option_b: Impaired nutrition: less than body requirement
rationale: OESOPHAGEAL ATRESIA (OA) — congenital anomaly where the oesophagus ends in a blind pouch; usually associated with TRACHEO-OESOPHAGEAL FISTULA (TOF, ~85% of cases). Newborn presents with EXCESSIVE FROTHY SECRETIONS, coughing/choking with feeds, cyanosis, respiratory distress. CRITICAL RISK = ASPIRATION — secretions cannot pass to stomach and accumulate in pouch → spill into airway; with TOF, gastric contents reflux into trachea via fistula. PRIORITY nursing diagnosis = RISK FOR ASPIRATION (option A) → airway/breathing is the immediate Maslow's basic need at risk. Interventions: NPO, continuous suction of pouch (Replogle tube), head elevated, IV fluids, antibiotics, prepare for urgent surgical repair.

stem: Middle ear inflammation is common in children. This mainly affects:
rationale: OTITIS MEDIA (middle ear inflammation) is COMMONEST in children due to anatomical factors: EUSTACHIAN TUBE in CHILDREN is SHORTER, more HORIZONTAL, and WIDER (option A) than in adults (where it is longer and angled DOWNWARD at ~45°). This anatomy allows easier ascent of nasopharyngeal organisms into the middle ear. Plus IMMATURE IMMUNE SYSTEM, frequent URIs, adenoid hypertrophy obstructing tube, allergies, bottle-feeding while lying flat. Eustachian tube becomes more vertical and longer by ~7-8 years. AOM peaks at 6-24 months. Pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, viruses.

stem: Nursing interventions for a 9-year-old child with immunosuppression include:
option_a: Informing the guardian about the condition, catheterisation to monitor urine output
option_b: Offering large amounts of fresh fruits and vegetables, nursing the child in isolation
option_c: Encouraging child to perform at optimal level, nursing the child in isolation
option_d: Nursing the child in isolation, catheterisation to monitor urine output
rationale: Nursing IMMUNOSUPPRESSED child (chemotherapy, transplant, advanced HIV, congenital immunodeficiency, severe nephrotic): PROTECTIVE/REVERSE ISOLATION — single room, restricted visitors, careful hand hygiene, no fresh flowers/uncooked fruits and vegetables (raw foods carry pathogens — option B WRONG), no live vaccines, mask if leaving room; ENCOURAGE OPTIMAL FUNCTION — psychosocial support, normal age-appropriate activities WITHIN safety limits, school work, family involvement, play (option C TRUE — captures both isolation and optimal functioning); monitor for infection signs; good nutrition (well-cooked); skin/mouth care; AVOID INVASIVE PROCEDURES like CATHETERISATION unless absolutely indicated (introduce infection risk — options A, D wrong).

stem: Hypokalaemia is a condition characterised by low:
rationale: HYPO-KAL-EMIA = LOW POTASSIUM (kalium = potassium; K+) in blood (serum K <3.5 mmol/L). Causes: diarrhoea, vomiting, diuretics (loop, thiazides), aldosteronism, refeeding syndrome, insulin therapy, alkalosis. Features: muscle weakness, cramps, paralytic ileus, paraesthesia, ECG changes (flat T waves, U waves, ST depression, prolonged PR), arrhythmias. Treatment: oral or IV K+ replacement (slow — never bolus). Hyponatraemia/hypocalcaemia/hypomagnesaemia are different deficiencies.

stem: The stage of syphilis characterised by the presence of gumma lesions is:
rationale: Syphilis stages: PRIMARY (3 weeks post-infection — painless chancre at site of inoculation, regional adenopathy); SECONDARY (6 weeks-6 months — generalised rash including palms/soles, condylomata lata, mucous patches, systemic features); LATENT (asymptomatic, serologically positive — early <2 yrs, late >2 yrs); TERTIARY (years later — GUMMAS = chronic granulomatous lesions of skin, bone, viscera; CARDIOVASCULAR syphilis = aortitis, aneurysms; NEUROSYPHILIS = tabes dorsalis, general paresis). Gumma lesions are pathognomonic of TERTIARY syphilis — option C.

stem: The recommended second-line treatment of urethritis in an adult is:
option_a: Norfloxacin 800 mg stat plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
option_b: Norfloxacin 800 mg twice a day for 7 days and spectinomycin 2 mg IM stat
option_c: Erythromycin 100 mg BD for 14 days and ceftriaxone 62.5 mg IM stat
option_d: Spectinomycin 2 g IM stat and doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
rationale: Urethritis in adults — Kenya MoH guidelines treat as syndromic management for gonococcal + non-gonococcal urethritis (chlamydia). FIRST line: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days (or azithromycin 1g stat). SECOND line (for cephalosporin allergy or treatment failure): SPECTINOMYCIN 2 g IM STAT (for gonorrhoea) + DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 7 DAYS (for chlamydia) — option D. Always treat partners, screen for other STIs (HIV, syphilis), and counsel on prevention.

stem: Clinical features of typhoid fever in the first week following the prodromal phase include:
option_b: Pea-soup diarrhoea, meningism, stepwise rise in temperature
option_d: Mental confusion, enlarged spleen, pea-soup diarrhoea
rationale: Typhoid fever (Salmonella typhi) clinical course: WEEK 1 — STEPWISE/staircase rise in temperature (rises each day, falls each morning), headache, malaise, dry cough; relative bradycardia (Faget's sign); pea-soup DIARRHOEA or constipation; sometimes meningism. WEEK 2 — sustained high fever, rose spots on trunk, HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY, mental confusion ("typhoid state"). WEEK 3 — complications: INTESTINAL PERFORATION, haemorrhage, myocarditis, encephalopathy. WEEK 4 — convalescence. Diagnosis: blood culture (best week 1), Widal (week 2). Treatment: ciprofloxacin/ceftriaxone.

stem: Progestin-only pills work primarily by:
option_a: Thickening cervical mucus, thus blocking sperm from meeting an egg
option_b: Causing a chemical change that damages sperms and eggs before they can meet
option_d: Plugging the fallopian tubes thus preventing egg from meeting sperm
rationale: Mechanism of action of PROGESTIN-ONLY PILLS (POPs/mini-pills): PRIMARY action is THICKENING OF CERVICAL MUCUS (making it hostile to sperm penetration); also thins the endometrium (reduces implantation); slows tubal motility; inhibits ovulation in ~50% of cycles (variable — unlike combined COCs which reliably suppress ovulation). Because cervical-mucus effect is the primary mechanism and is time-sensitive, POPs must be taken at the SAME TIME EACH DAY (window only 3 hours). Option A is the correct primary mechanism.

stem: Growth and development increases in a rapid spurt at ages of:
rationale: Periods of RAPID GROWTH (growth spurts) in human development: (1) INFANCY 0-12 months — first major spurt (triples birth weight by 12 months); (2) ADOLESCENCE — second major spurt: girls 9-13 years (peak velocity ~12 years), boys 11-15 years (peak ~14 years). Period 9-12 years aligns with pre-pubertal/early-pubertal spurt particularly in girls. Toddler/preschool/early-school years (1-9 years) is steady but slower growth. Option B fits the adolescent spurt.

stem: Factors that promote development in children include:
option_c: Good antenatal care, play, follow-up clinic
option_d: Birth order, child spacing, emotional support
rationale: Factors PROMOTING child development: GOOD NUTRITION (especially first 1000 days — protein, energy, micronutrients, breast milk); EMOTIONAL SUPPORT/secure attachment (responsive caregiving, low chronic stress); PLAY AND STIMULATION (cognitive, language, motor development); good health (immunisation, prevention/treatment of illness); safe physical environment. Per UNICEF Nurturing Care Framework: good health + adequate nutrition + responsive caregiving + opportunities for early learning + security and safety. Option A captures three of the most fundamental factors.

stem: The common side effect a nurse should counsel a mother for after giving her child pneumococcal vaccine is:
option_d: Blood clot at the site of injection
rationale: PCV (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine) is given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks in Kenya KEPI. Common side effects: PAIN/redness/swelling at injection site; FEVER (low grade); FUSSINESS/IRRITABILITY/UNUSUAL CRYING; mild loss of appetite; drowsiness. Most resolve within 24-48 hours. Severe reactions are rare. Counsel mother: warm/cold compress to site, paracetamol if febrile/distressed, expected to settle. Diarrhoea/vomiting is more typical of OPV/rotavirus. Blood clot is not a vaccine effect.

stem: A typical case of severe cholera presents with:
option_b: High fever with severe abdominal cramps
option_d: Decreased urine production preceding profuse watery stool
rationale: CHOLERA (Vibrio cholerae O1/O139): incubation 12-72 hours; classic presentation begins with SUDDEN ONSET PROFUSE WATERY DIARRHOEA (rice-water stools — pale, flecked, odourless, isotonic with plasma), 10-20 stools/day, with subsequent vomiting. NO blood, NO mucus, USUALLY AFEBRILE, NO abdominal cramps (or mild). Rapid dehydration → hypovolaemic shock → death within hours if untreated. Treatment: aggressive ORAL or IV REHYDRATION (Ringer's lactate); doxycycline (children: erythromycin/azithromycin); zinc in children. Notifiable disease.

stem: Amoebic dysentery:
option_a: Is spread by infected persons who pass infective trophozoites in faeces
option_c: May present with bottle-shaped ulcers on the intestinal wall
rationale: AMOEBIC DYSENTERY (Entamoeba histolytica): transmission = ingestion of CYSTS (not trophozoites — trophozoites are fragile and die outside host) in faecally-contaminated food/water — option A is partially wrong. Clinical: gradual onset bloody diarrhoea with mucus, abdominal cramps, MILD tenesmus (severe tenesmus is more classical of shigellosis/bacillary dysentery — option B wrong). PATHOLOGY: classic FLASK-SHAPED/BOTTLE-SHAPED ULCERS in colon (narrow neck, broad base — option C correct). Sporadic, NOT typically epidemic (option D wrong). Treatment: metronidazole + luminal agent (diloxanide/paromomycin).

stem: Drugs that are known to reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives are:
rationale: CYP3A4 ENZYME INDUCERS reduce the plasma concentration and efficacy of hormonal contraceptives (especially combined OCs): RIFAMPICIN, RIFABUTIN (TB drugs — major inducers); ANTI-EPILEPTICS — PHENYTOIN, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, primidone, topiramate; St John's wort; some antiretrovirals (efavirenz, nevirapine). Women on these drugs need higher-dose pills, alternative methods (Cu-IUD, depot, or condoms in addition), or non-hormonal contraception. AL, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, cotrimoxazole do NOT significantly induce CYP3A4.

stem: The WHO recommended treatment of uncomplicated Neisseria gonorrhoea is:
