option_a: Benzyl penicillin 3g intramuscularly as a single dose
option_b: Ofloxacin 400 mg orally as a single dose
option_c: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly as a single dose
option_d: Azithromycin 1g orally as a single dose
rationale: WHO/Kenya STI guidelines for UNCOMPLICATED GONOCOCCAL infection: CEFTRIAXONE 250 mg IM stat (some current protocols 500 mg-1g due to rising MICs) — single dose. Often given WITH AZITHROMYCIN 1 g orally stat (dual therapy — covers chlamydia co-infection AND helps slow resistance). Older fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin) NO LONGER RECOMMENDED — widespread resistance. Penicillin no longer effective due to PPNG (penicillinase-producing N. gonorrhoeae). Always treat partners, screen for other STIs, counsel on prevention.

stem: A child aged 9-12 months is able to:
option_a: Stand without assistance and throw balls
option_b: Walk without support and grasp small objects with thumb and fingers
option_c: Enjoy imitation and take objects out of a container
option_d: Walk and can say some sentences
rationale: Developmental milestones at 9-12 MONTHS: motor — crawls well, pulls to stand, stands holding on, cruises (walks holding furniture), some take first independent steps by 12 m; FINE motor — pincer grasp (thumb-index), bangs objects together, places/removes objects from container; LANGUAGE — first words ("mama", "dada") with meaning, responds to name; SOCIAL/COGNITIVE — IMITATES SIMPLE ACTIONS (waves bye-bye, claps), object permanence, plays peekaboo, ENJOYS IMITATION. Option C is the most age-typical. Walking unsupported (B) and sentences (D) are older skills.

stem: Non-organic growth failure (failure to thrive) in a child may be attributed to:
option_a: A poor mother-child bond of attachment
option_b: Altered physiology due to improper feeding
rationale: FAILURE TO THRIVE (FTT) classifications: ORGANIC FTT — identifiable medical/physiological cause (malabsorption, congenital heart disease, chronic infection like TB/HIV, metabolic disorders, GORD, neurological problems); NON-ORGANIC FTT (often called "psychosocial" FTT) — caused by PSYCHOSOCIAL FACTORS — POOR MOTHER-CHILD ATTACHMENT/bonding, neglect, maternal depression, poverty, food insecurity, inadequate feeding practices. Treatment requires multidisciplinary approach — feeding support, social work, mental health support, child protection if abuse. Option A is the classic non-organic cause.

stem: The dosage of drugs in primary level ARV prophylaxis for prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV is:
option_a: Nevirapine (NVP) 200mg to mother at onset of labour, infant NVP 2mg/kg as soon as possible within 72 hours of delivery
option_b: Nevirapine (NVP) 200mg to mother during labour, infant NVP 2mg/kg immediately after birth plus 4 weeks of AZT 4mg/kg BD
option_c: AZT 300mg BD plus NVP 200mg to mother during labour, infant 2mg/kg after birth plus AZT 4mg/kg BD for one week
option_d: AZT 600mg to mother at onset of labour, infant NVP 2mg/kg immediately after birth
rationale: This question references OLDER PMTCT prophylaxis regimens (Option A/Option B/Option B+ ladder, pre-2014). Single-dose Nevirapine (sdNVP) to mother + infant was a primary regimen historically but had resistance concerns. CURRENT Kenya PMTCT (since 2014, Option B+ then "Treat All" 2016): LIFELONG TRIPLE ART for all HIV+ pregnant women regardless of CD4 (first-line: TDF/3TC/DTG or TDF/3TC/EFV). INFANT prophylaxis: NVP daily for 6 weeks (high-risk: up to 12 weeks) for breastfeeding HIV-exposed infants. The question represents historical knowledge; option B approximates the older Option B regimen.

stem: Emergency hormonal contraception is usually effective following unprotected sex when taken within a period of:
rationale: Emergency contraception (EC) options and time windows: LEVONORGESTREL 1.5 mg single dose — most effective within 72 hours but can be used UP TO 120 HOURS (5 days) with declining efficacy; ULIPRISTAL ACETATE 30 mg single dose — effective up to 120 hours with sustained efficacy; YUZPE METHOD (combined COCs) — within 72 hours, less effective and more side effects; COPPER IUD — most effective method (>99%), within 120 HOURS (5 days). The widest window ("120 hours") covers ulipristal and copper IUD — option A. Time matters — sooner is more effective.

stem: Immunisation schedule for Rotavirus vaccine is:
option_a: 2 mls orally at 6 weeks and 10 weeks
option_b: 1.5 mls IM at 10 weeks and 14 weeks
option_c: 2 mls IM at 10 weeks and 14 weeks
option_d: 1.5 mls orally at 6 weeks and 10 weeks
rationale: Kenya KEPI ROTAVIRUS VACCINE (Rotarix monovalent) schedule: TWO DOSES, 1.5 mL ORALLY (NOT IM) at 6 weeks AND 10 weeks of age. Must complete by 24 weeks (latest) to minimise intussusception risk. CONTRAINDICATIONS: severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), history of intussusception, prior severe allergic reaction. Mild gastrointestinal symptoms after vaccination are common. Option D: 1.5 mL orally at 6 and 10 weeks.

stem: An example of a contraceptive method that falls in category 4 of the medical eligibility criteria includes:
option_a: Combined oral contraceptives for women with thalassaemia
option_b: Implants for women with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
option_c: Progestin-only contraceptives for women with sickle cell disease
option_d: Intra-uterine contraceptive device for women with valvular heart disease
rationale: WHO MEDICAL ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA (MEC) categories: 1 = use without restriction; 2 = advantages outweigh risks (use); 3 = risks outweigh advantages (generally not recommended); 4 = UNACCEPTABLE HEALTH RISK - DO NOT USE. CATEGORY 4 examples: COCs in active breast cancer, active DVT/PE, smokers >35 years smoking >15/day, hypertension >160/100, severe cirrhosis, migraine with aura. IUCD in COMPLICATED VALVULAR HEART DISEASE (with pulmonary HTN, AF, history of subacute bacterial endocarditis) - CATEGORY 4 due to RISK OF BACTERIAL ENDOCARDITIS during insertion - option D. Uncomplicated valvular heart disease is Category 2.

stem: Normal developmental milestone for an infant aged 1 month include:
option_b: Follow object with eyes, play with hands
option_c: Lifts head when prone, often smiles
rationale: Developmental milestones at 1 MONTH: GROSS MOTOR - when prone, lifts head briefly (option C); turns head side-to-side; FINE MOTOR - strong grasp reflex (not voluntary grasp); LANGUAGE - coos, gurgles; SOCIAL - first SOCIAL SMILES (often) by 4-6 weeks (option C); fixates on faces; follows objects briefly. Voluntary grasping (3-4 months), playing with hands (3 months), good head control (4 months) - these are later. Option C - lifts head when prone + early smiling - fits 1-month milestone.

stem: A patient with asthma is having an acute attack. The nurse should administer:
option_a: Oral prednisolone as the first-line treatment
option_b: Salbutamol (albuterol) via nebuliser or inhaler as the first-line bronchodilator
option_c: Aminophylline IV as the first-line treatment
option_d: Ipratropium bromide alone as the first-line treatment
rationale: In acute asthma, SHORT-ACTING BETA-2 AGONISTS (SABA) — SALBUTAMOL (albuterol) — are the FIRST-LINE bronchodilator. Administer via metered-dose inhaler (MDI) with spacer (2–4 puffs every 20 minutes for 3 doses) or nebuliser (2.5–5 mg). Add ipratropium bromide (anticholinergic) for moderate-severe attacks. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone oral or hydrocortisone IV) are given early to reduce airway inflammation but take 4–6 hours to work. Aminophylline is a third-line agent for severe/life-threatening asthma. Oxygen to maintain SpO2 94–98%.

stem: A patient with heart failure is prescribed furosemide. The nurse should monitor for which electrolyte imbalance?
rationale: FUROSEMIDE is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, causing excretion of sodium, potassium, chloride, and water. The most important electrolyte to monitor is POTASSIUM — furosemide causes HYPOKALAEMIA (K+ <3.5 mmol/L). Hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity and causes cardiac arrhythmias, muscle weakness, and cramps. Management: potassium-rich diet (bananas, oranges, potatoes), potassium supplements, or potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone). Also monitor sodium, magnesium, and renal function.

stem: A patient with peptic ulcer disease is prescribed omeprazole. The mechanism of action of this drug is:
option_a: It neutralises gastric acid in the stomach
option_b: It blocks H2 receptors on parietal cells to reduce acid secretion
option_c: It inhibits the proton pump (H+/K+ ATPase) on parietal cells
option_d: It coats the ulcer to protect it from acid
rationale: OMEPRAZOLE is a PROTON PUMP INHIBITOR (PPI). It irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) on the luminal surface of gastric parietal cells — the final common pathway of acid secretion. This produces the most potent and sustained acid suppression of any drug class. PPIs are first-line for peptic ulcer disease, GORD, H. pylori eradication (triple therapy), and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. H2 blockers (ranitidine, famotidine) block histamine H2 receptors. Antacids (magnesium hydroxide) neutralise existing acid. Sucralfate coats the ulcer.

stem: A patient with a urinary tract infection (UTI) is prescribed trimethoprim. The nurse should advise the patient to:
option_a: Take the medication with antacids to reduce stomach upset
option_b: Complete the full course of antibiotics even if symptoms resolve
option_c: Stop the medication as soon as symptoms improve
option_d: Take the medication only when symptoms are severe
rationale: Antibiotic adherence is critical: patients must COMPLETE THE FULL COURSE of antibiotics even when symptoms resolve (usually within 1–2 days). Stopping early allows surviving bacteria (which may be more resistant) to multiply, causing relapse and contributing to antibiotic resistance. For uncomplicated UTI in women, trimethoprim is typically prescribed for 3–7 days. Advise: take at regular intervals, drink plenty of fluids, avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, and return if symptoms worsen or do not resolve within 48 hours.

stem: A doctor orders amoxicillin 500 mg. The available stock is amoxicillin 250 mg/5 mL suspension. How many mL should the nurse administer?
rationale: Drug calculation: Volume to administer = (Dose required / Dose available) × Volume of stock. = (500 mg / 250 mg) × 5 mL = 2 × 5 mL = 10 mL. Always use the formula: What you WANT / What you HAVE × Volume. Double-check: 10 mL of 250 mg/5 mL suspension contains 500 mg. Verify the calculation independently, check the patient's allergy status, and use a calibrated oral syringe for liquid medications.

stem: The recommended treatment for uncomplicated malaria in a non-pregnant adult in Kenya is:
option_c: Quinine 600 mg three times daily for 7 days
rationale: Kenya Ministry of Health guidelines: ARTEMETHER-LUMEFANTRINE (AL/Coartem) is the first-line treatment for UNCOMPLICATED MALARIA in non-pregnant adults and children. Dosing: 6 doses over 3 days (0, 8, 24, 36, 48, 60 hours), taken with food or milk (fat enhances absorption). Chloroquine resistance is widespread in Kenya — no longer first-line. Quinine is reserved for severe malaria or when AL is unavailable. SP (Fansidar) is used for Intermittent Preventive Treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) — not first-line treatment. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are WHO-recommended globally.

stem: The composition of WHO standard oral rehydration salts (ORS) solution includes:
option_a: Sodium chloride, potassium chloride, sodium bicarbonate, glucose
option_b: Sodium chloride, potassium chloride, trisodium citrate, glucose
option_c: Sodium chloride, calcium chloride, sodium bicarbonate, sucrose
option_d: Sodium chloride, magnesium sulphate, trisodium citrate, glucose
rationale: WHO/UNICEF standard ORS (reduced osmolarity, 2002 formulation): SODIUM CHLORIDE 2.6 g/L, POTASSIUM CHLORIDE 1.5 g/L, TRISODIUM CITRATE 2.9 g/L (replaced sodium bicarbonate — more stable), GLUCOSE (anhydrous) 13.5 g/L. Total osmolarity: 245 mOsm/L (reduced from 311 mOsm/L — reduces stool output and vomiting). Glucose drives sodium-glucose cotransport (SGLT1) in the intestine, facilitating sodium and water absorption even during diarrhoea. ORS is the cornerstone of diarrhoea management — prevents dehydration deaths.

stem: When administering oxytocin for induction of labour, the nurse should monitor for:
option_b: Uterine hyperstimulation and fetal heart rate changes
rationale: Oxytocin (Syntocinon) stimulates uterine contractions. Key monitoring during induction/augmentation: UTERINE ACTIVITY — contractions should not exceed 5 in 10 minutes (hyperstimulation/tachysystole); each contraction should last <90 seconds with adequate relaxation between. FETAL HEART RATE — continuous CTG monitoring for decelerations (late decelerations indicate fetal hypoxia). If hyperstimulation occurs: STOP the oxytocin infusion, position left lateral, give oxygen, notify the obstetrician. Also monitor maternal BP (oxytocin has antidiuretic effect — risk of water intoxication with high doses in large volumes of fluid).

stem: The recommended minimum number of antenatal visits for a low-risk pregnancy according to WHO 2016 guidelines is:
rationale: The WHO 2016 ANC model recommends a MINIMUM OF 8 CONTACTS for a positive pregnancy experience (replacing the older 4-visit focused ANC model). Contacts at: <12 weeks, 20 weeks, 26 weeks, 30 weeks, 34 weeks, 36 weeks, 38 weeks, and 40 weeks. Each contact includes clinical assessment, screening, health promotion, and supportive care. Kenya MoH has adopted this model. More contacts allow earlier detection of complications, better birth preparedness, and improved maternal and neonatal outcomes.

stem: The vaccine given to a pregnant woman to protect her newborn against neonatal tetanus is:
rationale: TETANUS TOXOID (TT) is given to pregnant women to protect both the mother and the newborn against tetanus. Maternal antibodies (IgG) cross the placenta and protect the neonate during the vulnerable neonatal period. Kenya MoH schedule: TT1 at first ANC contact, TT2 at least 4 weeks later, TT3 at least 6 months after TT2, TT4 at least 1 year after TT3, TT5 at least 1 year after TT4 (provides lifelong protection). Neonatal tetanus (tetanus neonatorum) results from contaminated cord cutting — a major cause of neonatal mortality in low-income settings.

stem: The most advantageous therapy for a preschool-aged child with a history of physical and sexual abuse would be:
rationale: PLAY THERAPY (Axline, Landreth) is the BEST therapy for PRESCHOOL/younger children (developmentally under ~10 years) who lack verbal/cognitive maturity for talk therapy. Play is the child's natural medium for expressing feelings and processing trauma. Used in abuse, parental separation, illness, behavioural problems. Materials: dolls, art, sand tray, puppets. Psychodrama suits older adolescents/adults; group therapy is generally not first-line for traumatised pre-schoolers.

stem: When plotting a child's weight on a growth chart, a weight-for-age below -3 SD (Z-score) indicates:
rationale: WHO Child Growth Standards Z-score interpretation for weight-for-age: Above -2 SD = NORMAL; Between -2 and -3 SD = MODERATE UNDERWEIGHT; Below -3 SD = SEVERE UNDERWEIGHT (also called severe acute malnutrition when combined with MUAC <11.5 cm or bilateral oedema). Growth monitoring using the Road to Health booklet (Kenya) plots weight monthly. Faltering growth (crossing centile lines downward) requires investigation and intervention. MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) <11.5 cm in children 6–59 months = severe acute malnutrition.

stem: The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding for:
rationale: WHO and UNICEF recommend EXCLUSIVE BREASTFEEDING for the first 6 MONTHS of life — no other food, water, or liquids (except oral rehydration salts, vitamins, or medicines when medically indicated). After 6 months, introduce nutritionally adequate complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond. Benefits of exclusive breastfeeding: optimal nutrition, passive immunity (IgA, lactoferrin), reduced risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, otitis media, SIDS, obesity, and diabetes. Breastfeeding also benefits the mother (uterine involution, reduced breast/ovarian cancer risk, natural child spacing).

stem: According to the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines, a child aged 2–59 months with a respiratory rate of 50 breaths per minute should be classified as having:
option_c: Severe pneumonia or very severe disease
rationale: IMCI fast breathing thresholds: <2 months: ≥60 breaths/min; 2–11 months: ≥50 breaths/min; 12–59 months: ≥40 breaths/min. A child aged 2–59 months with RR 50 breaths/min meets the threshold for FAST BREATHING → classified as PNEUMONIA. Treatment: oral amoxicillin for 5 days, follow up in 2 days. SEVERE PNEUMONIA signs: chest indrawing, stridor at rest, inability to drink/breastfeed, convulsions, abnormally sleepy → refer urgently, give first dose of IM/IV antibiotic. No fast breathing + no chest indrawing = no pneumonia (cough or cold — symptomatic treatment only).

stem: A 10-month-old child with diarrhoea has sunken eyes, a very dry mouth, and is not able to drink. This child should be classified as having:
rationale: IMCI dehydration classification: NO DEHYDRATION — no signs; SOME DEHYDRATION — two or more of: restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly/thirsty, skin pinch goes back slowly; SEVERE DEHYDRATION — two or more of: lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, NOT ABLE TO DRINK or drinks poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly (>2 seconds). This child has sunken eyes + unable to drink = SEVERE DEHYDRATION. Treatment: Plan C — IV Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg over 3 hours (infants) or 30 mL/kg in 30 min then 70 mL/kg in 2.5 hours. Reassess every 30 minutes.

stem: Physiological jaundice in a term newborn typically appears:
option_a: Within the first 24 hours of life
option_b: Between 2–3 days of life and resolves by day 10–14
option_d: At birth and persists for 6 weeks
rationale: PHYSIOLOGICAL JAUNDICE: appears on DAY 2–3 (never in the first 24 hours — that is always pathological), peaks on day 3–5, and resolves by DAY 10–14 in term infants (up to 3 weeks in preterm). Caused by: high fetal haemoglobin breakdown, immature hepatic conjugation (low UDP-glucuronosyltransferase), increased enterohepatic circulation. Bilirubin rarely exceeds 200 µmol/L. PATHOLOGICAL jaundice: appears <24 hours (haemolytic disease — Rh/ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency), bilirubin rises >85 µmol/L/day, or persists >2 weeks (conjugated — investigate for biliary atresia, hypothyroidism). Treatment: phototherapy, exchange transfusion for severe cases.

stem: The recommended age for introduction of complementary foods alongside breastfeeding is:
rationale: WHO/UNICEF recommend introducing COMPLEMENTARY FOODS at 6 MONTHS while continuing breastfeeding. Before 6 months, the infant's gut is immature and exclusive breastfeeding meets all nutritional needs. Starting too early increases risk of infections, allergies, and displaces breast milk. Starting too late causes growth faltering and micronutrient deficiencies. Complementary foods should be: timely (at 6 months), adequate (energy, protein, micronutrients), safe (hygienically prepared), and appropriately fed (responsive feeding). Introduce one new food at a time, starting with iron-rich foods (fortified cereals, pureed meat).

stem: The part of the brain responsible for coordinating voluntary movement and maintaining balance is the:
rationale: CEREBELLUM ('little brain') — located in the posterior fossa — coordinates VOLUNTARY MOVEMENT (smooth, precise), maintains BALANCE and POSTURE, and regulates MUSCLE TONE. Cerebellar damage causes: ataxia (unsteady gait), dysmetria (past-pointing), intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia (inability to perform rapid alternating movements), nystagmus, dysarthria. CEREBRUM — higher functions (thought, speech, sensation, voluntary movement initiation). MEDULLA OBLONGATA — vital centres (breathing, heart rate, BP, swallowing). HYPOTHALAMUS — temperature regulation, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythm, hormone control.

stem: The enzyme responsible for the initial digestion of starch in the mouth is:
rationale: SALIVARY AMYLASE (ptyalin) is secreted by the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual salivary glands. It begins STARCH DIGESTION in the mouth by breaking alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds, converting starch → dextrins → maltose. Activity continues briefly in the stomach until inactivated by gastric acid (pH <4). Pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion in the small intestine. PEPSIN (gastric) digests proteins. LIPASE (pancreatic/lingual) digests fats. TRYPSIN (pancreatic) digests proteins in the small intestine.

stem: The foremost aetiology of schizophrenia today is the:
rationale: Current understanding of SCHIZOPHRENIA aetiology is predominantly BIOLOGICAL: (1) GENETIC — strong heritability (~80%), polygenic; (2) DOPAMINE HYPOTHESIS (excess mesolimbic dopamine → positive symptoms; deficient mesocortical → negative symptoms), glutamate (NMDA hypofunction), serotonin; (3) STRUCTURAL brain changes — enlarged ventricles, reduced cortical/hippocampal volume; (4) Neurodevelopmental — perinatal complications, prenatal infections. Psychoanalytic theories (option D) of "schizophrenogenic mother" are LONG DISCREDITED.

stem: A patient who had abdominal surgery 3 days ago develops a temperature of 38.5°C, productive cough, and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base. The most likely complication is:
rationale: The "5 W's" of post-operative fever: Wind (days 1–2: atelectasis/pneumonia), Water (days 3–5: UTI), Wound (days 5–7: wound infection), Walking (days 5+: DVT/PE), Wonder drugs (any time: drug fever). On day 3 with fever, productive cough, and decreased breath sounds at the lung base, POST-OPERATIVE PNEUMONIA or ATELECTASIS (collapsed alveoli → secondary infection) is most likely. Risk factors: general anaesthesia, abdominal/thoracic surgery, immobility, pain limiting deep breathing. Prevention: early ambulation, incentive spirometry, deep breathing exercises, adequate analgesia. Treatment: physiotherapy, antibiotics if pneumonia confirmed.

stem: A patient with acute appendicitis has pain that started around the umbilicus and has now shifted to the right iliac fossa. This migration of pain is due to:
option_a: Spread of infection to the peritoneum
option_b: Involvement of the parietal peritoneum as inflammation progresses
rationale: Classic appendicitis pain migration: INITIAL PAIN — periumbilical/central (visceral pain — poorly localised, transmitted via T10 visceral afferents from the appendix). As inflammation progresses and involves the PARIETAL PERITONEUM overlying the appendix, pain MIGRATES to the RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA (McBurney's point — 1/3 of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus). Parietal peritoneal pain is well-localised, sharp, and worsened by movement. Rebound tenderness (Blumberg's sign) and guarding indicate peritoneal irritation. Rovsing's sign: pressure in LIF causes pain in RIF.

stem: The most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage is:
rationale: PRIMARY PPH (blood loss ≥500 mL within 24 hours of vaginal delivery, or ≥1000 mL after caesarean section) causes — the 4 T's: TONE (UTERINE ATONY — 70–80% of cases, most common cause), TISSUE (retained placenta/membranes — 10%), TRAUMA (lacerations of cervix, vagina, perineum — 10%), THROMBIN (coagulation disorders — rare). Uterine atony = failure of the uterus to contract after delivery. Risk factors: grand multiparity, overdistended uterus (twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia), prolonged labour, oxytocin augmentation, general anaesthesia. Prevention: AMTSL. Treatment: uterine massage, oxytocin, ergometrine, misoprostol, bimanual compression, surgical intervention.

stem: The definitive treatment for severe pre-eclampsia is:
option_c: Delivery of the baby and placenta
option_d: Corticosteroids to mature the fetal lungs
rationale: Pre-eclampsia is a placental disease — the only DEFINITIVE CURE is DELIVERY OF THE BABY AND PLACENTA (removal of the trophoblast). All other treatments (antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate, corticosteroids) are supportive measures to stabilise the mother and optimise fetal maturity before delivery. Delivery timing depends on gestational age and severity: severe pre-eclampsia at ≥34 weeks → deliver; <34 weeks → consider expectant management with close monitoring in a tertiary centre. Magnesium sulphate prevents/treats seizures but does not treat the underlying disease. Antihypertensives protect against stroke but do not cure pre-eclampsia.

stem: The first stage of labour is defined as:
option_a: From the onset of regular contractions to full dilatation of the cervix
option_b: From full dilatation of the cervix to delivery of the baby
option_c: From delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta
option_d: From the onset of contractions to delivery of the placenta
rationale: Stages of labour: FIRST STAGE — from onset of regular uterine contractions to FULL CERVICAL DILATATION (10 cm). Divided into: latent phase (0–4 cm, slow dilatation) and active phase (4–10 cm, ≥1 cm/hour). SECOND STAGE — from full dilatation to DELIVERY OF THE BABY (pushing phase). THIRD STAGE — from delivery of the baby to DELIVERY OF THE PLACENTA AND MEMBRANES (normally within 30 minutes; active management reduces to <5 minutes). FOURTH STAGE — first 1–2 hours after delivery (monitoring for PPH). The partograph is used to monitor progress in the first stage.

stem: When a cord prolapse is detected during labour, the nurse's immediate action is to:
option_a: Prepare the patient for immediate caesarean section
option_b: Manually push the cord back into the uterus
option_c: Elevate the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand and call for help
option_d: Apply a warm saline compress to the cord and wait for the obstetrician
rationale: CORD PROLAPSE management: the cord is compressed between the presenting part and the pelvis → fetal hypoxia → death within minutes. IMMEDIATE actions: (1) CALL FOR HELP (emergency team); (2) ELEVATE THE PRESENTING PART manually with a gloved hand inserted into the vagina — maintain this until delivery; (3) Position: knee-chest or Trendelenburg (gravity reduces pressure on cord); (4) Fill the bladder with 500–700 mL saline (lifts presenting part); (5) Keep the cord warm and moist (wrap in warm saline gauze — do not handle excessively); (6) EMERGENCY CAESAREAN SECTION unless vaginal delivery is imminent. Do NOT push the cord back — risk of vasospasm and injury.

stem: The direct causes of maternal mortality include:
option_b: Haemorrhage, sepsis, complications of induced abortion
rationale: DIRECT maternal deaths result from obstetric complications of the pregnancy state, interventions, omissions, or incorrect treatment. Classic direct causes: HAEMORRHAGE (antepartum and postpartum), SEPSIS (puerperal, septic abortion), HYPERTENSIVE DISORDERS (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia), OBSTRUCTED LABOUR (ruptured uterus), UNSAFE/COMPLICATIONS OF INDUCED ABORTION, embolism. INDIRECT causes = pre-existing diseases worsened by pregnancy: anaemia, malaria, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, cardiac disease. Option B names three pure direct causes.

stem: When dealing with addiction, the word "drug" means:
option_a: An illegal substance that activates the pleasure centre in the brain
option_b: A substance that activates the pleasure centre in the brain
option_c: A chemical that produces a pharmacological action when ingested
option_d: Any kind of pill that is broken down in the stomach by digestive action
rationale: In the context of ADDICTION, a "drug" = any SUBSTANCE (legal OR illegal) that ACTIVATES THE BRAIN'S REWARD/PLEASURE CENTRE (mesolimbic dopamine pathway, particularly nucleus accumbens). Includes ILLICIT drugs (cocaine, heroin), PRESCRIPTION drugs (opioids, benzodiazepines), LEGAL substances (alcohol, nicotine, caffeine). Option A restricts to illegal — incorrect (alcohol/nicotine are legal but highly addictive). Option B is the broadest, most accurate definition for addiction.

stem: Which of the following statements about birth polio and streptomycin is CORRECT?
option_a: Birth polio can be given at 3 weeks of age; streptomycin does NOT cause fetal deafness
option_b: Birth polio must be given within 2 weeks of birth; streptomycin can cause deafness to the unborn baby
option_c: Birth polio can be given at any time in the first 6 months; streptomycin can cause deafness to the unborn baby
option_d: Birth polio must be given within 2 weeks of birth; streptomycin does NOT cause fetal deafness
rationale: Per Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunisation (KEPI) schedule, BIRTH POLIO (OPV0) is given within the FIRST 2 WEEKS of life. After 14 days the birth dose is no longer effective and is skipped; the baby joins the routine schedule (OPV1 at 6 weeks). STREPTOMYCIN and other aminoglycosides (gentamicin, kanamycin) cross the placenta and are OTOTOXIC to the fetus, causing eighth nerve damage and SENSORINEURAL DEAFNESS. Therefore aminoglycosides are AVOIDED in pregnancy unless absolutely necessary.

stem: The prophylactic drugs given to a term new born at birth are:
option_a: 3% tetracycline eye ointment, vit. K 0.5mg i.m. stat
option_b: Gentamycin eye drops, vit K. i.m. stat
option_c: 1% tetracycline eye ointment, vit K, 1 mg i.m. stat
option_d: Gentamycin eye drop, vit. K 1 mg i.m. stat
rationale: Per Kenya MoH/WHO Essential Newborn Care: (1) EYE PROPHYLAXIS — 1% TETRACYCLINE EYE OINTMENT (or 0.5% erythromycin, or 2.5% povidone-iodine) applied to both eyes within 1 hour of birth — prevents ophthalmia neonatorum from gonococcal/chlamydial infection in the birth canal. (2) VITAMIN K — 1 mg IM stat (0.5 mg for preterm <1500 g) — prevents Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding (VKDB). (3) BCG and OPV0 vaccinations within first 14 days. Gentamicin drops are not used as prophylaxis (only for treatment of conjunctivitis).

stem: The causes of indirect maternal deaths include:
option_b: Malaria, diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease
option_d: Tuberculosis, road traffic accident, puerperal sepsis
rationale: INDIRECT maternal deaths result from pre-existing diseases or diseases that developed during pregnancy (not due to direct obstetric causes) but aggravated by pregnancy: MALARIA, ANAEMIA, HIV/AIDS, TUBERCULOSIS, DIABETES MELLITUS, CARDIAC DISEASE, SICKLE CELL DISEASE, hepatitis, epilepsy. DIRECT causes (= obstetric — haemorrhage, sepsis, eclampsia, obstructed labour, ruptured uterus, complications of abortion) are excluded. INCIDENTAL/coincidental causes = unrelated to pregnancy (e.g. RTA). Option B lists three classic indirect causes.

stem: The presumptive signs of second stage of labour include:
option_b: Rupture of the forewaters, expulsive uterine contractions
rationale: Second stage of labour (full dilatation to delivery of baby). Presumptive (suggestive but not diagnostic) signs include: RUPTURE of the forewaters (membranes), EXPULSIVE/bearing-down uterine contractions, urge to push, anal dilatation, gaping of the vulva, perineal bulging, appearance of the presenting part. The DEFINITIVE (positive) sign is full cervical dilatation (10 cm) on vaginal examination. Show and progressive dilatation are first-stage features.

stem: Following rupture of membranes during labour, drainage of golden yellow amniotic fluid could be due to:
option_d: Previous distress which the fetus overcame
rationale: Amniotic fluid colour: CLEAR = normal; GREEN/MECONIUM-STAINED = current or recent fetal distress; GOLDEN YELLOW ("old gold") = PREVIOUS fetal distress that the fetus has survived (old meconium that has been broken down/oxidised), or chronic placental insufficiency; PORT WINE/red-brown = abruptio placentae; YELLOW with brown flecks = rhesus iso-immunisation (haemolysis). The "golden yellow" colour is most associated with previous, resolved meconium staining — option D.

stem: When the sagittal suture is found in transverse diameter with both fontanelles palpable during vaginal examination, this is diagnostic of:
rationale: In DEEP TRANSVERSE ARREST (occipito-transverse position): the fetal head fails to rotate from the transverse to anterior/posterior position. On vaginal examination, the sagittal suture lies in the transverse diameter of the pelvis, and BOTH the anterior and posterior fontanelles are palpable (because the head is deflexed and neither pole has dropped below the level of the ischial spines). This is an abnormal labour pattern needing rotation (manual, vacuum or forceps) or caesarean section.

stem: The definite indications of elective caesarean section are:
option_a: Intrauterine growth retardation, antepartum haemorrhage, cephalopelvic disproportion
option_b: Placenta praevia type II posterior, cord presentation, diabetes mellitus
option_c: Fulminating pregnancy induced hypertension, diabetes mellitus, breech presentation in a primigravida
option_d: Placenta praevia Type III, cephalopelvic disproportion, multiple pregnancy with three or more fetuses
rationale: ABSOLUTE/DEFINITE indications for elective caesarean section: PLACENTA PRAEVIA TYPE III/IV (major praevia — completely covering the os); proven CEPHALOPELVIC DISPROPORTION (CPD); transverse lie; previous classical caesarean or uterine rupture; HIGHER-ORDER MULTIPLE PREGNANCY (triplets or more); some maternal cardiac/HIV conditions; active genital HSV. IUGR, APH, diabetes and breech are RELATIVE indications, not absolute. Cord PROLAPSE (not presentation alone) is an emergency CS indication.

stem: Presence of a hole in the membranes on examination of a placenta is indicative of:
rationale: SUCCENTURIATE PLACENTA: an accessory lobe of placental tissue lies separate from the main placenta, connected by blood vessels running through the membranes. After delivery, the main placenta is delivered but the succenturiate lobe may be retained — leaving a HOLE in the membranes (the spot where the vessels passed to the accessory lobe) and vessels ending mid-membrane. This is dangerous because the retained lobe causes postpartum haemorrhage and infection — must be manually removed. VELAMENTOUS = cord inserts on membranes; BATTLEDORE = cord at placental margin; BIPARTITE = two equal lobes joined by membranes.

stem: The general danger signs in a sick child include:
rationale: IMNCI general danger signs are: not able to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions (current or history), and lethargy or unconsciousness. Option B correctly lists three recognized IMNCI general danger signs. Ref: Kenya IMNCI guidelines (MOH Division of Child and Adolescent Health).

stem: The muscle layer of the uterus that contracts and retracts during labour to force the fetus into the receptive lower uterine segment is:
rationale: The myometrium has 3 layers: OUTER LONGITUDINAL (subserous) — fibres run from cervix up the front, over the fundus, down the back of the uterus — these CONTRACT and RETRACT during labour, shortening progressively to expel the fetus and create the upper segment; MIDDLE OBLIQUE (figure-of-eight around blood vessels) — "living ligatures" that compress vessels after delivery to control bleeding; INNER CIRCULAR — concentrated at internal os, holds the cervix closed in pregnancy. The endometrium is not muscle. Hence C for fetal expulsion.

stem: Puerperal sepsis should always be suspected when a mother has:
option_a: Foul smelling discharge, abdominal tenderness, adnexal tenderness
option_b: Septic wound, odourless discharge, urinary tract infection
option_c: Breast infection, urinary tract infection, abdominal tenderness
option_d: Maternal tachycardia, purulent discharge from genital tract, septic wound
rationale: PUERPERAL SEPSIS is infection of the genital tract within 42 days of delivery. WHO criteria for diagnosis include: fever ≥38.5°C, PELVIC PAIN, ABNORMAL/FOUL VAGINAL DISCHARGE (offensive lochia), abnormal uterine sub-involution, ABDOMINAL/UTERINE TENDERNESS, sometimes adnexal tenderness (if parametritis/salpingitis). Wound infection, mastitis and UTI are POSSIBLE sources of puerperal sepsis but are SEPARATE entities. Option A captures the diagnostic features of genital tract sepsis itself.

stem: The trophoblastic layer responsible for nourishing the growing organism during embedment process is:
rationale: During implantation (embedment, ~6-7 days post-fertilisation), the outer SYNCYTIOTROPHOBLAST invades the maternal endometrium, erodes maternal capillaries, and forms lacunae filled with maternal blood — this provides nutrients and oxygen to the developing embryo (haemotrophic nutrition). The syncytiotrophoblast is also the hormone-producing layer. The cytotrophoblast lies underneath and provides the cellular reservoir. Mesoderm and ectoderm are embryonic germ layers, not trophoblastic.

stem: Client Mi's weight is 50 kgs at 20 weeks gestation. At 36 weeks she will weigh approximately:
rationale: Expected weight gain in pregnancy averages ~0.5 kg/week from week 20 onwards. From 20 to 36 weeks = 16 weeks × 0.5 kg/week = ~8 kg gain. 50 + 8 = 58 kg minimum. The typical answer including the slightly higher rate during mid-pregnancy is ~10 kg gain = 60 kg. The exam-expected answer is B (60 kg), reflecting standard expected gain. Total pregnancy gain target ~11-16 kg for normal BMI.

stem: Mrs Ra, para 0+0 gravida 1 visits antenatal clinic with complaints of increased vaginal discharge. The specific intervention would include:
option_a: Advice her to bring her partner for investigations, perform urinalysis
option_b: Exclude possibility of infection, advice on hygiene
option_c: Advice her to start douching, commence antifungal treatment
option_d: Advice her to avoid tight inner wears, commence antibacterial therapy
rationale: Increased vaginal discharge in pregnancy is usually PHYSIOLOGICAL (leucorrhoea — from oestrogen-induced increased cervical mucus and vaginal transudate). The midwife should first EXCLUDE INFECTION (Candida, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, STIs — speculum examination, wet mount, high vaginal swab if indicated) and only treat if infection confirmed. ADVISE ON HYGIENE: cotton underwear, avoid douching (alters vaginal flora, predisposes to infection), avoid scented soaps. Empirical antifungal or antibacterial therapy without diagnosis is inappropriate.

stem: The importance of assessing the state of the cervix during labour is:
option_a: To determine adequacy of the pelvis
option_b: For accurate measurement of the cervix
option_d: To determine if the woman meets criteria for implementation of partogram
rationale: Per WHO/Kenya labour management, the PARTOGRAM (partograph) is started ONCE THE WOMAN IS IN ACTIVE PHASE of labour — defined by cervical DILATATION ≥ 4 cm (older criteria) or ≥ 5 cm (current WHO 2018 update) with regular contractions. Cervical assessment is therefore the gateway to partogram use. The partogram tracks progress (cervical dilatation, descent, contractions), fetal wellbeing (heart rate, membranes, moulding) and maternal wellbeing (pulse, BP, temperature, urine) and prompts action when alert/action lines are crossed.

stem: On diagnosis of fetal distress, the fluid of choice to administer is:
option_a: 1 litre of 5% dextrose for 30 minutes, then evaluate foetal well being
option_b: 500 mls of 10% dextrose for one hour, followed by 500 mls of normal saline
option_c: 1 litre of normal saline for 30 minutes, then evaluate foetal heart rate
option_d: 50 mls of 50% dextrose as bolus then 5% dextrose for two hours
rationale: INTRAUTERINE RESUSCITATION for fetal distress: position mother LEFT LATERAL (relieves caval compression), give 100% OXYGEN by mask, STOP oxytocin if running, give a CRYSTALLOID FLUID BOLUS — typically 1 LITRE OF NORMAL SALINE (or Ringer's lactate) over 20-30 minutes to improve uteroplacental perfusion. Treat hypotension. Re-evaluate fetal heart pattern; if no improvement, proceed to urgent delivery. Dextrose solutions are AVOIDED — they cause fetal hyperglycaemia, hyperinsulinaemia and neonatal hypoglycaemia/acidosis.

stem: Following administration of epidural anaesthesia during labour, the blood pressure should be recorded every:
option_a: 5 minutes for the initial 20 minutes, then at 15 minutes interval
option_b: 10 minutes for the first 2 hours, then half hourly
option_c: 15 minutes until the anaesthesia wears off
option_d: 10 minutes until the blood pressure reading is satisfactory
rationale: Epidural anaesthesia causes SYMPATHETIC BLOCKADE → vasodilation → hypotension (common in obstetric epidurals). Standard monitoring: BP every 5 MINUTES for the first 15-20 MINUTES after epidural insertion or top-up dose (the period of maximum risk of hypotension), then every 15 minutes thereafter. Continuous CTG monitoring. Pre-loading with 500-1000 mL crystalloid reduces hypotension risk. Treat hypotension with left lateral tilt, IV fluids, and ephedrine if needed.

stem: By 9th to 10th day postnatally the uterus is usually palpated:
option_b: Midway between umbilicus and symphysis pubis
rationale: Uterine INVOLUTION milestones: immediately after delivery — fundus at umbilicus; day 1 — 1 finger-breadth below umbilicus; descends approximately 1 cm (1 finger-breadth) per day. Day 7 — uterus at midway between umbilicus and symphysis pubis; DAY 10-14 — uterus has descended into the pelvis and is NO LONGER PALPABLE per abdomen. By 6 weeks postpartum it has returned to pre-pregnancy size. Persistent palpability beyond day 10-14 suggests SUB-INVOLUTION.

stem: Mrs. Wi a previous caesarean section mother para 2+0 gravida 3 comes to your health facility at 36 weeks gestation with complaints of intermittent right abdominal pain for three days. The probable diagnosis would be:
rationale: In a multipara with previous caesarean section, scar dehiscence/rupture is a major concern. PRESENTATION: scar tenderness — INTERMITTENT or persistent pain over the previous CS scar (lower abdomen, often right side or scar line); occurs late pregnancy or during labour; if untreated progresses to uterine rupture with maternal shock, fetal distress and death. "Impending rupture" is the warning phase — the woman is alert, vital signs may be normal, scar is tender. Action: urgent admission, IV access, blood preparation, monitor closely, plan elective/early CS.

stem: Which of the following statements about twin delivery management is CORRECT?
option_a: After delivery of the 1st twin, if presentation is cephalic, encourage pushing — TRUE; After 2nd twin, wait for placental separation before giving uterotonic — TRUE
option_b: After delivery of the 1st twin, if presentation is cephalic, encourage pushing — TRUE; After 2nd twin, wait for placental separation before giving uterotonic — FALSE
option_c: After delivery of the 1st twin, if presentation is cephalic, encourage pushing — FALSE; After 2nd twin, wait for placental separation before giving uterotonic — TRUE
option_d: After delivery of the 1st twin, if presentation is cephalic, encourage pushing — FALSE; After 2nd twin, wait for placental separation before giving uterotonic — FALSE
rationale: After delivery of the first twin: abdominal exam confirms longitudinal lie of twin 2; if cephalic and engaged, gentle pushing/oxytocin can establish contractions for vaginal delivery — TRUE. After delivery of the SECOND TWIN, OXYTOCIC (10 IU oxytocin IM or as IV infusion) is given IMMEDIATELY (with the anterior shoulder of the second twin or after delivery of the baby) — DO NOT wait for placental separation. Twin pregnancies have a markedly higher risk of PPH (due to overdistended uterus), so active management of the third stage with immediate oxytocics is mandatory — FALSE to wait.

stem: The immediate interventions following development of urine retention after delivery include:
option_a: Running tap water, sitting in a bath tub
option_c: Applying warm compresses on perineum, catheterization
option_d: Sitz bath, applying warm compresses on perineum
rationale: Postpartum urinary retention is common after vaginal delivery (perineal oedema/trauma, epidural effects, bladder atony). FIRST-LINE conservative measures: PRIVACY, AMBULATION, sounds of RUNNING WATER, warm SITZ BATH or warm COMPRESSES to the perineum (promote relaxation of perineal muscles and urethral sphincter), pouring warm water over the vulva while she tries to void, encouraging adequate oral fluids and timed voiding. If conservative measures fail → catheterisation (in-out or short-term indwelling). Option D captures the conservative first-line approach.

stem: The role of the midwife in relieving after pain during puerperium includes:
option_b: Encouraging bed rest, advising the mother not to breastfeed until pains reduce
option_d: Encouraging frequent urination, administering appropriate analgesics
rationale: Afterpains (uterine cramping during puerperal involution, particularly during breastfeeding due to oxytocin release) are managed by: APPROPRIATE ANALGESIA (paracetamol; mefenamic acid/ibuprofen are particularly effective for uterine cramps); FREQUENT URINATION (a FULL BLADDER displaces the uterus and worsens afterpains — keep bladder empty); ambulation is ENCOURAGED (improves involution, prevents DVT — not restricted); breastfeeding should CONTINUE (afterpains accompany breastfeeding but breastfeeding promotes involution). Most afterpains settle by day 4-5.

stem: The diameter of the pelvic brim that plays a role in determining the outcome of occipito posterior position is:
rationale: In occipito-posterior (OP) position, the fetal head occupies the SACROCOTYLOID DIAMETER (from the sacro-iliac joint to the iliopectineal eminence on the opposite side — about 9.5 cm) — narrow space. If this diameter is contracted, descent and rotation are impeded, leading to deep transverse arrest or persistent OP. The OBSTETRIC CONJUGATE (anteroposterior — sacral promontory to back of symphysis pubis, 11 cm) is the most important for ALL labours but not the specific one tested in OP. Hence the answer is D sacrocotyloid.

stem: The positive signs of pregnancy include:
option_a: Visualization of fetus by x-ray at 16 weeks, foetal heart sound by Doppler at 5+ weeks
option_b: Visualization of gestational sac by trans-vaginal ultrasound at 4-5 weeks, foetal heart sound by foetal scope at 20 weeks
option_c: Uterine souffle at 12-16 weeks, Braxton Hicks at 16 weeks
option_d: Visualization of foetal pulsation by trans-abdominal ultrasound at 5 weeks, foetal heart sound by foetal scope at 16+ weeks
rationale: POSITIVE (definitive) signs of pregnancy: (1) FETAL HEART AUSCULTATION — by Doppler from ~10-12 weeks, by Pinard fetal scope from 20-24 weeks; (2) FETAL MOVEMENTS palpable by examiner from ~20 weeks; (3) ULTRASOUND visualisation of GESTATIONAL SAC (4-5 weeks trans-vaginal, 5-6 weeks trans-abdominal) and fetal cardiac activity (from 6 weeks). Option B names two valid positive signs with correct timings. Uterine souffle and Braxton Hicks are PROBABLE signs, not positive.

stem: Mrs. Y comes for her first antenatal clinic. On history taking her last menstrual period was 25.4.2011. Her expected date of confinement will be:
rationale: NAEGELE'S RULE for calculating expected date of delivery (EDD): add 7 days to the first day of the last menstrual period, subtract 3 months, add 1 year. LMP = 25.4.2011. Add 7 days → 2.5.2011. Subtract 3 months → 2.2.2011. Add 1 year → 2.2.2012. By strict Naegele's rule, the correct date is 2.2.2012, option B.

stem: The definite indications for an episiotomy include:
option_b: Scarring from female genital cutting, foetal distress
rationale: RESTRICTIVE (definite) indications for episiotomy: maternal — RIGID/scarred PERINEUM (e.g., previous Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting), perineum about to tear catastrophically; fetal — FETAL DISTRESS requiring expedited delivery, shoulder dystocia (provides room for manoeuvres), instrumental delivery (forceps/vacuum). Episiotomy is NO LONGER routine for first delivery (WHO and Kenya MoH discourage routine episiotomy — restrictive use is associated with less perineal trauma overall). Option B lists two valid current indications.

stem: Mrs. K. begins to bleed heavily immediately after delivery of the baby. In sequence, your actions as a midwife would be:
option_a: Call for help, make rapid evaluation of Mrs K's general condition, massage uterus, give oxytocin 10 I.U.
option_b: Massage uterus give oxytocin 20 I.U, perform urinary bladder catheterization, take blood to rule out blood disorders
option_c: Call for help, perform urinary bladder catheterization, deliver placenta, examine birth canal
option_d: Start I.V. line with crystalloids, deliver placenta if in-situ, examine birth canal, give ergometrine 0.5mg I.V. stat
rationale: Immediate PPH management — systematic approach: (1) CALL FOR HELP (resuscitation requires a team); (2) RAPID ASSESSMENT (ABC — airway, breathing, circulation; vital signs; level of consciousness; estimated blood loss); (3) Determine the cause (4 Ts — TONE atonic uterus, TRAUMA lacerations, TISSUE retained placenta/clots, THROMBIN coagulopathy); for atonic uterus — UTERINE MASSAGE/bimanual compression, OXYTOCIN 10 IU IM/slow IV; ergometrine if oxytocin fails (CI in HTN); misoprostol; tranexamic acid; (4) IV access (2 large-bore), crystalloids, blood. Option A starts with the correct sequence.

stem: In the course of managing 2nd stage of labour, you realize that after delivery of the head, it tries to return in the vagina. Your immediate action in sequence would be:
option_a: Apply McRoberts Manoeuvre, perform episiotomy, apply supra-pubic pressure, apply Rubin's Manoeuvre, apply Woods Manoeuvre
option_b: Reassure the mother/partner summon for help, perform an episiotomy, change position of the mother, attempt Rubin's Manoeuvre
option_c: Summon for help, reassure Mother and partner, attempt change of position, apply McRoberts Manoeuvre, apply supra-pubic pressure
option_d: Summon for help, attempt Rubin's Manoeuvre, apply supra-pubic pressure, attempt Woods Manoeuvre, give an episiotomy
rationale: The "TURTLE SIGN" (head retracting against the perineum after delivery) is pathognomonic of SHOULDER DYSTOCIA. Management algorithm (HELPERR): H — Call for HELP (announce dystocia, recruit team); E — EVALUATE for episiotomy (consider but not always needed); L — LEGS into McRoberts (hyperflexion of thighs); P — Suprapubic PRESSURE; E — ENTER manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, reverse Woods); R — REMOVE the posterior arm; R — ROLL the mother to all fours (Gaskin). Option C most closely matches this sequence: summon help, reassure, position change, McRoberts, suprapubic pressure.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes fundal dominance in labour?
option_a: Contractions start at the lower uterine segment and spread upward
option_b: Contractions last longer and are more intense at the fundus, with the peak reached simultaneously over the whole uterus
option_c: Contractions are equal in intensity throughout the uterus
option_d: Contractions start at the fundus but are strongest in the lower uterine segment
rationale: FUNDAL DOMINANCE: contractions in normal labour BEGIN at the fundus, are STRONGEST AND LAST LONGEST at the fundus, but the contraction peaks SIMULTANEOUSLY across the whole uterus — this ensures the fundus pushes downward against the relaxed lower segment to deliver the fetus. RETRACTION RING: the physiological RIDGE marking the junction between the actively contracting/retracting UPPER UTERINE SEGMENT and the passively dilated LOWER UTERINE SEGMENT. If labour is obstructed, the upper segment becomes thicker and the ring rises abnormally high — the PATHOLOGICAL retraction ring of Bandl — warning sign of impending uterine rupture.

stem: In breech delivery the principle of hands off the breech as the baby progressively descends is to:
option_b: Allow enough room for the foetus to pass
option_c: Allow gravitating descent of the foetus
rationale: "HANDS OFF THE BREECH" (a cardinal principle of assisted vaginal breech delivery): the midwife/obstetrician does NOT pull on the baby's body once it has been delivered up to the umbilicus — TRACTION on the breech causes the head to extend, leading to head entrapment (NUCHAL ARMS) which is catastrophic. Instead the baby is allowed to deliver by maternal expulsive effort and gravity, with the operator's hands ready to perform specific manoeuvres only as needed (Lovset's for extended arms, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit/Burns-Marshall for the after-coming head). Avoid traction — option D.

stem: On abdominal examination during labour, the sinciput is felt and occiput just felt. The descent is:
rationale: Descent on abdominal palpation is recorded as how many FIFTHS of the fetal head are STILL palpable ABOVE the pelvic brim (0/5 = fully descended, 5/5 = floating). When ONLY the SINCIPUT is palpable (the occiput has descended below the brim and only "just felt" or not at all), the descent is 1/5 — most of the head is below the pelvic brim and engagement is complete. Used together with vaginal exam findings (station relative to ischial spines) to monitor labour progress on the partogram.

stem: On vaginal examination during labour, you elicit the following: Sagittal suture is in the left oblique diameter at the pelvis, occiput points to the right iliopectineal eminence. The position of the vertex presentation is:
rationale: Position is defined by the relationship of the OCCIPUT to the maternal PELVIS. The OCCIPUT points to the RIGHT ILIOPECTINEAL EMINENCE (right anterior) → RIGHT OCCIPITO-ANTERIOR (ROA) position. The sagittal suture lies in the LEFT oblique diameter (the diameter perpendicular to the line from right anterior to left posterior). ROA is a less favourable position than LOA (left occipito-anterior, the commonest position), but still permits vaginal delivery — the head usually rotates to OA before delivery.

stem: The maternal danger signs that a midwife should concern her/himself with during labour include:
option_a: Meconium stained liquor, falling blood pressure, abnormal lower abdominal contour
option_b: Pulse rate of 70-80 BPM, rising blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg, hyperactivity
option_c: Increasing apprehension, inadequate contraction, abnormal lower abdominal contour
option_d: Pathological retraction ring, falling blood pressure, meconium stained liquor
rationale: MATERNAL DANGER SIGNS in labour requiring urgent action: PATHOLOGICAL/BANDL'S RETRACTION RING (impending uterine rupture); FALLING BP (shock — APH, PPH, ruptured uterus); rising pulse, FEVER, abnormal abdominal contour (transverse lie, ruptured uterus), severe persistent abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, eclamptic seizures, severe headache/visual changes. MECONIUM-STAINED LIQUOR is primarily a fetal danger sign but also has maternal implications. Option D lists three classic maternal danger signs (ring, hypotension, meconium liquor).

stem: The humanistic theory of counselling was developed by:
rationale: Carl Rogers developed person-centred humanistic counselling. Maslow = humanistic psychology broadly; Ellis = REBT; Freud = psychoanalysis. Ref: Counselling theory; nursing education.

stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes cephalohaematoma from caput succedaneum?
option_a: Cephalohaematoma crosses suture lines and is present at birth; caput succedaneum is limited by suture lines
option_b: Cephalohaematoma is blood between the pericranium and skull, limited by suture lines; caput succedaneum is oedema of tissues superficial to the pericranium
option_c: Both cephalohaematoma and caput succedaneum are present at birth and cross suture lines
option_d: Caput succedaneum is blood between the pericranium and skull; cephalohaematoma is scalp oedema
rationale: CEPHALOHAEMATOMA: subperiosteal collection of BLOOD lying between the PERICRANIUM (periosteum) and the SKULL bone — therefore LIMITED BY SUTURE LINES (does not cross them), develops over hours after birth, firm, slow to resolve (weeks-months), may cause jaundice; rarely needs intervention. CAPUT SUCCEDANEUM: OEDEMA of soft tissues SUPERFICIAL to the pericranium (scalp tissue oedema from pressure during labour) — therefore CROSSES SUTURE LINES, present AT birth, soft and pitting, resolves in 1-3 days.

stem: The physical examination done on a newborn baby during a home visit on 3rd day of life includes:
option_a: Temperature, respiration, skin turgor and jaundice
option_b: Breast engorgement, weight gain, range of movement
option_c: Pus swab for culture and sensitivity, feeding pattern, wake and sleep pattern
option_d: Ecchymotic mark, colour and odour of stool, weight gain
rationale: Day-3 home visit newborn examination focuses on the COMMONEST PROBLEMS AT THIS AGE: TEMPERATURE (sepsis, hypothermia — leading neonatal killer), RESPIRATION (rate, retractions — pneumonia/sepsis signs), SKIN TURGOR/hydration (feeding adequacy, dehydration), JAUNDICE (physiological jaundice peaks day 3-5 — assess level/severity and look for danger signs); plus feeding, cord examination, eyes, weight. Option A lists the four core day-3 assessments.

stem: The Apgar score for the baby born at term with heart rate 110 bpm, gasping respiration, blue extremities, some flexion of limbs and minimal grimace at 1 minute is:
rationale: APGAR scoring (each 0, 1 or 2): APPEARANCE (skin colour) — blue extremities, body pink = 1; PULSE — HR 110 (>100) = 2; GRIMACE (reflex irritability) — minimal grimace = 1; ACTIVITY (muscle tone) — some flexion = 1; RESPIRATION — gasping (slow, irregular) = 1. Total = 1+2+1+1+1 = 6. APGAR 4-6 at 1 min = moderately depressed (needs resuscitation/stimulation); APGAR <4 severe depression; APGAR 7-10 normal.

stem: The amount of 3 hourly feeds appropriate for a baby whose weight is 1600 grams on day two is:
rationale: Preterm/LBW feeding (per Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols): Day 1 = 60 mL/kg/day; Day 2 = 80 mL/kg/day; Day 3 = 100; Day 4 = 120; Day 5 = 140; Day 6 = 150; Day 7+ = 160-180 mL/kg/day. Day 2 for 1.6 kg baby = 80 × 1.6 = 128 mL/day. 3-hourly feeds = 8 feeds/day = 128 / 8 = 16 mL per feed. Answer C.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes hereditary spherocytosis?
option_a: Caused by fragile red blood cells due to membrane protein defects
option_b: Caused by G6PD enzyme deficiency leading to oxidative haemolysis
option_d: Caused by iron deficiency leading to microcytic anaemia
rationale: HEREDITARY SPHEROCYTOSIS: defect in red-cell membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin) causes the RBC to assume a sphere shape — these spherocytes are osmotically fragile and trapped/destroyed in the spleen, causing haemolytic anaemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, gallstones. G6PD deficiency: X-linked enzyme deficiency; G6PD normally produces NADPH which MAINTAINS INTEGRITY of the RBC against oxidative stress; deficient cells haemolyse on exposure to oxidants (fava beans, primaquine, sulpha drugs, infection). Common cause of neonatal jaundice in Africa/Mediterranean.

stem: The common complications of a light for dates baby include:
option_a: Polycythaemia, congenital abnormalities, fetal alcohol syndrome
option_c: Twin to twin transfusion, asphyxia, poor temperature control
option_d: Polycythemia, meconium aspiration, twin to twin transfusion
rationale: Light-for-dates / small-for-gestational-age (SGA) babies (birth weight <10th centile) face the consequences of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and placental insufficiency: HYPOGLYCAEMIA (low glycogen stores), HYPOTHERMIA (low fat, large surface area), MECONIUM ASPIRATION (chronic hypoxia → in-utero passage of meconium), perinatal ASPHYXIA, polycythaemia (chronic hypoxia → ↑erythropoietin), INFECTION (reduced immune competence), poor feeding, increased mortality. Option B captures three core complications. Twin-twin transfusion is specific to monozygotic monochorionic twin pregnancies.

stem: A baby whose birth weight is 1800 gm is admitted in newborn unit with apnoeic attacks. The baby should be nursed in:
rationale: NEUTRAL THERMAL ENVIRONMENT: the range of environmental temperature at which the infant maintains normal body temperature with minimum metabolic oxygen consumption. For 1500-2000g preterm, the appropriate incubator temperature is ~31-33°C and room temperature ~28-30°C. The optimal incubator temperature is set BY weight and DAY OF AGE (the WHO/Kenya tables). The closest match for an 1800 g baby is option D — incubator 31-32°C and room 28-30°C. Aim to keep baby's axillary temperature 36.5-37.5°C.

stem: Side effects that a midwife should look for while nursing a baby under conventional phototherapy include:
option_b: Hypothermia, lethargy, alteration in neuro-behaviour organization
rationale: Side effects of PHOTOTHERAPY: thermoregulation problems (HYPOTHERMIA or hyperthermia — strip baby down but maintain warmth), increased insensible water losses (dehydration), loose stools (degraded bilirubin in gut), skin rashes, retinal damage (must cover eyes with patches), "BRONZE BABY syndrome" if conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, LETHARGY/sleepiness, ALTERED NEURO-BEHAVIOUR (irritability or lethargy, poor feeding), SEPARATION from mother (interferes with breastfeeding/bonding). Option B captures three recognised side effects.

stem: The infective stage of Taenia species is:
rationale: Humans acquire Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) or Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) by eating undercooked meat containing the cysticercus larva, which is the infective stage for the definitive host. The oncosphere/hexacanth is the form in the egg that infects the intermediate host. Rhabditiform is a hookworm/Strongyloides larval stage. Ref: Parasitology.

stem: The initial symptoms of lithium toxicity include:
option_b: Stiff neck, occipital headache and increased blood pressure
option_c: Ataxia, blurred vision and severe nausea
option_d: Fever, sore throat and cardiac arrhythmias
rationale: LITHIUM has a NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX (0.6-1.2 mEq/L; toxic >1.5 mEq/L). EARLY/MILD TOXICITY (1.5-2.0 mEq/L): COARSE TREMOR, nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea, slurred speech, ATAXIA, BLURRED VISION, drowsiness, muscle weakness — option C. MODERATE (2.0-2.5): confusion, dysarthria, hyperreflexia, clonus, marked ataxia. SEVERE (>2.5): seizures, coma, cardiac arrhythmias, renal failure, death. Risk factors: dehydration, NSAIDs/thiazides/ACE-inhibitors (reduce renal clearance), low sodium. Treatment: stop lithium, IV fluids, dialysis if severe.

stem: In acute mania a patient presents with:
rationale: ACUTE MANIA (DSM-5) — distinct period of abnormally elevated/expansive/IRRITABLE mood + INCREASED ENERGY, with ≥3 of: inflated self-esteem/grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas/racing thoughts, distractibility, PSYCHOMOTOR AGITATION/EXCESSIVE ACTIVITY, excessive involvement in pleasurable risky activities. Mood is often LABILE (not just cheerful — can be irritable/hostile). Thought process is DISORGANISED (flight of ideas — NOT organised, option D wrong). EXCESSIVE psychomotor activity (option B) is more specific and characteristic than just "increased" motor activity (option C).

stem: In narcissistic personality disorder there is a pervasive pattern of:
option_a: Social discomfort, fear of negative evaluation and timidity
option_b: Grandiosity, lack of empathy and hypersensitivity to evaluation by others
option_c: Dependence and submissive behaviour beginning by early adulthood
option_d: Indifference to social relationships and restricted range of emotional experience and expression
rationale: DSM-5 PERSONALITY DISORDERS (Cluster B — dramatic/erratic): NARCISSISTIC — pervasive pattern of GRANDIOSITY (in fantasy or behaviour), need for admiration, LACK OF EMPATHY, HYPERSENSITIVITY to criticism/evaluation, sense of entitlement, exploitative — option B. CLUSTER C: AVOIDANT (option A — social discomfort, fear of negative evaluation, timidity), DEPENDENT (option C — submissive, clinging). CLUSTER A: SCHIZOID (option D — detachment from social relationships, restricted emotion).

stem: Anonymity in research is aimed at:
option_b: Conferring protection to the source of information
option_c: Selectively disclosing information to specific individuals
option_d: Keeping names of respondents only known to the research supervisor
rationale: ANONYMITY = the researcher CANNOT LINK data back to the individual respondent — no identifying information collected or completely de-identified. PROTECTS the SOURCE/respondent from any consequence of their participation — option B. CONFIDENTIALITY = data may be identifiable but is protected from disclosure to others. Option D (names known to supervisor only) is closer to confidentiality, not anonymity. Both are pillars of research ethics under autonomy/respect for persons.

stem: The study design that is appropriate in observing the behaviour changes of drug addicts under rehabilitation is:
rationale: LONGITUDINAL design tracks SAME subjects OVER TIME — ideal for tracking CHANGES over the rehabilitation period (option B). PROSPECTIVE is similar but emphasises forward direction. CROSS-SECTIONAL = snapshot at one point in time — cannot show changes. RETROSPECTIVE = look back at past records. For tracking change over time during rehabilitation, longitudinal is the best fit.

stem: The total number of new cases of HIV infection reported in the month of March from X village was 50. This is referred to as:
rationale: EPIDEMIOLOGICAL MEASURES: INCIDENCE = number of NEW cases of disease arising in a defined population during a specified time period (e.g. 50 new HIV cases in March in X village). Used to study disease aetiology, evaluate prevention. PREVALENCE = TOTAL number of EXISTING cases (new + old) at a point in time - useful for chronic disease burden. MORBIDITY is a broader term for disease frequency. PANDEMIC = worldwide epidemic. The question describes new cases in a defined time period = INCIDENCE.

stem: The components of home-based care include:
option_b: Clinical care, nursing care, social support
rationale: HOME-BASED CARE (HBC) per Kenya MoH guidelines — CORE COMPONENTS: (1) CLINICAL CARE — medical management, symptom relief, palliative care, treatment monitoring; (2) NURSING CARE — wound care, hygiene, positioning, feeding; (3) PSYCHOSOCIAL/SOCIAL SUPPORT — counselling, family support, spiritual care, livelihood; (4) Referrals/linkages to formal health services. Option B — clinical + nursing + social support — captures three of these pillars. HBC team: patient, family caregiver, CHW, nurse, doctor, counsellor, social worker.

stem: The main reason for carrying out a home visit is to:
option_a: Meet the family at home and tell them how to solve their health problems
option_b: Assess social economic status and educational level of the family
option_c: Assess family structure and their health behaviour
option_d: Establish a working relationship with the family
rationale: The MAIN PURPOSE of home visiting in community health nursing is to ASSESS THE FAMILY IN THEIR NATURAL ENVIRONMENT — observing family structure, health behaviours, environment, resources, hygiene practices — option C. This enables individualised care planning. Other purposes: health education, continuity of care, follow-up of chronic patients, support for vulnerable groups. Establishing relationship (option D) is supportive but the OBJECTIVE is the assessment for care planning.

stem: In taeniasis infection, the adult worm lives in the:
rationale: TAENIASIS — infection with adult tapeworm (T. saginata — beef tapeworm, up to 10m; T. solium — pork tapeworm, up to 5m). ADULT WORM lives in the HUMAN SMALL INTESTINES (typically jejunum/ileum) — option C — attached by scolex to mucosa, releasing proglottids/eggs in faeces. Most adults are asymptomatic carriers; mild abdominal discomfort, weight loss, malnutrition possible. CYSTICERCOSIS occurs when humans ingest T. solium EGGS — autoinfection or faecal-oral. Treatment: praziquantel or niclosamide single dose.

stem: The main goal of the Kenyan Government in disaster management is to:
option_b: Take a leading role when disasters occur
option_c: Minimise losses and disruptions to the population and economy
option_d: Give early warning information on impending disasters
rationale: Per Kenya's National Disaster Management Policy and the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), the overarching goal of disaster management is to MINIMISE THE LOSS OF LIFE, PROPERTY AND DISRUPTION to the population, economy and environment — through a CYCLE of prevention, mitigation, preparedness (option A), response (option B), recovery, and rehabilitation. Early warning (option D) is a tool within preparedness. Option C — minimising losses and disruptions — captures the OVERARCHING goal.

stem: When using the 3-pot system for water purification, the water is considered safe for drinking after standing for:
rationale: THREE-POT SYSTEM for household water treatment: water is collected and progressively settles/disinfects through three pots over 48 HOURS. Pot 1 (today) - fresh water added; Pot 2 (yesterday's water) - being used currently; Pot 3 (2 days ago / 48-hour-old water) - at the end of the day this is transferred and used; refilled each day. The 48-hour standing allows sedimentation of particles, pathogen die-off, and water becomes safer to drink. A simple, low-cost intervention for rural settings. Should be combined with chlorination, boiling or SODIS for best safety.

stem: Babies of mothers on anti-TB treatment should not be immunised with BCG because:
option_a: Anti-TB drugs can neutralise BCG vaccine administered
option_b: The babies have low immunity which can make them develop tuberculosis
option_c: They can develop massive drug resistance
option_d: They are immune to TB due to maternal antibodies
rationale: BCG is a LIVE ATTENUATED bovine TB strain. If administered to a baby whose mother is on isoniazid/rifampicin (or whose baby is receiving INH preventive therapy), the anti-TB drugs WILL KILL/NEUTRALISE the live BCG organisms, preventing the desired immune response — option A. Approach: DELAY BCG until the infant has completed INH prophylaxis (3-6 months), then assess and give BCG if mother is TB-negative. The baby is NOT immune from maternal antibodies (option D wrong) — TB immunity is cell-mediated, not transferable transplacentally.

stem: Community mobilisation is the process:
option_a: In which the community is fully involved in identifying their problem and providing solutions
option_b: Of raising awareness on specific issues among community members
option_c: Of bringing members of the community together for the purpose of taking common action
option_d: Of moving the community members from a risky environment to a less risky one
rationale: COMMUNITY MOBILISATION = a comprehensive process where the community is FULLY INVOLVED in: (1) IDENTIFYING THEIR OWN PROBLEMS (assessing needs); (2) prioritising; (3) PROVIDING SOLUTIONS (planning interventions); (4) implementing and (5) evaluating — option A captures this empowerment model. Option B is awareness-raising (a tool within mobilisation but narrower); option C is bringing together for common action (a step in mobilisation); option D misinterprets "mobilisation" literally as physical movement. The defining feature is COMMUNITY OWNERSHIP and full participation throughout.

stem: An example of an intervention study design is:
rationale: STUDY DESIGNS by type: OBSERVATIONAL — researcher OBSERVES without intervening (cross-sectional, case-control, cohort); INTERVENTIONAL/EXPERIMENTAL — researcher INTRODUCES AN INTERVENTION: TRUE EXPERIMENT/RCT (with randomisation and control); QUASI-EXPERIMENT — has intervention and (often) control group but NO RANDOMISATION — option A. QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL examples: non-equivalent control group, interrupted time series, before-after with control. Useful when randomisation is unethical/impractical. EXPLORATORY, DESCRIPTIVE, EVALUATIVE are research PURPOSES, not specifically interventional designs.

stem: In longitudinal research, a cohort can be defined as a sample:
option_a: Chosen by certain criteria and followed up for a specified period
option_b: With shared characteristics like age or date of birth
rationale: COHORT (epidemiology) = a GROUP OF PEOPLE WHO SHARE A COMMON CHARACTERISTIC OR EXPERIENCE within a defined time period — typically BIRTH COHORT (same year of birth), exposure cohort, occupational cohort, disease cohort. Option B captures the defining feature — SHARED CHARACTERISTICS. Cohort STUDY = follow-up of such a group over time to determine incidence of outcomes. Option A describes follow-up of a sample but doesn't capture the SHARED CHARACTERISTIC essence.

stem: Descriptive research:
option_a: Refers to the direct study of people in their natural everyday settings
option_b: Systematically investigates relations between two or more variables of interest
option_c: Involves observation for a specific purpose to test cause and effect relation between variables
option_d: Involves collection of data that will provide an account of individuals, groups or situations
rationale: DESCRIPTIVE research = systematically COLLECTING and ORGANISING DATA to provide a detailed ACCOUNT/PICTURE of individuals, groups, situations or phenomena — answers "WHAT IS" rather than "WHY" — option D. Examples: prevalence surveys, KAP studies, case studies, situation analyses. Distinct from: ANALYTICAL/EXPLANATORY research (options B/C — examines RELATIONSHIPS and CAUSATION); ETHNOGRAPHIC research (option A — naturalistic study in cultural settings). Descriptive is foundational — basis for further analytical work.

stem: A measurable characteristic that assumes different values among subjects is referred to as:
rationale: VARIABLE = a CHARACTERISTIC that can take DIFFERENT VALUES across subjects/observations (height, age, blood pressure, disease status, sex). Types: INDEPENDENT (manipulated/exposure); DEPENDENT (outcome measured); CONFOUNDING (associated with both IV and DV — distorts relationship); EXTRANEOUS; MODERATING; mediator. OPERATIONAL DEFINITION = how a variable is measured in a specific study (option A, different concept). PARAMETER = population value (vs statistic = sample). STUDY UNIT = the individual subject/element studied.

stem: The following is associated with intussusception in a 2-year-old:
rationale: Intussusception classically presents with red-currant jelly (blood-stained, mucoid) stools, colicky abdominal pain and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass in the right upper quadrant. Projectile vomiting is characteristic of pyloric stenosis; ribbon-like stools suggest Hirschsprung disease. Ref: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols; paediatric surgical nursing.

stem: The following is true concerning observation as a research method:
option_a: It takes less time than self-report approaches
option_b: It costs less money than self-report approaches
option_c: It is often not possible to determine exactly why the people behave as they do
rationale: OBSERVATION as a research method — advantages: direct, no recall bias, captures non-verbal behaviour, natural setting, suitable for those who cannot self-report. DISADVANTAGES: (1) MORE time-consuming and EXPENSIVE than self-report surveys (options A, B WRONG — observation typically MORE time/money intensive); (2) OBSERVATION captures WHAT people do but NOT WHY (the underlying motivation, beliefs, emotions) — option C TRUE; (3) Hawthorne effect; (4) observer bias; (5) ethical issues with concealed observation. Option C is the true statement; D is wrong because A and B are false.

stem: When constructing a questionnaire one should:
option_d: Use multiple items to measure a single construct
rationale: QUESTIONNAIRE DESIGN — what to AVOID: LEADING/loaded questions (suggest desired answer — option A — AVOID); DOUBLE-BARRELLED questions (asking 2 things in 1 — option B — AVOID); double negatives (confusing — option C — AVOID); ambiguous terms; jargon. RECOMMENDED: clear simple language; one idea per question; balanced response options; USE MULTIPLE ITEMS TO MEASURE A SINGLE CONSTRUCT (option D — TRUE) — improves reliability/internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), captures different facets of complex concepts (e.g. depression scales use 10-21 items).

stem: When an extraneous variable systematically varies with the independent variable and influences the dependent variable, it is called:
rationale: TYPES OF EXTRANEOUS VARIABLES: CONFOUNDING variable — associated with BOTH the INDEPENDENT variable (exposure) AND the DEPENDENT variable (outcome), distorting the apparent relationship between them (option B). E.g. studying coffee → cancer, smoking is a confounder if smokers also drink more coffee. Must be CONTROLLED through randomisation, matching, restriction, or statistical adjustment. MODERATING variable (option C) — affects the STRENGTH/direction of the IV-DV relationship (interaction). MEDIATING variable — lies in the CAUSAL pathway between IV and DV.

stem: The following is necessary in obtaining informed consent for research:
option_a: A description of the statistical analyses that will be carried out
option_b: A description of the purpose of the research
option_c: A description of the reliability and validity of test instruments
option_d: A list of publications that the researcher has had in the last ten years
rationale: ELEMENTS OF INFORMED CONSENT (per Belmont Report, Helsinki, GCP): (1) PURPOSE of the research (option B — REQUIRED); (2) Procedures involved; (3) Duration/time commitment; (4) RISKS and DISCOMFORTS; (5) BENEFITS; (6) ALTERNATIVES; (7) CONFIDENTIALITY assurances; (8) Voluntariness — right to refuse/WITHDRAW anytime without penalty; (9) CONTACT info for questions; (10) Compensation/costs. Statistical analyses (option A), reliability/validity details (option C), researcher publications (option D) are NOT routinely required in lay-language consent forms.

stem: The following are high-level disinfectants:
rationale: DISINFECTANT CLASSIFICATION by Spaulding: HIGH-LEVEL disinfectants (HLD) — kill ALL microorganisms EXCEPT high numbers of bacterial spores: GLUTARALDEHYDE 2% (Cidex), ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA), HYDROGEN PEROXIDE 6-7.5%, PERACETIC ACID, hypochlorite at higher concentrations (CHLORINE/JIK at 5000 ppm or 0.5% concentration). Used for SEMI-CRITICAL items (endoscopes, respiratory equipment). INTERMEDIATE-level — phenolics like LYSOL, iodophors. LOW-LEVEL — QUATERNARY AMMONIUM — HIBITATE/chlorhexidine, ethanol. Option B — chlorine + Cidex + Jik (concentrated) — three high-level disinfectants.

stem: Tertiary phase of cancer prevention involves:
option_a: Asking people to stop smoking and ingestion of alcohol
option_b: Regular screening of people at risk of cancer diseases
option_c: Early and quick treatment for those diagnosed
option_d: Setting facilities with ionising radiation far from settlements
rationale: LEVELS OF CANCER PREVENTION: PRIMORDIAL — preventing the EMERGENCE of risk factors (option D — environmental/regulatory). PRIMARY — preventing CANCER from occurring in those at risk (option A — health promotion, lifestyle, immunisation). SECONDARY — early DETECTION through screening (option B — Pap smear, VIA/VILI, mammography). TERTIARY — preventing complications/disability/death once cancer is diagnosed — EARLY/PROMPT TREATMENT (option C — surgery, chemo, radiotherapy), palliative care, rehabilitation, prevention of recurrence.

stem: Crude birth rate (CBR) measures:
option_a: Number of births per 5000 population in a specified period
option_b: Number of newborns per 1000 mothers in a year
option_c: Number of births per 1000 population in a specified period
