option_d: Number of births in 100,000 populations in a year
rationale: CRUDE BIRTH RATE (CBR) = LIVE BIRTHS in 1 year / TOTAL MID-YEAR POPULATION × 1000 — option C. Reflects the OVERALL birth rate including non-childbearing population. Kenya CBR ~28/1000 (declining). GENERAL FERTILITY RATE = births / women 15-49 years × 1000 — more refined. TOTAL FERTILITY RATE = average number of children a woman would have if she went through her childbearing years at current age-specific fertility rates (TFR for Kenya ~3.4 per KDHS 2022). CRUDE DEATH RATE = deaths / population × 1000.

stem: The steps followed in carrying out a community diagnosis are:
option_a: Survey, exploration, develop pre-test tools and report writing
option_b: Developing pre-testing survey tools, exploration, plan time survey and report writing
option_c: Exploration, develop and pre-test tools, survey, report writing and dissemination
option_d: Develop and pre-test survey tools, execute the survey, exploration and report dissemination
rationale: COMMUNITY DIAGNOSIS STEPS in correct sequence: (1) EXPLORATION/situational analysis — preliminary visit, community entry, gather background info; (2) PLANNING — formulate objectives, choose methodology, determine sample, draft tools; (3) DEVELOP AND PRE-TEST INSTRUMENTS — questionnaires, checklists, FGD guides; pilot for clarity, reliability; (4) EXECUTION/SURVEY — data collection; (5) Data ANALYSIS; (6) REPORT WRITING; (7) DISSEMINATION to community and stakeholders; (8) ACTION PLANNING. Option C follows this correct sequence.

stem: The following are activities carried out during school health services EXCEPT:
rationale: SCHOOL HEALTH PROGRAMME activities (per Kenya MoH/MoEST): (1) HEALTH APPRAISAL/SCREENING — vision, hearing, dental, growth, nutrition; (2) IMMUNISATION catch-up, HPV vaccination for girls 10 years; (3) Deworming; micronutrient supplementation; (4) Treatment of minor ailments and FIRST AID; (5) REFERRAL of identified cases (option A — IS done); (6) HEALTH EDUCATION/MESSAGES (option C — IS done); (7) HEALTHY school ENVIRONMENT — water, sanitation, food safety, INSPECTION of premises (option B — IS done); (8) Mental health support. REHABILITATION OF HANDICAPPED CHILDREN (option D) is NOT typically a school health service — handled by specialised services. The "EXCEPT" answer = D.

stem: The following guidelines should be considered when choosing a site for a pit latrine EXCEPT:
option_a: Pit latrines and cesspools to be at least 3 metres above the water table
option_b: Latrines should be 6 metres away from buildings
option_d: Pit latrines should be at least 20 feet deep and 10 metres above water table
rationale: PIT LATRINE SITING GUIDELINES (per Kenya Public Health Act/MoH Sanitation): (1) Pit BOTTOM should be at least 1.5-3 METRES ABOVE highest WATER TABLE (option A — generally correct); (2) Distance from dwellings — at least 6 metres (option B — correct); (3) WELLS UPSTREAM (option C — correct); (4) Pit depth typically 2-3 metres (6-10 feet) — NOT 20 FEET; the 20-feet depth + 10-metre water-table specification in option D is INCONSISTENT and overly deep — practical pit latrines are not excavated 20 feet (~6 m). The "EXCEPT" answer = D — incorrect specification.

stem: The following are roundworms EXCEPT:
rationale: Helminth classification: NEMATODES (ROUNDWORMS) — ASCARIS LUMBRICOIDES (option A), ENTEROBIUS vermicularis (pinworm — option B), STRONGYLOIDES stercoralis (option C), Trichuris, hookworms, Wuchereria, Loa loa, Onchocerca, Trichinella. CESTODES (TAPEWORMS, flat segmented) — Taenia saginata, T. solium, Hymenolepis nana, Diphyllobothrium latum, ECHINOCOCCUS GRANULOSUS (option D — causes hydatid cysts — CESTODE not roundworm). TREMATODES (FLUKES) — Schistosoma, Fasciola, Clonorchis, Paragonimus. The "EXCEPT" = D.

stem: The following are true about rabies EXCEPT:
option_b: Presents with seizures in acute stage
option_c: Sensitivity to light presents in early stage
option_d: Death occurs within 3 days from onset of symptoms
rationale: RABIES CLINICAL COURSE: INCUBATION 1-3 months (range 4 days to >1 year); PRODROMAL phase 2-10 days (option A — TRUE) — fever, malaise, headache, paraesthesia/tingling at bite site, anxiety, sensitivity to light/photophobia (option C — TRUE); ACUTE NEUROLOGIC phase 2-7 days — furious (hyperexcitability, hydrophobia, aerophobia, hypersalivation, SEIZURES — option B TRUE) or paralytic; COMA and DEATH within 7-14 DAYS of symptom onset, NOT 3 days (option D FALSE — death takes longer than 3 days). The "EXCEPT" = D.

stem: Self-concept comprises of the following:
option_a: Body image, ego, and ideal self
option_c: Self image, body image and ideal self
rationale: SELF-CONCEPT (Stuart-Sundeen/Townsend framework) — the totality of how one perceives oneself. COMPONENTS: (1) BODY IMAGE — perception of one's physical self; (2) SELF-ESTEEM — overall evaluation of self-worth; (3) ROLE PERFORMANCE — how well one performs life roles; (4) PERSONAL IDENTITY — sense of who one is; (5) IDEAL SELF — perception of who one would LIKE TO BE; (6) EGO (Freudian — the executive of personality mediating id/superego/reality). Option A — body image + ego + ideal self — captures three core components. Self-concept disturbances underlie many psychiatric conditions.

stem: The psychological conceptual theory of psychiatric nursing assumes that:
option_a: Mental illness is as a result of altered levels of neurotransmitters
option_b: Abnormal behaviour is learnt and it can therefore be unlearnt
option_c: Mental illness originates from repressed feelings and experiences
option_d: Abnormal behaviour is as a result of poorly socialised superego
rationale: CONCEPTUAL/THEORETICAL MODELS in psychiatric nursing (Townsend): (1) PSYCHOANALYTIC/PSYCHODYNAMIC (Freud, Erikson, Sullivan) — focus on UNCONSCIOUS conflicts and REPRESSED FEELINGS/EXPERIENCES from past (especially childhood) — option C. (2) BEHAVIOURAL (Skinner, Pavlov, Bandura) — abnormal behaviour is LEARNED and can be UNLEARNED (option B — behavioural model). (3) COGNITIVE (Beck, Ellis) — thoughts → feelings → behaviour. (4) BIOLOGICAL/NEUROCHEMICAL (option A — neurotransmitter imbalance). The "psychological/PSYCHODYNAMIC" approach emphasises repressed feelings/conflicts.

stem: Dysthymia mood disorder:
option_a: Is a less severe form of chronic depression
option_b: Is diagnosed when a client has had a depressed mood for more than 3 years
option_d: Is treated using psychoanalysis and group therapy
rationale: DYSTHYMIA / PERSISTENT DEPRESSIVE DISORDER (DSM-5) = a CHRONIC, LESS SEVERE form of depression — depressed mood for MOST of the day, more days than not, for ≥ 2 YEARS (not 3 — option B wrong) in adults (1 year in children/adolescents), plus ≥2 of: poor appetite/overeating, insomnia/hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness. Option A — TRUE description. Treatment: SSRIs/SNRIs (first-line antidepressants), psychotherapy (CBT, interpersonal therapy) — NOT primarily ECT (option C — reserved for severe/treatment-resistant major depression).

stem: In mild mental retardation (MR) there is:
option_a: IQ of 50-70, the child is educable and can live independently
option_b: IQ is 35-50, the child is trainable and only speaks few words
option_c: IQ is 20-34, child is unable to have structured living but is trainable
option_d: IQ is below 20, child unable to relate verbally but can live independently
rationale: INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY severity (DSM-IV based on IQ): MILD — IQ 50-70 (option A) — "EDUCABLE" — can achieve basic academic skills (up to 6th grade), live and work INDEPENDENTLY with support, often go undetected in early childhood; comprise ~85% of intellectual disability cases. MODERATE — IQ 35-49 (option B) — "TRAINABLE" — basic communication and self-help, supervised work, sheltered employment. SEVERE — IQ 20-34 (option C) — limited speech, requires significant support. PROFOUND — IQ <20 — minimal communication, requires total care (option D wrong in saying can live independently). DSM-5 emphasises adaptive functioning over IQ alone.

stem: Milieu therapy includes:
option_a: Providing a supportive environment for positive adaptation and personal growth
option_b: Teaching skills of everyday living to improve a patient's general performance
option_c: Use of various recreational activities to meet patient treatment goals
option_d: Focusing on the here and now interactions rather than repressed childhood experiences
rationale: MILIEU THERAPY ("therapeutic environment/community" — Maxwell Jones) = USE OF THE PHYSICAL AND SOCIAL ENVIRONMENT OF THE WARD/UNIT as a THERAPEUTIC TOOL — providing a SUPPORTIVE, SAFE, STRUCTURED ENVIRONMENT that promotes POSITIVE ADAPTATION, recovery and PERSONAL GROWTH (option A) — captures the essence. Key principles: safety; clear structure and rules; therapeutic relationships; group activities; community meetings; patient involvement in unit management; consistency; respect; modelling healthy interactions. Option B describes OCCUPATIONAL therapy/life-skills training; option C describes RECREATIONAL therapy; option D describes a focus on PRESENT (here-and-now therapies, e.g. Gestalt).

stem: The mode of action of antipsychotics includes:
option_a: Blockage of dopamine receptors in the brain
option_b: Stimulation of serotonin receptors in the brain
option_c: Blockage of adrenaline and noradrenaline receptors
option_d: Stimulation of dopamine receptors in the brain
rationale: ANTIPSYCHOTICS — mechanism: BLOCKADE OF DOPAMINE D2 RECEPTORS in the mesolimbic pathway (responsible for positive symptoms — hallucinations, delusions) — option A. TYPICAL (first-generation) — chlorpromazine, haloperidol, fluphenazine — strong D2 blockade, more EPS (extrapyramidal side effects — Parkinsonism, dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia), hyperprolactinaemia. ATYPICAL (second-generation) — risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine, aripiprazole — block D2 AND 5-HT2A serotonin, fewer EPS, but more metabolic side effects (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia). NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME (NMS) — rare, life-threatening — fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness.

stem: Principles of PHC are:
rationale: PRINCIPLES of PRIMARY HEALTH CARE (Alma Ata 1978): EQUITABLE distribution - services accessible to all; APPROPRIATE TECHNOLOGY - scientifically sound, acceptable, affordable, locally feasible; COMMUNITY participation; INTERSECTORAL coordination - health works with education, agriculture, housing, water; FOCUS ON PREVENTION; HUMAN POWER/MANPOWER DEVELOPMENT - training appropriate cadre at appropriate level. Option A lists 3 of these principles.

stem: The correct order of community mobilisation steps:
option_c: Making reinforcement, community entry, planning, conducting
rationale: COMMUNITY MOBILISATION STEPS in sequence: (1) COMMUNITY ENTRY - establish rapport with gatekeepers (chief, religious leaders, opinion leaders), introduce purpose, get permission/acceptance; (2) PLANNING - together with the community identify needs, set objectives, plan activities, mobilise resources; (3) CONDUCTING/IMPLEMENTING - execute planned activities with community involvement; (4) MONITORING AND EVALUATION - track progress against objectives, document outcomes; (5) reinforcement and sustainability. Option B follows the correct order.

stem: Absorption of iron is enhanced by:
rationale: IRON ABSORPTION enhancers and inhibitors: ENHANCERS - VITAMIN C (ascorbic acid - in citrus fruits, guavas, dark green vegetables) - converts ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous (Fe2+) form which is better absorbed; ANIMAL PROTEINS (haem iron well absorbed). INHIBITORS - TEA AND COFFEE (tannins/polyphenols form insoluble complexes with iron); CALCIUM (milk, dairy, antacids); PHYTATES (whole grains, legumes); fibre; ANTACIDS (reduce gastric acidity needed for iron solubility). Counsel: take iron 1 hour BEFORE OR 2 hours AFTER meals (especially dairy/tea/coffee/antacids), with vitamin C source (orange juice).

stem: Green tags in disaster management means:
option_b: Victims can wait up to 3 hours
option_c: The victims can wait up to 1 hour
rationale: DISASTER TRIAGE TAGS (START system): RED = IMMEDIATE - life-threatening but salvageable - treat first; YELLOW = DELAYED - serious but stable, can WAIT UP TO 1 HOUR for treatment; GREEN = MINOR/WALKING WOUNDED - can wait several hours (commonly up to 3 hours per some protocols) - least urgent; BLACK = EXPECTANT/DECEASED - no signs of life, or unsurvivable injuries given current resources. Option B - 3-hour green-tag waiting time - is a common quoted figure for minor injuries.

stem: The first step when organising a school health programme is:
option_d: Establishing partnerships between teachers and health workers
rationale: ORGANISING A SCHOOL HEALTH PROGRAMME - sequence: (1) GATHERING INFORMATION/BASELINE ASSESSMENT - situational analysis of school (number of pupils, current health status, existing facilities, problems, environment); without this baseline, planning is uninformed; (2) Stakeholder engagement and partnerships (teachers, parents, MOH, NGOs); (3) Awareness creation; (4) Joint planning with stakeholders; (5) Implementation; (6) Monitoring and evaluation. Option B - information-gathering - should always precede planning.

stem: Community health:
option_a: Is concerned more with health of individuals
option_d: Can be affected by education levels
rationale: COMMUNITY HEALTH: focuses on health of GROUPS/COMMUNITIES (not just individuals - option A wrong); emphasises HEALTH PROMOTION, PREVENTION - not just curative (option B wrong); CLOSELY RELATED TO public health/population health/community medicine - overlapping concepts (option C wrong); influenced by SOCIAL DETERMINANTS - EDUCATION level, income, housing, employment, gender etc. (option D TRUE). Educated communities have better health-seeking behaviour, lower fertility, better nutrition.

stem: Elements of culture include:
rationale: ELEMENTS OF CULTURE: VALUES (shared ideas about what is good/desirable); BELIEFS (ideas about reality, including religious beliefs); NORMS (rules and expectations - folkways, mores, taboos, laws); SYMBOLS and language; MATERIAL CULTURE (artefacts, technology); ROLES; rituals/customs; arts; social institutions (family, religion, education). Option B - VALUES, BELIEFS, ROLES - captures three core non-material elements of culture.

stem: Socio-economic factors that have a bearing on health include:
rationale: The classic SOCIO-ECONOMIC DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH include: EDUCATION (literacy, health-seeking behaviour, child survival); HOUSING (overcrowding, ventilation, sanitation — affecting TB, ARI); FOOD AND NUTRITION (security and quality); income, employment, occupation; access to safe water; gender; culture and beliefs. Live birth and blood test are individual outcomes/investigations, not socio-economic determinants. Option C — housing + education + food — captures three core socio-economic determinants.

stem: The type of immunity a child acquires after receiving measles vaccine is:
rationale: Types of acquired immunity: NATURAL ACTIVE — from infection (e.g. having measles); NATURAL PASSIVE — transplacental IgG, breast milk; ARTIFICIAL ACTIVE — VACCINATION (immune system makes its own antibodies in response to vaccine antigen) — applies to measles vaccine — option B; ARTIFICIAL PASSIVE — immunoglobulin (e.g. rabies, tetanus immunoglobulin). Measles vaccine = artificial active immunity because the child's own immune system is stimulated to produce antibodies and memory cells.

stem: Vaccine potency can be maintained in the refrigerator by:
option_a: Placing vaccines in the correct compartments, defrosting the refrigerator regularly, ensuring the maintenance of ideal temperature of 0° to 8°C
option_b: Defrosting the refrigerator regularly, packing vaccines with enough space in-between to allow circulation of air, opening refrigerator only when necessary
option_c: Avoiding contact of vaccines with evaporator, regulating the thermostat regularly, lining frozen icepacks in the inner walls of the refrigerator
option_d: Ensuring the maintenance of ideal temperature of between +2° to +8°C, lining frozen icepacks in the inner walls of the refrigerator, placing vaccines in the correct compartments
rationale: KEPI cold-chain standards: vaccines stored at +2 to +8°C in the refrigerator (NOT 0-8°C — freezing damages DPT, Hib, Hepatitis B, Pentavalent, PCV); ice packs lined in inner walls (cold-life buffer for power outages); BCG and measles in TOP shelf; OPV in middle; DPT/HepB/Penta on lower shelf (AWAY from evaporator/freezer); cold-chain monitor (VVM); never re-freeze freeze-sensitive vaccines (Shake test). Option D lists the correct temperature range (+2 to +8°C) with proper storage practices.

stem: Deficiency of vitamin B1 (Thiamine) leads to:
option_a: Heart failure, abnormal nerve and brain function, emotional disturbances
option_b: Rupture of red blood cells, muscle spasm, bleeding
option_c: Night blindness, heart failure, impaired sensory perception
option_d: Emotional disturbances, rupture of red blood cells, nerve damage
rationale: Thiamine (Vit B1) deficiency causes BERIBERI: WET beriberi — cardiovascular (high-output HEART FAILURE, peripheral oedema, dilated cardiomyopathy); DRY beriberi — neurological (peripheral polyneuropathy, paresthesia, weakness, foot drop — ABNORMAL NERVE AND BRAIN FUNCTION); CEREBRAL beriberi (Wernicke-Korsakoff in alcoholics) — confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, memory loss (EMOTIONAL DISTURBANCES). Sources: whole grains, legumes, pork. Risk groups: alcoholics, infants of malnourished mothers, polished-rice diets, hyperemesis gravidarum. Option A captures all three manifestations.

stem: The occupational disease that persons working in information technology are likely to develop is:
rationale: Occupational diseases by sector: IT/clerical/repetitive keyboard work — CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME (median nerve compression at wrist from repetitive movements — numbness, tingling, weakness in thumb/index/middle fingers); also neck/back pain, computer vision syndrome. Lead poisoning — battery workers, painters. Radiation sickness — radiographers, nuclear workers. Mesothelioma — asbestos-exposed workers (mining, construction, insulation). Carpal tunnel is the classic IT-related occupational disease.

stem: The principle of unity of command in any organisation is important because:
option_a: The superior is able to assign part of his job domain to his/her subordinate, thus avoids overworking
option_b: It avoids divided loyalty since each employee receives orders from one superior
option_c: Employees are self-disciplined and self-controlled, so require very little supervision
option_d: It ensures smooth working at all levels of the organisation
rationale: Fayol's 14 PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT: UNITY OF COMMAND = each employee should receive orders from ONLY ONE SUPERIOR — avoids conflicts, divided loyalty, confusion, contradictory instructions. Distinct from UNITY OF DIRECTION = all activities working toward same objective should have one head and one plan. Option B captures the essence — single line of authority preserves accountability and clear loyalty. This principle is fundamental to classical management theory and remains relevant in nursing management.

stem: Which of the following is correct? (a) According to Douglas McGregor's Theory X, an employee will exercise self-discipline and self-control in certain circumstances. (b) When reprimanding an employee, the supervisor should avoid arguments and listen carefully to all comments.
rationale: (a) FALSE — McGregor's THEORY X assumes employees DISLIKE work, AVOID responsibility, NEED COERCION, threats and CLOSE SUPERVISION (because they will NOT exercise self-discipline). THEORY Y is the opposite — assumes employees enjoy work, are self-motivated, seek responsibility and exercise self-control. So self-discipline belongs to Theory Y, not X. (b) TRUE — effective reprimanding: be private, factual, prompt, listen carefully to the employee's perspective, avoid arguments, focus on behaviour not personality, end positively. Option B: (a) FALSE and (b) TRUE.

stem: Methods of food preservation which inhibit multiplication of bacteria include:
rationale: Food preservation methods: KILL bacteria — pasteurisation, canning, irradiation, sterilisation. INHIBIT MULTIPLICATION (bacteriostatic) — DRYING (removes water — pathogens need water), FREEZING (low temperature halts enzymatic and microbial activity), SMOKING (combination of dehydration and antimicrobial chemicals from smoke); SALTING (high osmotic pressure draws water out of microbes). Blanching is a brief pre-treatment, not preservation per se. Option D — all three INHIBIT multiplication without necessarily killing. Pasteurisation and canning KILL bacteria, so options A, B, C are incorrect.

stem: The goals of triaging in disaster management are:
option_a: Early patient assessment, control infection, determination of urgency of need of care
option_b: Document initial patient assessment, teach health care to the patient, notify care providers of incoming patients
option_c: Obtain past history records if needed, teach health care to patient, control infection
option_d: Brief overall patient assessment, control the flow of patients and visitors, take phone calls regarding incoming patients
rationale: TRIAGE (French for "to sort") in disasters/emergencies: rapid INITIAL ASSESSMENT of all incoming casualties, DETERMINING URGENCY of treatment, prioritising those most likely to benefit from limited resources. Standard triage categories (e.g. START): RED (immediate, life threats); YELLOW (delayed — serious but stable); GREEN (minor — "walking wounded"); BLACK (expectant/deceased). Also includes infection control, identification and documentation. Option A — early patient assessment + infection control + determination of urgency — captures the three core goals.

stem: A tooth cavity that gets close to or reaches the pulp causes:
option_a: Pain only when one drinks something cold or eats candy
option_b: Sensitivity to the tooth when one bites
option_c: Lingering pain even after a stimulus (e.g. cold water) is removed
option_d: Swelling due to pus in the adjacent gum
rationale: Dental caries progression: ENAMEL caries (superficial) = no symptoms or transient cold/sweet sensitivity that resolves immediately. DENTIN caries = sharper pain to cold/sweet, brief, resolves on removal of stimulus. PULPAL involvement (PULPITIS) — early reversible = transient sensitivity; LATE/IRREVERSIBLE PULPITIS = LINGERING PAIN after the stimulus is removed (sometimes spontaneous, throbbing), heat-aggravated — needs root canal or extraction. PERIAPICAL ABSCESS = gum swelling with pus — option D. Option C correctly describes irreversible pulpitis.

stem: Primary Health Care activities at the district level are co-ordinated by the:
rationale: Per Kenya health system structure, at the DISTRICT (now COUNTY/sub-county) level, the DISTRICT HEALTH MANAGEMENT TEAM (DHMT) coordinates all health activities — chaired typically by the District Medical Officer of Health, but it is a TEAM (DMOH, nursing officer, public health officer, pharmacist, finance officer, health records officer, etc.) that collectively coordinates planning, supervision, monitoring, and implementation. The DHMT is the operational coordinating body for PHC at district level. With devolution, equivalent bodies are at sub-county level (SCHMT) and County Health Management Team (CHMT).

stem: Activities of the pre-visit phase of home visiting include:
option_a: Sharing information on reason and purpose of visit with the family, gathering information on the location of the house, assessing the family needs and planning nursing care with them
option_b: Recording important events about the family, gathering some information on need of visit, introducing oneself to the family
option_c: Gathering information on the location of the house, gathering some information on need of visit, assembling supplies needed for the visit
option_d: Investigating community resources, establishing nurse-patient relationship, transferring the client to another nurse for care
rationale: Phases of HOME VISITING: (1) PRE-VISIT — REVIEW CLIENT RECORDS/find out client/family background, GATHER INFORMATION on the need and purpose of visit, plan objectives, contact family to schedule visit, ASSEMBLE SUPPLIES (home-visiting bag with relevant equipment), get directions/LOCATION of house, transport arrangements. (2) IN-HOME (initiation) — greet, introduce self, establish rapport. (3) IMPLEMENTATION — assessment, intervention, health education. (4) TERMINATION — summary, plan next visit. (5) POST-VISIT — DOCUMENTATION, plan follow-up. Option C lists three classic pre-visit activities.

stem: Community diagnosis is carried out:
option_a: With active participation of members of the community
option_b: With active participation of the leaders in the community
option_c: With active participation of health workers only
option_d: By strictly looking at medical problems
rationale: COMMUNITY DIAGNOSIS (community health assessment) is the process of identifying the health status, needs and priorities of a community. The KEY PRINCIPLE is ACTIVE COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION — community members must be partners in identifying their own problems, ranking priorities, and developing solutions (per Alma Ata declaration). Health workers facilitate and bring technical expertise but the process is community-led. Community diagnosis goes beyond medical problems to encompass SOCIAL, ENVIRONMENTAL, ECONOMIC determinants.

stem: Incidence rate:
option_a: Is used to record protracted diseases
option_b: Shows the magnitude/burden of disease in the community
option_c: Is useful for planning and administration of health care services
option_d: Shows the rate of development of disease in the community
rationale: INCIDENCE RATE = (number of NEW cases occurring in a defined population over a specified time period) / (population at risk during that period). Measures the RATE OF DEVELOPMENT of new disease cases — useful for ACUTE diseases, outbreak detection, and epidemiology research. PREVALENCE (option B) = total cases existing at a point — shows burden — useful for chronic diseases and service planning. Incidence is preferred for studying causation and acute disease dynamics.

stem: A special consideration for immunocompromised persons regarding immunisation is that:
option_a: Asymptomatic HIV-infected children should not receive BCG vaccine
option_b: Live vaccines can safely be given to persons on corticosteroid therapy
option_c: Asymptomatic children infected with HIV should receive all standard KEPI vaccines
option_d: Pentavalent vaccine can be administered to a child with neurologic disease so long as they are monitored closely
rationale: Per Kenya MoH PMTCT and KEPI guidelines for HIV-EXPOSED/INFECTED children: ASYMPTOMATIC HIV-INFECTED CHILDREN should RECEIVE ALL STANDARD KEPI VACCINES at the routine times (including LIVE vaccines — BCG, OPV, measles) — the benefits outweigh the risks. SYMPTOMATIC HIV infection or severe immunosuppression — DEFER live vaccines (BCG, OPV, measles, yellow fever). Persons on high-dose corticosteroids — DEFER live vaccines. Children with progressive neurological disease — defer pertussis-containing (DPT/Penta) until stable. Option C is the correct general rule for asymptomatic HIV.

stem: The following is associated with intussusception in a 2-year-old:
rationale: Intussusception classically presents with red-currant jelly (blood-stained, mucoid) stools, colicky abdominal pain and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass in the right upper quadrant. Projectile vomiting is characteristic of pyloric stenosis; ribbon-like stools suggest Hirschsprung disease. Ref: Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols; paediatric surgical nursing.

stem: When constructing a septic tank for 15 users, the recommended dimensions are:
option_a: Length 300 cm, Breadth 60 cm, Width 150 cm
option_b: Length 200 cm, Breadth 60 cm, Width 100 cm
option_c: Length 360 cm, Breadth 60 cm, Width 160 cm
option_d: Length 450 cm, Breadth 60 cm, Width 150 cm
rationale: Per Kenya public health/environmental health design standards, a septic tank for 15 users is typically designed using formulae based on daily sewage production (~120 L/person) and required retention time (~24 hours), plus sludge storage capacity. Standard dimensions for ~15-user household septic tank: LENGTH ~3 m (300 cm), BREADTH ~0.6 m (60 cm), DEPTH/WIDTH ~1.5 m (150 cm). Length:breadth ratio typically 2:1 to 3:1; depth 1.5-2 m. Two-chamber design for solids settling and liquid effluent.

stem: A child who presents with widening of the wrists, recurrent pneumonia and has prominent costochondral joints is likely to have:
rationale: VITAMIN D DEFICIENCY in children → RICKETS. Classic clinical features: WIDENED WRISTS AND ANKLES (epiphyseal widening); RACHITIC ROSARY (prominent costochondral junctions); pigeon-chest, Harrison's sulcus; bowed legs/knock knees (genu varum/valgum); craniotabes; delayed dental eruption; SHORT STATURE/delayed milestones; muscle weakness; RECURRENT CHEST INFECTIONS (PNEUMONIA — soft chest wall and weak muscles). Causes: lack of sunlight exposure, dietary deficiency, malabsorption, dark skin, breastfed beyond 6 months without supplementation. Treatment: vitamin D + calcium supplementation.

stem: Measurement of the mid-upper arm circumference is performed:
option_a: When the child's age is under one year
option_b: With or without a weighing scale
option_c: As a screening method for in-patients
rationale: MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) is a quick, simple, low-tech NUTRITIONAL SCREENING tool. Best used in CHILDREN 6-59 MONTHS for screening acute malnutrition. WHO/Kenya cut-offs: <11.5 cm = SEVERE acute malnutrition (red zone); 11.5-12.5 cm = moderate (yellow); ≥12.5 cm = normal (green). Used in FIELD SURVEYS, mass screening, mother-led screening ("family MUAC"), and emergency settings — IDEAL where weighing scales and height boards are impractical. NOT specifically for under-1s (used 6-59 months); CAN be done without scale (its strength); used both inpatient and outpatient.

stem: When managing accidental exposure to body fluids and possible HIV infection after a needle prick, the action that should be taken in correct sequence is:
option_a: Wash the wound under running water with soap, take emergency ARVs, undergo HIV test
option_b: Take emergency ARVs, wash the wound under running water with soap, undergo HIV test
option_c: Wash the wound under running water with soap, undergo HIV test, take emergency ARVs
option_d: Undergo HIV test, wash the wound under running water with soap, take emergency ARVs
rationale: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) protocol for needlestick injury: (1) IMMEDIATE FIRST AID — encourage bleeding (don't squeeze tissue), WASH the wound thoroughly with SOAP AND RUNNING WATER for several minutes; irrigate eyes with saline if eye exposure; (2) RISK ASSESSMENT — type of exposure, source patient HIV/HBV/HCV status; (3) Source patient HIV test (with consent); EXPOSED PERSON BASELINE HIV TEST; (4) Start PEP if indicated (within 72 hours, ideally 1-2 hours) — TDF/FTC + DTG for 28 days; (5) Follow-up HIV testing at 6 weeks and 3 months. Option C reflects this sequence: wash → test → PEP.

stem: Controlling function in management involves:
option_b: Determining philosophy and goals, managing action
rationale: MANAGEMENT FUNCTIONS (Fayol/POSDCORB): PLANNING (philosophy, goals, objectives — option B); ORGANISING (structures, grouping — option D); STAFFING (recruiting, interviewing, orientating — option C); DIRECTING/LEADING (motivating, supervising, communicating); CONTROLLING (monitoring performance against standards) — includes PERFORMANCE APPRAISAL, QUALITY MANAGEMENT/audits, budget monitoring, taking corrective action — option A. Controlling closes the feedback loop and ensures organisational goals are being met.

stem: After the Alma Ata Declaration, three elements of primary health care that were added in Kenya are:
option_b: Mental health, HIV and AIDS, dental health
option_c: Mental health, provision of essential drugs, HIV and AIDS
option_d: Mental health, provision of essential drugs, immunisation
rationale: Original 8 ELEMENTS of PHC (Alma Ata 1978): Education on health problems, Locally endemic disease control, MCH including family planning, Essential drugs, Nutrition, Treatment of common conditions, Sanitation and safe water, Immunisation. Kenya added 3 more (totalling 11): MENTAL HEALTH, DENTAL HEALTH, HIV AND AIDS — option B. Some references also cite community-based rehabilitation. Immunisation and essential drugs are part of the original 8, not added.

stem: Community participation in organisation of health services in ascending order includes:
rationale: LADDER/CONTINUUM OF COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION (ascending — lowest to highest involvement): (1) INFORMATION (one-way — community told what's happening); (2) CONSULTATION (community asked for views — final decision elsewhere); (3) DISCUSSION/dialogue (two-way exchange, community input considered); (4) PARTNERSHIP/joint decision; (5) FULL CONTROL/empowerment (community decides and acts). Lowest = tokenism; highest = empowerment. Option D correctly orders: information → consultation → discussion → full control.

stem: Specific functions of school health include:
option_a: Conducting special screening programs, treatment of cases by teachers and school nurse
option_b: Determining the health status of each child, continuously appraising changes in health status of a child
option_c: Continuously appraising changes in each child, case management of a sick child
option_d: Determining the health status of each child, case management of a sick child
rationale: SCHOOL HEALTH PROGRAMME functions (per Kenya MoH/MoEST): (1) school HEALTH ASSESSMENT/screening — DETERMINING HEALTH STATUS at entry and periodically; (2) CONTINUOUS MONITORING — APPRAISING CHANGES in health, growth and development; (3) immunisation catch-up; (4) deworming, micronutrient supplementation; (5) treatment of minor ailments; (6) health education (life skills, hygiene, nutrition, SRH); (7) healthy school environment (sanitation, water); (8) referral. Option B captures the surveillance functions of school health most accurately.

stem: Primary prevention of occupational health care hazards includes:
option_a: Emphasis on first aid to minimise complications
option_b: Dealing with substances inhaled or contracted because of employee's poor attitudes
option_c: General screening of non-occupational illness before a person is hired
option_d: Screening of the working environment to check that recommended preventive measures are put in place
rationale: Levels of prevention applied to occupational health: PRIMARY = preventing disease from occurring — workplace hazard identification/assessment, ENGINEERING controls, administrative controls (job rotation, shorter shifts), PPE, employee training, ENVIRONMENTAL SCREENING/monitoring of workplace (noise, dust, chemicals — option D). SECONDARY = early detection and treatment — periodic medical examination, biological monitoring. TERTIARY = preventing complications and disability after disease — rehabilitation, return-to-work, first aid (option A is tertiary, not primary). PRE-EMPLOYMENT screening (option C) is more selection/baseline, not prevention.

stem: An example of a disease that does not pass from human to human is:
rationale: Modes of disease transmission: HUMAN-TO-HUMAN (communicable) — TB (airborne droplets), diphtheria (respiratory droplets), measles, cholera, HIV, etc. ARTHROPOD VECTOR-borne (often human-to-human via vector) — malaria (anopheles), dengue (aedes), trypanosomiasis (tsetse). ENVIRONMENTAL (NOT human-to-human) — TETANUS (Clostridium tetani spores in soil/dust enter via wounds — no human-to-human transmission), botulism, brucellosis (animal source). Tetanus is the only one in the list that is acquired from the ENVIRONMENT (soil), not from another human.

stem: In the treatment of tuberculosis "DOT" means:
option_a: Patient getting TB treatment as close to home as possible
option_b: Patient adheres to treatment during the intensive phase only
option_c: Directly observed treatment with weekly monitoring
option_d: Patient takes every drug dosage under supervision during the intensive phase
rationale: DOT = DIRECTLY OBSERVED TREATMENT — a TB treatment strategy where a trained observer (health worker or trained treatment supporter) WATCHES THE PATIENT SWALLOW EVERY DOSE of anti-TB medication, especially during the INTENSIVE PHASE (first 2 months — 2HRZE). Continuation phase (4HR) is usually self-administered with periodic follow-up. DOT improves adherence, reduces relapse, prevents drug resistance, and is one of the five elements of WHO's DOTS strategy (commitment, case detection by smear, DOT, drug supply, monitoring). Option D is most precise — every dose under supervision during intensive phase.

stem: All health care services and activities within the district are monitored and supervised by the district:
rationale: The DISTRICT HEALTH MANAGEMENT TEAM (DHMT) is the multidisciplinary body coordinating, monitoring and supervising ALL district-level health services and activities. Chaired by DMOH but it is a team (DMOH, DNO, DPHO, DCO, DPHN, finance, pharmacy, health records, etc.) — collectively responsible. With Kenya's devolved system since 2013, equivalent bodies are at sub-county level (SCHMT) and County Health Management Team (CHMT).

stem: Triaging may best be defined as the process of:
option_a: Assessing all incoming casualties of a disaster
option_b: Initiating diagnostic measures for casualties of a disaster
option_c: Determining the urgency of need of care for casualties of a disaster
option_d: Setting priorities and assigning urgency ratings for casualties of a disaster
rationale: TRIAGE = the process of SORTING/CATEGORISING casualties based on URGENCY OF NEED FOR CARE, ASSIGNING PRIORITY RATINGS and RESOURCES based on likelihood of benefit — particularly when resources are limited. Option D is more complete than C — triage includes BOTH determining urgency AND assigning priority ratings/category (red/yellow/green/black). Various triage tools: START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) for adults; JumpSTART for paediatrics; SALT (Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment/Transport).

stem: The acid-generating bacterium in our mouth that is the most common cause of tooth decay (dental caries) is the:
rationale: DENTAL CARIES (tooth decay) pathogenesis: bacterial PLAQUE (biofilm) metabolises dietary sugars producing ACIDS that demineralise tooth enamel. The primary cariogenic bacterium is STREPTOCOCCUS MUTANS — converts sucrose to lactic acid (and synthesises insoluble glucans that anchor plaque). Lactobacilli also contribute, particularly in advanced caries. Prevention: oral hygiene (brushing with FLUORIDE toothpaste, flossing); REDUCED FREQUENCY of sugar consumption; FLUORIDE (water fluoridation, varnish); fissure sealants on molars; regular dental check-ups.

stem: The term "role" may be defined as:
option_a: Community's expectation of a trained person
option_b: Legal and moral binding of a professional
option_c: Capacity to run health care activities
option_d: Activities one is expected to perform as a professional
rationale: ROLE (sociology/professional) = the SET OF EXPECTED ACTIVITIES, BEHAVIOURS and RESPONSIBILITIES that a person is expected to perform by virtue of their POSITION (e.g., nurse, doctor, teacher). Includes role expectations from self, colleagues, patients, profession, employer, society. SCOPE OF PRACTICE is the legally-defined role boundary. Role conflict, role strain, role ambiguity are challenges. Option D is the most precise professional definition. Option A is closer to a layperson's view; option B is professional accountability; option C is competence/capability.

stem: Currently in Kenya the problems associated with old age are made worse by the:
option_b: Inability to acquire new marketable skills
option_d: Disintegration of traditional social support systems
rationale: Kenya's elderly population (≥60 years) is growing rapidly. PROBLEMS faced: poverty (no/inadequate pension), declining health (NCDs, sensory loss, mobility), social isolation, neglect, elder abuse, lack of geriatric services. The DISTINCTIVE CONTEMPORARY FACTOR making things worse is the DISINTEGRATION OF TRADITIONAL SOCIAL SUPPORT SYSTEMS — traditionally elders were cared for within extended family/communal structures. Urbanisation, migration, modernisation, smaller families have eroded these systems, leaving many elders without care or support. National Older Persons Cash Transfer (Inua Jamii) and the Older Persons Act 2014 aim to address gaps.

stem: A major cause of "missed opportunity" in the immunisation programme is:
option_b: Use of vaccines that have lost potency
option_c: High drop-out of immunisable target group
rationale: MISSED OPPORTUNITIES in immunisation (per WHO/KEPI): occasions when an eligible child/woman comes into contact with a health service but DOES NOT RECEIVE the vaccines they need. Major causes: HIGH DROP-OUT/incomplete immunisation (started but didn't return for later doses — option C); not screening for vaccination status at every contact; service contraindications/myths; provider not knowing schedule; vaccine stock-outs at the visit (option D also a cause). High dropout (especially between Penta 1 and 3, or measles) is the LEADING cause of incomplete immunisation. Strategies: defaulter tracing, every-contact screening, integrated services.

stem: The process in community diagnosis in which data is separated and categorised in order to help one understand its meaning is known as data:
rationale: Data processing stages: COLLECTION → CLEANING (option C — checking for errors, missing values, inconsistencies) → ANALYSIS (option B — SEPARATING, CATEGORISING, CALCULATING, INTERPRETING data to extract meaning — descriptive statistics, comparisons, trends, hypothesis testing) → PRESENTATION (option D — graphs, tables, narratives for dissemination); HANDLING (option A — broad term, less specific). Analysis is the cognitive step transforming raw data into INFORMATION → understanding.

stem: Vitamins found in the watery parts of the foods we eat:
option_a: Vit K, Niacin, Riboflavin, pantothenic acid
option_b: Pantothenic acid, Thiamine, Pyridoxine, Vit E
option_c: Vit K, Pantothenic acid, Thiamine, Pyridoxine
rationale: Vitamins are classified by solubility: WATER-SOLUBLE — B-complex vitamins (B1 THIAMINE, B2 RIBOFLAVIN, B3 niacin, B5 pantothenic acid, B6 pyridoxine, B7 biotin, B9 FOLATE/folic acid, B12 CYANOCOBALAMINE) and Vitamin C. Found in "watery" parts of food. Not stored extensively (except B12 in liver) — daily intake needed; excess excreted in urine. FAT-SOLUBLE — A, D, E, K — found in fatty parts, stored in liver/adipose, risk of toxicity at high doses. Option D lists 4 water-soluble vitamins (folate, B12, B1, B2). Options A and C contain Vit K (fat-soluble — incorrect). Option B contains Vit E (fat-soluble — incorrect).

stem: Essential amino acids can be defined as amino acids that:
option_a: Cannot be made by the body
option_b: Body can make if nitrogen is available
option_c: Are unique in their primary structure
option_d: Are the basic building blocks of proteins
rationale: Amino acids classified by dietary requirement: ESSENTIAL (indispensable) amino acids — CANNOT BE SYNTHESISED BY THE BODY in sufficient quantities and MUST BE OBTAINED FROM THE DIET. 9 essential AAs: HISTIDINE, ISOLEUCINE, LEUCINE, LYSINE, METHIONINE, PHENYLALANINE, THREONINE, TRYPTOPHAN, VALINE. Conditionally essential — needed extra under stress/disease (e.g. arginine in burns/sepsis; cysteine/tyrosine in liver disease). NON-ESSENTIAL — synthesised from other AAs/nitrogen. Complete protein sources contain all 9 essential AAs (animal proteins, soya); plant proteins often have one limiting AA.

stem: Water-related diseases include:
rationale: WHO classification of water and disease: (1) WATER-BORNE — pathogen in water — cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, dysentery, polio (faecal-oral); (2) WATER-WASHED (water-scarce) — diseases of poor personal hygiene from inadequate water for washing — trachoma, scabies, skin/eye infections; (3) WATER-BASED — pathogen has obligate aquatic host — SCHISTOSOMIASIS (snail intermediate host), guinea worm; (4) WATER-RELATED (vector breeds in/near water) — MALARIA (anopheles in water), DENGUE, ONCHOCERCIASIS (simulium near fast-flowing rivers), filariasis, trypanosomiasis. Option D lists three vector-related/water-based diseases.

stem: When health care is geographically, financially and culturally within easy reach to the entire community the service is said to be:
rationale: The "4 As" framework of health service quality/access: AVAILABILITY — services exist (clinic open, drugs in stock, staff present); ACCESSIBILITY — services are within REACH — GEOGRAPHIC (distance, transport), FINANCIAL (cost-affordability), socio-CULTURAL/SOCIAL acceptability (option C — comprehensive concept); ACCEPTABILITY — services align with cultural beliefs, dignity, language; AFFORDABILITY — services not financially prohibitive. Option C encompasses all dimensions of "easy reach" — geographic, financial, cultural — by definition of accessibility (a broader concept than just affordability or acceptability alone).

stem: The purpose of a screening test is to:
option_b: Detect persons with risk factors of sub-clinical disease
option_c: Check whether a population is at risk of a disease
option_d: Collect the data for a mass campaign
rationale: SCREENING vs DIAGNOSTIC TESTS: SCREENING — applied to ASYMPTOMATIC persons to IDENTIFY THOSE AT HIGHER RISK or with SUB-CLINICAL DISEASE (pre-clinical detectable phase) — does NOT diagnose, only identifies people needing further evaluation. Examples: Pap smear, VIA/VILI, mammography, HIV testing, BP screening. DIAGNOSTIC — applied to SYMPTOMATIC or screen-positive people to CONFIRM diagnosis. Wilson-Jungner criteria for good screening: important condition, accepted treatment, facilities for diagnosis/treatment available, recognisable latent/early phase, suitable test, acceptable to population.

stem: Herd immunity may be said to exist in a community when:
option_a: Both dead and live antigens are used to immunise
option_b: Vaccination is stopped in a community that has been well vaccinated
option_c: The incidence of the disease decreases to a very low level
option_d: A high percentage of people are immune to an infection
rationale: HERD (community) IMMUNITY = the indirect protection of unimmunised individuals when a SUFFICIENTLY HIGH PROPORTION of the population is IMMUNE (via vaccination or natural infection), interrupting transmission chains. Required threshold (the "herd immunity threshold") varies by R0: measles (R0 12-18) requires ~95%; pertussis ~94%; polio ~80%; influenza ~70%. Protects: those who can't be vaccinated (infants, immunocompromised), vaccine failures, those refusing. Disease cases drop sharply, sometimes to elimination. Option D is the definition.

stem: Principles of community health nursing include:
option_a: Prioritising on curative and preventive aspects of health
option_d: Utilising of only health professionals in health care delivery
rationale: COMMUNITY HEALTH NURSING (CHN) PRINCIPLES: emphasis on PREVENTION and HEALTH PROMOTION (not curative-first); HOLISTIC care; FAMILY and COMMUNITY-CENTRED; DECENTRALISATION (services brought close to communities - option C wrong); MULTIDISCIPLINARY teams INCLUDING community health volunteers/workers (NOT only professionals - option D wrong); INTEGRATION of services / minimisation of vertical (single-disease) programmes - favours horizontal integrated approach - option B TRUE; equity, accessibility, intersectoral collaboration, evidence-based practice.

stem: Management roles include:
rationale: MINTZBERG'S 10 MANAGERIAL ROLES grouped into 3 categories: INTERPERSONAL - figurehead, leader, LIAISON; INFORMATIONAL - MONITOR, disseminator, spokesperson; DECISIONAL - entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator (i.e. DECISION-MAKING). Option C includes MONITORING, LIAISON, DECISION-MAKING - fits Mintzberg roles. Options A and D list management FUNCTIONS (Fayol's POLC - planning, organising, leading/directing, controlling), not specifically Mintzberg roles.

stem: The following theorist emphasised on the use of rules, regulations and policies to govern employees:
rationale: MANAGEMENT THEORISTS: FREDERICK TAYLOR - SCIENTIFIC management (time-motion studies, efficiency, piece-rate pay); HENRI FAYOL - 14 principles of management, classical administrative theory (POLC functions); MAX WEBER - BUREAUCRATIC theory: emphasised RULES, REGULATIONS, POLICIES, hierarchy of authority, impersonality, formal procedures, merit-based selection, division of labour - option B; DOUGLAS McGREGOR - Theory X and Y of human behaviour at work; ELTON MAYO - Hawthorne studies, human relations; ABRAHAM MASLOW - hierarchy of needs; HERZBERG - two-factor theory.

stem: Tactical plans in an organisation:
option_b: Are concerned on how to implement operational plans
option_d: Are mainly developed from the major organisation goals
rationale: TACTICAL PLANS are MIDDLE-LEVEL plans of INTERMEDIATE TIME FRAME (1-3 years), bridging strategic and operational. They specify HOW to implement parts of the strategic plan - option B is reversed (tactical guides operational, not vice versa). Develop FROM STRATEGIC plans (which embody major organisational goals - option D describes strategic plans). Daily action plans are OPERATIONAL not tactical (option A). The defining feature of tactical plans is INTERMEDIATE time frame - option C.

stem: The following leadership style has the greatest regard for organisational policies and rules:
rationale: LEADERSHIP STYLES: AUTOCRATIC - leader makes decisions unilaterally, strict control; DEMOCRATIC/participative - involves team in decisions; LAISSEZ-FAIRE - minimal direction, team autonomy; BUREAUCRATIC - leader manages by-the-book, STRICT ADHERENCE TO RULES, REGULATIONS AND POLICIES, formal procedures - option C; transformational - visionary, inspires change; transactional - rewards/sanctions. Bureaucratic style is best in high-risk standardised settings (safety-critical) but can stifle innovation.

stem: Auto-infection is commonly seen in:
rationale: AUTO-INFECTION (self re-infection) is commonly seen in ENTEROBIASIS (pinworm, Enterobius vermicularis): female worm migrates to perianal area at night to lay eggs, scratching transfers eggs to hands, hand-to-mouth ingestion, continuous self-infection cycle. Eggs are immediately infectious. Strongyloides stercoralis also has classic autoinfection (eggs hatch and re-invade host). Trichuriasis, ascariasis, schistosomiasis require an external maturation period before becoming infective.

stem: Examples of cestodes include:
option_a: Hymenolepis nana, Taenia saginata, Diphyllobothrium latum
option_b: Necator americanus, Ankylostoma duodenale, Taenia solium
option_c: Echinococcus granulosus, Brugia malayi, Wuchereria bancrofti
option_d: Ankylostoma duodenale, Loa loa, Onchocerca volvulus
rationale: Classification of helminths: NEMATODES (roundworms) - Ascaris, Trichuris, Enterobius, hookworms (Ancylostoma, Necator), Strongyloides, Loa loa, Wuchereria, Brugia, Onchocerca, Trichinella; CESTODES (tapeworms - flat segmented) - TAENIA (saginata = beef tapeworm; solium = pork tapeworm), HYMENOLEPIS NANA (dwarf tapeworm), DIPHYLLOBOTHRIUM LATUM (fish tapeworm), ECHINOCOCCUS granulosus (hydatid); TREMATODES (flukes) - Schistosoma, Fasciola, Clonorchis, Paragonimus. Option A lists 3 pure cestodes.

stem: Drug of choice for all Schistosomal species is:
rationale: PRAZIQUANTEL is the DRUG OF CHOICE for ALL species of schistosomiasis (S. haematobium, mansoni, japonicum, intercalatum) - single oral dose 40 mg/kg (60 mg/kg for S. japonicum). Used in WHO mass drug administration programmes (preventive chemotherapy). OXAMNIQUINE - older drug effective only against S. mansoni. METRIFONATE - older drug for S. haematobium only. NICLOSAMIDE - for tapeworms (cestodes), not schistosomes. Praziquantel is also effective for tapeworms - broad antihelminthic.

stem: A disease pandemic is one that:
option_a: Few persons acquire over a short period of time
option_b: Is always present in a population
rationale: DISEASE OCCURRENCE TERMINOLOGY: SPORADIC - occurs OCCASIONALLY/scattered (option C); ENDEMIC - habitually PRESENT in a defined area/population at expected levels (option B); HYPER-ENDEMIC - persistently high level; EPIDEMIC/outbreak - occurrence in EXCESS of expected; PANDEMIC - EPIDEMIC SPREAD OVER MULTIPLE COUNTRIES/CONTINENTS/WORLDWIDE affecting LARGE NUMBERS OF PEOPLE (option D). Examples of pandemics: 1918 influenza, HIV/AIDS, COVID-19. WHO declares pandemics.

stem: A nurse finds an oxygen saturation of 78% in a 9-year-old child with asthma; the best action to take would be:
option_b: Do nothing as this is normal
rationale: SpO2 of 78% represents severe, life-threatening hypoxaemia. The immediate priority following the ABC principle is to administer oxygen, then notify the physician. Any delay in oxygenation risks rapid deterioration and cardiac arrest. Ref: Emergency paediatric nursing; Kenya Paediatric Protocols; ABC priority framework.

stem: Symptoms in stage 2 of WHO clinical staging of HIV/AIDS for adults include:
rationale: WHO HIV CLINICAL STAGING for adults: STAGE 1 - asymptomatic, generalised lymphadenopathy. STAGE 2 - moderate unexplained weight loss <10%, recurrent respiratory infections (sinusitis, otitis, pharyngitis), HERPES ZOSTER, angular cheilitis, recurrent oral ulcers, papular pruritic eruption, fungal nail infections, SEBORRHOEIC DERMATITIS - option A. STAGE 3 (advanced) - weight loss >10%, chronic diarrhoea >1 month, persistent fever, oral candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia, PULMONARY TB, severe bacterial infections (pneumonia, pyomyositis), thrombocytopenia <50, neutropenia - these are STAGE 3, not 2. STAGE 4 (AIDS) - wasting, PCP, oesophageal candida, extrapulm TB, Kaposi's, toxoplasmosis.

stem: Angular stomatitis in children is as a result of deficiency in:
rationale: ANGULAR STOMATITIS (cheilitis, perlèche) = cracking, fissuring at the corners of the mouth - classic feature of RIBOFLAVIN (VITAMIN B2) DEFICIENCY (other features: glossitis, magenta tongue, seborrhoeic dermatitis around nose/eyes, photophobia, corneal vascularisation). May also occur with iron deficiency, other B-vitamin deficiencies, Candida albicans infection, denture-related drooling. Treatment: vitamin B2 supplementation, identify and treat secondary cause (iron, candida). Sources of B2: milk, eggs, liver, green vegetables, whole grains.

stem: Gradual social change that occurs with very little or no human effort is referred to as:
rationale: TYPES OF SOCIAL CHANGE: EVOLUTION - GRADUAL, NATURAL, often unintentional change over long periods (e.g. demographic transitions, technological evolution) - option A; REFORM - planned, gradual, deliberate change within existing system (e.g. educational reform, health-sector reform); REVOLUTION - RADICAL, ABRUPT change overthrowing existing order; DIFFUSION - spread of cultural traits, innovations or behaviours from one group/society to another (e.g. spread of mobile phones, dietary trends).

stem: Identify the correct statement below concerning malaria:
option_a: Humans are the definitive host for plasmodium
option_b: Symptoms appear in the hepatic stage
option_c: Malignant type is caused by falciparum species
option_d: Artemether lumefantrine is the 1st line therapy for complicated malaria
rationale: MALARIA LIFE CYCLE: the MOSQUITO (Anopheles) is the DEFINITIVE host (sexual reproduction occurs there); HUMAN is the INTERMEDIATE host (asexual reproduction). Symptoms appear in the ERYTHROCYTIC (blood) stage, NOT hepatic (silent phase). PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM causes MALIGNANT/SEVERE/COMPLICATED malaria - cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, multi-organ failure, ARDS - option C TRUE. ARTEMETHER-LUMEFANTRINE (AL) is 1st line for UNCOMPLICATED falciparum malaria; IV ARTESUNATE is 1st line for SEVERE/COMPLICATED malaria - option D wrong.

stem: The indications for surgery in trachoma include:
rationale: TRACHOMA (chronic conjunctivitis from Chlamydia trachomatis) progression and WHO SAFE strategy: S - SURGERY for late-stage scarring complications: TRICHIASIS (inwardly turned lashes scratching cornea) and ENTROPION (inwardly turned eyelid margin) - both threaten vision and need surgical correction (bilamellar tarsal rotation); A - ANTIBIOTICS (azithromycin mass treatment); F - FACIAL cleanliness; E - ENVIRONMENTAL improvement (clean water, sanitation, fly control). Pannus and follicles are EARLIER active stages, treated with antibiotics not surgery.

stem: The elements of Primary Health Care are:
option_a: Maternal child health, nutrition, appropriate technology
option_c: Malaria control, essential drugs supply, equitable distribution of resources
option_d: Mental health, integration of services, local disease control
rationale: ALMA ATA 8 ELEMENTS of PHC: Education on health problems; Locally endemic disease control; Expanded programme on IMMUNISATION; Maternal and child health (MCH/FP); Essential drugs supply; Nutrition; Treatment of common illnesses; Sanitation and safe water supply. Kenya added 3 more: Mental health, Dental health, HIV/AIDS - plus community-based rehabilitation. Option B lists immunisation, education, community rehabilitation - three accepted elements. APPROPRIATE TECHNOLOGY and EQUITABLE DISTRIBUTION (in options A and C) are PRINCIPLES, not elements.

stem: The number of deaths from typhoid divided by the total deaths in a year multiplied by 100 is an example of:
rationale: MORTALITY RATIOS/RATES: PROPORTIONAL MORTALITY RATIO = deaths from a specific cause / TOTAL DEATHS x 100 - shows what proportion of all deaths are due to that cause (option C - cause-specific proportion); CASE FATALITY RATE = deaths from a disease / cases of that disease x 100 - measures lethality of a disease; CRUDE DEATH RATE/MORTALITY RATE = total deaths / total population x 1000; CAUSE-SPECIFIC DEATH RATE = deaths from a cause / total population x 100,000 (population-based). The question matches the proportional mortality definition - best fitting option C.

stem: In occupational health, deployment of epileptics away from areas where they can easily injure themselves is an example of:
rationale: Applying LEVELS OF PREVENTION to occupational health: PRIMARY = preventing injury/disease BEFORE it occurs - pre-placement matching, engineering controls, PPE, training, ENVIRONMENTAL/job modification (e.g. KEEPING EPILEPTICS AWAY FROM heights, machinery, water where they could injure themselves during a seizure) - option A. SECONDARY = early detection (medical exams, screening). TERTIARY = rehabilitation after disease/injury. Pre-placement screening and job allocation to avoid risk = PRIMARY prevention.

stem: An employee of a milk processing industry sustained a frost bite while putting milk in a deep freezer. This is an example of:
rationale: OCCUPATIONAL HAZARDS classification: PHYSICAL - TEMPERATURE EXTREMES (heat/COLD - including frost bite), noise, vibration, radiation, illumination; CHEMICAL - solvents, dusts, fumes, gases; BIOLOGICAL - bacteria, viruses, fungi (e.g. healthcare-associated infections); MECHANICAL - slips/falls, machinery injuries; ERGONOMIC - repetitive strain, posture; PSYCHOSOCIAL - stress, harassment. Frost bite from sub-zero temperatures is a PHYSICAL hazard - option B.

stem: The infective stage of Taenia species is:
rationale: TAENIA SAGINATA (beef tapeworm) and TAENIA SOLIUM (pork tapeworm) life cycle: HUMAN ingests undercooked meat containing CYSTICERCI (larval stage encysted in muscle), cysticerci attach to small intestine and mature into adult tapeworms, release proglottids/eggs in faeces, eggs ingested by intermediate host (cow for saginata, pig for solium), ONCOSPHERE/HEXACANTH embryo released, invades muscle, encysts as CYSTICERCI. So for HUMANS the INFECTIVE STAGE = CYSTICERCI in meat. Note: T. solium EGGS can also infect humans if ingested causing cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis.

stem: Anthropometry is the science of measuring:
option_a: Size and make-up of the body and specific body parts
option_b: Nutritional factors needed for growth and development
option_c: Patients' habitual intake of food and liquids
option_d: Physical signs and symptoms of inadequate nutrition
rationale: ANTHROPOMETRY (anthropos = man, metron = measure) = science of measuring the SIZE AND PROPORTIONS of the human body - weight, height/length, MUAC, head circumference, skinfold thickness, BMI. Used for nutritional assessment, growth monitoring, screening for malnutrition (Z-scores against WHO/CDC growth standards). Distinct from: BIOCHEMICAL assessment (lab tests), CLINICAL assessment (signs/symptoms - option D), DIETARY assessment (food intake - option C - 24-hour recall, food frequency).

stem: A community may be defined as:
option_a: Individuals and groups living and interacting within certain boundaries
option_b: Groups of people sharing common health problems
rationale: COMMUNITY definitions in community health: a GROUP OF INDIVIDUALS AND/OR GROUPS LIVING IN A DEFINED GEOGRAPHICAL AREA who INTERACT and have shared interests, characteristics, values, or institutions. Key elements: people + location/boundaries + INTERACTION + sense of belonging. Communities can be: GEOGRAPHIC (village, neighbourhood), FUNCTIONAL (school, workplace), CULTURAL (ethnic, religious), VIRTUAL (online). Option A captures the people + boundaries + interaction triad most completely.

stem: Cold chain is defined as a system of:
option_a: Immunising children and expectant mothers with a potent vaccine in the facility
option_b: Maintaining vaccines in a potent state from the manufacturer to the consumer
option_c: Maintaining the vaccine in a potent state in a health facility
option_d: Transporting vaccines from the manufacturer to the consumer
rationale: COLD CHAIN = the SYSTEM (people, equipment, procedures) for MAINTAINING VACCINES at the RECOMMENDED TEMPERATURE (+2 to +8 degrees C, or frozen for some) FROM MANUFACTURER to AIRPORT to CENTRAL STORE to REGIONAL/COUNTY to SUB-COUNTY to FACILITY to CHILD (point of use). All links must be maintained. Tools: refrigerators with thermometers, cold boxes, vaccine carriers, ice packs, VVMs (vaccine vial monitors), temperature charts, freeze indicators. Break in cold chain leads to loss of vaccine potency and vaccination failures.

stem: The following plasmodia develop hypnozoites:
rationale: PLASMODIUM species: P. FALCIPARUM (commonest in Kenya, causes severe malaria, no hypnozoites); P. VIVAX (HYPNOZOITES = dormant liver forms causing relapses weeks-months-years later); P. OVALE (also HYPNOZOITES - relapses); P. MALARIAE (causes quartan fever, may recrudesce from low-level erythrocytic infection but NO hypnozoites); P. KNOWLESI (zoonotic). HYPNOZOITES require PRIMAQUINE (or tafenoquine) for radical cure to prevent relapses - testing for G6PD deficiency first because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients.

stem: Post-visit activities in home visiting:
option_d: Are done during every home visit
rationale: HOME VISITING PHASES and POST-VISIT activities: pre-visit (preparation), in-home (entry, implementation), termination (in-home - concluding the visit with client/family), POST-VISIT (back at the office) - includes DOCUMENTING the visit in client records, SHARING REPORTS/feedback with team and supervisor, PLANNING the NEXT visit, supplies replenishment, supervision/debrief. Evaluating the client (option C) happens DURING the in-home phase. Option B sharing reports - captures the key post-visit activity.

stem: Equity in primary health care means:
option_a: Every area should get same quantity of services
option_b: Health resources and services should be distributed to everyone fairly
option_c: All sectors should be involved in health care delivery
option_d: The community should participate in their health
rationale: EQUITY (fairness) in health: distributing resources and services FAIRLY ACCORDING TO NEED - providing MORE to those with greater need and less to those with lesser need, to achieve equal HEALTH OUTCOMES. Distinct from EQUALITY (same amount to all regardless of need - option A - but this is not equity). Intersectoral collaboration (option C) is another PHC principle. Community participation (option D) is another PHC principle. Equity is about JUST distribution according to need - option B.

stem: Diseases transmitted through the faecal-oral route include:
option_b: Poliomyelitis, bacillary dysentery, viral hepatitis A
rationale: FAECAL-ORAL transmitted diseases: VIRAL - POLIOMYELITIS, ROTAVIRUS, HEPATITIS A, HEPATITIS E, enteroviruses; BACTERIAL - CHOLERA, TYPHOID, BACILLARY DYSENTERY (shigella), E. coli, salmonella; PROTOZOAL - AMOEBIASIS, giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis; HELMINTHS - ascariasis, trichuriasis, enterobiasis, hookworm. MUMPS is DROPLET/airborne (option A wrong). SCHISTOSOMIASIS is via CERCARIAE in water through skin (option D wrong). Option B - poliomyelitis + bacillary dysentery + viral hepatitis A - all faecal-oral.

stem: Enteric fevers are usually common at:
option_a: Start of the rains and middle of dry season
option_c: Middle of the dry season till the end
option_d: End of the dry season and at the start of the rains
rationale: ENTERIC FEVERS (typhoid, paratyphoid) - Salmonella typhi/paratyphi A,B,C - transmitted via contaminated food/water. Epidemiologically common at the END OF THE DRY SEASON (when water becomes scarce and contaminated) AND THE START OF THE RAINS (when surface contamination is washed into water sources, but sanitation systems are overwhelmed) - option D. Hence outbreaks often follow these seasonal transitions. Prevention: safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene, food safety, vaccination (Vi polysaccharide or Ty21a oral).

stem: The migratory phase of Ascaris is associated with:
rationale: ASCARIS LUMBRICOIDES life cycle: ingested eggs hatch in small intestine, larvae penetrate intestinal wall, MIGRATE via portal vein to LIVER, HEART, LUNGS (during which they cause PNEUMONITIS - LOFFLER'S SYNDROME with cough, wheeze, eosinophilia, transient lung infiltrates), ascend trachea, swallowed, mature into adult worms in small intestine (causing abdominal discomfort, malnutrition, intestinal obstruction). Option A captures pneumonitis + cough + vague abdominal discomfort of migratory phase. Treatment: albendazole or mebendazole.

stem: The epidemiological triad includes:
rationale: EPIDEMIOLOGICAL TRIAD (also called epidemiologic triangle of disease causation): the THREE INTERACTING COMPONENTS necessary for disease: (1) AGENT (the cause - biological, chemical, physical, nutritional, social); (2) HOST (the susceptible individual - age, sex, genetics, immunity, behaviour); (3) ENVIRONMENT (the surroundings - physical, biological, socioeconomic, climate). Disease arises from the interaction. Public health interventions can target any vertex. Vectors and routes of transmission are sub-components of the agent-host-environment interaction.

stem: Active immunity:
option_a: Is acquired after several doses of a vaccine
option_b: Is acquired after vaccination with a live vaccine
option_c: Is only acquired when organisms invade the body
rationale: ACTIVE IMMUNITY = host's own immune system produces antibodies/memory cells in response to antigen - NATURAL (after recovery from infection) or ARTIFICIAL (after vaccination, live or killed); develops over WEEKS but is LONG-LASTING, often LIFELONG (option D - generally true for many vaccines/infections; some require boosters). PASSIVE IMMUNITY = pre-formed antibodies transferred (transplacental, breast milk, immunoglobulin injection) - immediate but SHORT-LIVED (weeks-months). Active immunity from a SINGLE dose can suffice (live vaccines often single dose - option A/B not always true) and is NOT limited to live vaccines or natural infection (options B/C too narrow).

stem: The diseases caused by flukes/worms include:
rationale: FLUKES/WORMS (HELMINTHS): SCHISTOSOMIASIS (TREMATODE/fluke); ONCHOCERCIASIS (NEMATODE filaria); DRACUNCULIASIS (NEMATODE, guinea worm); ascariasis, hookworm, filariasis (lymphatic - Wuchereria/Brugia), Loa loa, etc. PROTOZOAL diseases (NOT worms): LEISHMANIASIS (Leishmania); TRYPANOSOMIASIS (Trypanosoma); malaria; amoebiasis; giardiasis. Option C - schistosomiasis + onchocerciasis + dracunculiasis - all worms. Options A and B include protozoal diseases (leishmaniasis, trypanosomiasis).

stem: Zoonotic diseases include:
rationale: ZOONOTIC diseases = transmitted from VERTEBRATE ANIMALS to humans: BRUCELLOSIS (cattle, goats, sheep - unpasteurised milk, contact); ANTHRAX (cattle, sheep, goats); RABIES (dogs, bats, wildlife); plague (rodents/fleas); leptospirosis (rats); Q fever; viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola/Marburg - bats; Lassa - rodents); avian flu (birds); SARS-CoV/CoV-2 (bats/civet/pangolin); zoonotic TB (cattle - M. bovis); echinococcosis; toxoplasmosis. Option B lists three classic bacterial zoonoses. AMOEBIASIS (option A) is human-to-human faecal-oral, not strictly zoonotic. TETANUS is environmental, not zoonotic.

stem: In occupational health, secondary prevention services include:
option_a: Training of the workforce on how to work with machines
option_b: Screening employees at risk of a particular hazard
option_c: Provision of crutches for the injured workers
option_d: Utilisation of protective clothing in industries
rationale: OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH PREVENTION levels: PRIMARY = preventing disease/injury BEFORE it occurs - training workforce (option A), PPE (option D), engineering controls, job redesign, pre-placement assessment, immunisation. SECONDARY = EARLY DETECTION and prompt treatment of disease in pre-symptomatic stage - PERIODIC HEALTH SCREENING, biological monitoring, AUDIOMETRY for noise-exposed workers, SPIROMETRY for dust-exposed, PERIODIC examinations (option B). TERTIARY = limiting disability after disease - REHABILITATION, crutches for injured (option C), return-to-work programmes, compensation.

stem: The anti-tuberculosis drug that is known to damage vision is:
rationale: FIRST-LINE TB drugs and major adverse effects: ISONIAZID (H) - hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine); RIFAMPICIN (R) - hepatotoxicity, ORANGE secretions, drug interactions (enzyme inducer); PYRAZINAMIDE (Z) - hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia/gout; ETHAMBUTOL (E) - RETROBULBAR OPTIC NEURITIS leading to DECREASED VISUAL ACUITY, RED-GREEN COLOUR BLINDNESS, central scotoma - option D. Hence patients on ethambutol need baseline and periodic VISUAL ACUITY and colour vision testing; should report any vision changes immediately - usually reversible if stopped early. STREPTOMYCIN - ototoxicity (8th nerve damage, deafness), nephrotoxicity, NOT visual.

stem: Signs and symptoms of rabies include:
option_a: History of a dog bite, dribbling of saliva, difficulty in swallowing
option_b: Itching at the site of the wound, fever, irritation and skin rash
option_c: Difficulty in swallowing, history of dog bite, slow pulse
option_d: Severe pain at site of the wound, difficulty in swallowing, saliva dribbling
rationale: RABIES clinical features after dog (or other mammal) bite, after incubation of weeks-months-years: PRODROMAL - fever, malaise, paraesthesia at bite site; EXCITATIVE/FURIOUS (commonest) - HYDROPHOBIA (fear of water - spasm of pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles when trying to drink leading to DIFFICULTY SWALLOWING and DRIBBLING OF SALIVA - option A), aerophobia, hyperactivity, hallucinations, seizures, autonomic dysfunction; PARALYTIC (dumb) - ascending paralysis, less common; COMA then DEATH (100% fatal once symptoms appear). PREVENTION: pre-exposure prophylaxis (high-risk groups); POST-EXPOSURE - IMMEDIATE wound washing with soap and water for 15 minutes + rabies immunoglobulin into wound + 4-dose vaccine schedule. Option A captures three classic features.

stem: According to KEPI schedule of immunisation, the correct dose for vitamin A at six months is:
rationale: KENYA MoH VITAMIN A SUPPLEMENTATION schedule (per Kenya Demographic Health Surveys and KEPI): 6-11 MONTHS - 100,000 IU (oral) every 6 months (option B); 12-59 MONTHS - 200,000 IU every 6 months; POSTPARTUM mothers within 8 weeks of delivery - 200,000 IU single dose. Vitamin A reduces child mortality (especially from measles and diarrhoeal disease), prevents xerophthalmia/night blindness. Question option B 100,000 IU is correct for 6-month dose.

stem: According to the Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunisation (KEPI), the pentavalent vaccine given at 6, 10, and 14 weeks protects against:
option_a: Diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b
option_b: Diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, and measles
option_c: Tetanus, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae, meningococcus, and pneumococcus
option_d: Diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, rotavirus, and hepatitis B
rationale: The PENTAVALENT VACCINE (DTP-HepB-Hib) protects against FIVE diseases: DIPHTHERIA, TETANUS, PERTUSSIS (whooping cough), HEPATITIS B, and HAEMOPHILUS INFLUENZAE TYPE B (Hib — causes meningitis and pneumonia). Given at 6, 10, and 14 weeks in Kenya. The KEPI schedule also includes: BCG and OPV0 at birth; OPV1-3 and PCV1-3 at 6, 10, 14 weeks; IPV at 14 weeks; Rotavirus vaccine at 6 and 10 weeks; Measles-Rubella at 9 months and 18 months; Yellow fever at 9 months (in endemic areas).

stem: The most effective method of water purification at household level in a resource-limited setting is:
option_d: Allowing water to settle for 24 hours
rationale: BOILING is the most reliable household water treatment method — kills ALL pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa including Cryptosporidium and Giardia cysts) when water is brought to a ROLLING BOIL for at least 1 minute (3 minutes at altitudes >2,000 m). Other household water treatment options: chlorination (sodium hypochlorite — effective against bacteria and viruses but not Cryptosporidium), solar disinfection (SODIS — 6 hours in clear PET bottles in sunlight), ceramic filtration. Cloth filtration removes only large particles. Settling removes suspended solids but not pathogens.

stem: The DOTS strategy for tuberculosis control stands for:
rationale: DOTS = DIRECTLY OBSERVED THERAPY SHORT-COURSE. The five components of the WHO DOTS strategy: (1) Government commitment to TB control; (2) Case detection by quality sputum smear microscopy; (3) Standardised short-course chemotherapy (6 months) under DIRECT OBSERVATION — a health worker or trained community member watches the patient swallow each dose; (4) Regular uninterrupted supply of quality anti-TB drugs; (5) Recording and reporting system for programme monitoring. Direct observation prevents treatment interruption and reduces drug resistance. Kenya uses the NTLD (National TB and Lung Disease) programme.

stem: A child with bilateral pitting oedema, moon face, and sparse, discoloured hair is most likely suffering from:
rationale: KWASHIORKOR is severe acute malnutrition (SAM) caused primarily by PROTEIN DEFICIENCY (with relatively adequate caloric intake). Classic features: BILATERAL PITTING OEDEMA (from hypoalbuminaemia — reduced oncotic pressure), MOON FACE (facial oedema), SKIN CHANGES (flaky paint dermatosis, hyperpigmentation), HAIR CHANGES (sparse, straight, discoloured — flag sign), HEPATOMEGALY (fatty liver), misery/apathy. MARASMUS is severe caloric deficiency — wasted, "skin and bones," no oedema. MARASMIC-KWASHIORKOR has features of both. Treatment: F-75 then F-100 therapeutic feeds, RUTF (Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food).

stem: A patient with a panic attack presents with palpitations, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and fear of dying. The nurse's priority intervention is:
option_b: Stay with the patient, speak calmly, and guide slow deep breathing
option_c: Leave the patient alone in a quiet room to calm down
option_d: Administer oxygen at 10 L/min via non-rebreather mask
rationale: Panic attacks are intense episodes of fear with physical symptoms (palpitations, dyspnoea, chest pain, dizziness, paraesthesia, depersonalisation) that peak within 10 minutes. Priority nursing interventions: STAY WITH THE PATIENT (presence reduces fear), SPEAK CALMLY and reassuringly, GUIDE CONTROLLED BREATHING (slow diaphragmatic breathing — 4 seconds in, hold 2, 6 seconds out — reduces hyperventilation and CO2 washout that worsens symptoms). Reassure the patient they are not dying. Benzodiazepines are used for severe/refractory cases, not as first-line. Leaving the patient alone worsens anxiety.

stem: A patient with major depressive disorder is started on fluoxetine (an SSRI). The nurse should counsel the patient that:
option_a: The full antidepressant effect is felt within 24–48 hours
option_b: The medication should be stopped immediately if side effects occur
option_c: It may take 2–4 weeks before the full therapeutic effect is noticed
option_d: The medication can be taken only when feeling depressed
rationale: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram) are first-line antidepressants. Key patient education: (1) DELAYED ONSET — therapeutic effect takes 2–4 WEEKS (sometimes up to 6–8 weeks for full effect) — patients must be counselled not to stop early thinking it is not working; (2) SUICIDE RISK — monitor closely in the first 2 weeks, especially in adolescents (SSRIs can initially increase energy before mood lifts, potentially enabling suicidal plans); (3) SIDE EFFECTS — nausea, insomnia, sexual dysfunction (usually transient); (4) DO NOT STOP ABRUPTLY — taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome; (5) Take daily, not PRN.

stem: A patient in alcohol withdrawal develops tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and seizures 24 hours after stopping alcohol. The nurse should:
option_a: Administer haloperidol to control the seizures
option_b: Administer a benzodiazepine (e.g., diazepam) as prescribed and monitor vital signs
option_c: Restrain the patient and wait for the seizures to stop
option_d: Administer naloxone to reverse the alcohol effects
rationale: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME (AWS) occurs 6–72 hours after cessation in dependent drinkers. Severity: mild (tremor, anxiety, diaphoresis, tachycardia) → moderate (hallucinations) → severe (DELIRIUM TREMENS — confusion, agitation, hyperthermia, seizures — mortality 5–15% if untreated). Treatment: BENZODIAZEPINES (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are the gold standard — they cross-react with GABA-A receptors (same as alcohol), preventing and treating seizures and delirium. Thiamine 100 mg IV/IM BEFORE glucose (prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy). Naloxone reverses opioids, not alcohol.

stem: The most hygienic method of human waste disposal in a rural community without piped water is:
option_a: Open defecation in a designated field
option_c: Use of a properly constructed pit latrine
option_d: Burying waste in shallow pits near the homestead
rationale: A PROPERLY CONSTRUCTED PIT LATRINE is the recommended sanitation solution for rural areas without sewerage. Requirements: pit depth ≥3 metres (below groundwater table), slab with a hole (prevents flies and odour), superstructure for privacy, hand-washing facility nearby. Prevents faecal-oral disease transmission (cholera, typhoid, dysentery, polio, hepatitis A, intestinal worms). Open defecation contaminates soil and water sources.
